t: 58 BC: the Helvetii and Ariovistus
intro:
In early 58 BC Caesar, consul of the previous year, received the governorship of Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum for five years, and by a decision of the Senate Transalpine Gaul as well. That year he fought two wars, both described in the first book of the Gallic War: first he stopped the migrating Helvetii, then he turned against the Suebian king Ariovistus, who had crossed the Rhine.

The Helvetii – according to Caesar on the plan of one of their nobles, Orgetorix – decided to leave what is now Switzerland and settle in the west, in the land of the Santones. Two routes lay before them: the narrow pass between the Jura and the Rhodanus through the Sequani, or through the Roman province. Caesar closed the latter, then followed and defeated them as they passed through the land of the Sequani. Afterwards, at the request of Gallic nobles, he marched against the Germans who had come from beyond the Rhine.

The walk follows the places named in Caesar’s text. Dates are Julian, after the 2017 chronology of John T. Ramsey and Kurt A. Raaflaub; the Roman calendar was then a few days ahead. There were no Roman roads in Gaul yet: the line follows the later Roman road network (Itiner-e), which often reused older routes, but Caesar’s actual route is not known. Several sites (the crossing of the Arar, the battle with the Helvetii and the battle with Ariovistus) are uncertain; for these the text says what the marker is based on. The figures come from Caesar’s own account, written to justify his wars to the Roman public; scholars generally regard the large numbers as exaggerated. For two marching legs the legion calculator can compare the time given in the source with the estimated marching time.

s.d: 12 March 58 BC (15 March in the Roman calendar)
s.t:
Caesar spent the first months of the year just outside Rome: he could not cross the sacred boundary of the city without losing his military command (imperium). From there he watched Cicero go into exile under the law of Clodius. Then came the news that the Helvetii wanted to march through the province.

According to Caesar he set out for Further Gaul “by the longest marches he could” and hurried to Genava (Gallic War 1.7). Plutarch writes that he reached the Rhodanus on the eighth day (Caesar 17); Ramsey and Raaflaub refer this rather to Arelate (Arles), since Genava could not have been reached in that time. Only one legion was stationed in the province, so Caesar at once ordered new levies.

Genava, the frontier town of the Allobroges, lay where the Rhodanus leaves Lake Lemannus (Lake Geneva), and a bridge linked it to the land of the Helvetii. Caesar had the bridge broken down. The Helvetii had fixed 28 March (Roman calendar) for gathering on the bank of the Rhodanus (1.6), and sent two envoys, Nammeius and Verucloetius, to ask leave to pass.

Caesar remembered that in 107 BC the Helvetii had killed the consul Lucius Cassius and sent his army under the yoke, so he did not want to give way; to gain time he answered that he would consider it and that they should return on the Ides of April (1.7). Meanwhile he had a rampart sixteen feet high and a ditch built for nineteen miles from the lake to the Jura, with guard posts and forts (1.8). When the envoys returned, he refused the passage. The Helvetii tried to cross on rafts and boats lashed together and through fords, by day and more often by night, but the rampart and the soldiers drove them back. Then, with the consent of the Sequani, they set out westward through the pass of the Jura (1.9).

He entrusted the rampart to Titus Labienus and hurried by forced marches to Italy. There he enrolled two new legions and led out from winter quarters the three legions that had wintered around Aquileia (1.10). Aquileia lay on the north-eastern edge of Cisalpine Gaul, where the roads towards Illyricum began.

At this time Caesar learned that the Helvetii intended to march through the lands of the Sequani and the Aedui to the Santones, whose territory lay not far from the Tolosates, who belonged to the province. He judged that a warlike people hostile to Rome would be a great danger next to the open, grain-rich country of the province. In the chronology of Ramsey and Raaflaub the Aquileia legions set out westward on 11 May by the Roman calendar and reached Ocelum on 21 May.

s.d: late May – early June 58 BC (from 21 May in the Roman calendar)
s.t:
Ocelum was, in Caesar’s words, “the farthest town of the Hither Province”, at the mouth of the valley of the Durias (Susa valley); the marker follows the location given by Pleiades. From here he crossed the Alps with five legions by the shortest route, probably over the Mont Genèvre pass. The mountain peoples – the Ceutrones, the Graioceli and the Caturiges – tried to stop him by seizing the heights; Caesar routed them in several engagements and on the seventh day from Ocelum reached the land of the Vocontii in the Further Province (1.10).

Ramsey and Raaflaub put this at about 195 km, roughly 28 km a day. From there he led his army through the land of the Allobroges across the Rhodanus into the territory of the Segusiavi, the first people outside the province. By early June he thus had six legions: the five brought from Italy and the legion of the province.

The Aedui, the Ambarri and the Allobroges sent envoys: the Helvetii were laying waste their lands. The Helvetii were then crossing the Arar (Saône), which according to Caesar flows “with incredible slowness”, so that the eye cannot tell in which direction (1.12). Caesar does not name the place of the crossing; the marker points to the stretch of the river near Cabillonum (Chalon-sur-Saône) and shows only where the river is.

When scouts reported that three quarters of the Helvetii had crossed, Caesar marched out at night with three legions and cut to pieces the part still on the near bank, the canton of the Tigurini. He adds that in this he avenged a personal wrong as well: the Tigurini had killed Lucius Piso, the grandfather of his father-in-law, in 107 BC. He then had a bridge built across the river in a single day, a crossing that had taken the Helvetii twenty days (1.13). Alarmed, the Helvetii sent an embassy led by Divico, who had fought against Cassius. The talks came to nothing.

s.h: Bibracte: the battle with the Helvetii
s.t:
For fifteen days Caesar followed the Helvetii so closely that no more than five or six miles lay between their rearguard and his vanguard (1.15). His four thousand horsemen were routed by five hundred Helvetian horse. Supplies faltered because the Aedui delayed the grain; according to Caesar the Aeduan Dumnorix secretly helped the Helvetii, but at the request of his brother Diviciacus he forgave him (1.16–20).

Since grain had to be issued in two days and Bibracte, by far the largest and richest town of the Aedui, was only eighteen miles away, Caesar turned away from the Helvetii (1.23). Bibracte lay on top of Mont Beuvray; archaeologists have excavated the oppidum. The Helvetii turned back and attacked his rearguard. Caesar sent away the horses, his own first, so that all would share the same danger and no one could think of flight (1.25). The fighting lasted from the seventh hour until evening, and at the wagon laager late into the night (1.26). The exact site of the battle is disputed; the marker shows Bibracte.

According to Caesar about 130,000 people survived; they marched all night and on the fourth day reached the land of the Lingones. Because of the wounded and the dead Caesar did not follow them for three days.

img.c: The reconstructed gate of the oppidum of Bibracte (Mont Beuvray), the Porte du Rebout.

s.t:
Caesar sent a letter to the Lingones not to help the fugitives with grain, or he would treat them as enemies too. When he set out after them, envoys of the Helvetii met him and surrendered: they had to give up hostages, arms and the slaves who had deserted to them (1.26–27). We do not know exactly where in the land of the Lingones this happened; the marker shows the later capital of the Lingones, Andematunnum (Langres).

A group of about six thousand, the Verbigeni, fled at night towards the Rhine; Caesar had them brought back and – he writes – treated them as enemies. He sent the rest back to their homes so that the Germans would not take over their land, and ordered the Allobroges to supply them with grain. At the request of the Aedui the Boii were settled on Aeduan land (1.28).

In the Helvetian camp lists written in Greek letters were found: according to them 368,000 had set out, among them 92,000 able to bear arms; when those returning home were counted, there were 110,000 (1.29). Scholars mostly regard the figures as exaggerated.

At an assembly of Gallic nobles Diviciacus complained that the Sequani and the Arverni had once called in Germans against the Aedui; since then the German king Ariovistus had seized a third of the land of the Sequani, and some 120,000 Germans now lived in Gaul (1.31). Caesar sent envoys to Ariovistus, who coolly refused to come to him (1.34–36).

When Caesar heard that Ariovistus was heading for Vesontio, the largest town of the Sequani, he forestalled him by marching night and day (1.38). The Dubis (Doubs) almost encircles the town, and a high hill, ringed by a wall, closes the open side; the citadel of Besançon stands there today. A panic lasting several days broke out in the camp: traders and Gauls talked of the huge stature and terrible look of the Germans; according to Caesar soldiers sealed their wills and officers asked for leave (1.39). Caesar called a council and declared that if no one else came, he would set out with the tenth legion alone; Caesar says he had especially favoured this legion and trusted it most (1.40).

calc.src: According to Ramsey and Raaflaub Caesar left Bibracte about 16 August and reached Vesontio on 20 August: 4 days, the last stretch marching night and day (1.38).

s.n: Defeat of Ariovistus (assumed site: near Belfort)
s.t:
Caesar left Vesontio on 24 August. To avoid wooded country he followed Diviciacus’ reconnaissance on a detour of more than fifty miles through open land, and on the seventh day was told that Ariovistus was twenty-four miles away (1.41). Caesar does not name the site of the battle; according to Ramsey and Raaflaub the area of modern Belfort is most likely, and the marker shows it.

They parleyed on a mound rising from a large plain, each side with ten horsemen. Instead of Gallic cavalry Caesar mounted soldiers of the tenth legion; one of them joked that Caesar had done more than he promised: he had raised the tenth legion to the rank of knights (1.42). The parley broke off when German horsemen attacked with stones and missiles. Ariovistus marched past Caesar’s camp and cut his grain supply; six thousand horse and as many foot fought the skirmishes (1.48). From prisoners Caesar learned why the Germans would not give battle: the German matrons had prophesied that they could not win if they fought before the new moon (1.50).

Caesar then marched on the German camp and forced a battle. When the left wing wavered, the young commander of the cavalry, Publius Crassus, sent in the third line (1.52). The Germans fled to the Rhine, which according to the manuscripts was five or fifty miles away. Ariovistus escaped in a small boat; his two wives and one of his daughters perished. His envoy Gaius Valerius Procillus, whom the Germans had bound in triple chains, was found by Caesar himself as he pursued the fugitives; Caesar says this gave him as much pleasure as the victory (1.53). He put the army into winter quarters among the Sequani under Labienus and went to Cisalpine Gaul to hold the assizes (1.54).

calc.src: According to Caesar, on the seventh day (30 August) he was twenty-four miles from Ariovistus, after a detour of more than fifty miles (1.41). The calculator uses the Roman roads, without the detour, to the assumed battle site.

t: 57 BC: the Belgae
intro:
The second book of the Gallic War is a single campaign: Caesar marched against the Belgae, who lived in the northern third of Gaul between the Sequana (Seine), the Matrona (Marne) and the Rhine. According to Caesar the Belgae feared that the Roman army would subdue them too, and resented its wintering in Gaul; so they formed an alliance and exchanged hostages (2.1).

The campaign began with the Remi, who submitted of their own accord, and went on from their land: at the Axona (Aisne) the united army of the Belgae broke up, and Caesar, moving from tribe to tribe, received the surrender of the Suessiones, the Bellovaci and the Ambiani. He fought his hardest battle on the bank of the Sabis (Sambre) against the Nervii, and finally took the stronghold of the Atuatuci. At the end of the year one of his legates, Servius Galba, fought in the Alps.

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017); by this year the Roman calendar was more than two weeks ahead. The exact sites of several battles are disputed; the text says what the marker is based on. The line follows the later Roman road network.

s.t:
The army had wintered among the Sequani under Labienus. In Cisalpine Gaul Caesar learned of the Belgic alliance from Labienus’ letters. He raised two new legions and in spring sent them to Gaul with Quintus Pedius; as soon as there was fodder he himself joined the army (2.2). According to Ramsey and Raaflaub the winter quarters were probably around Vesontio.

Caesar asked the Senones and other Gauls bordering on the Belgae to find out what was happening among them. They all reported that the Belgae were raising troops and that an army was gathering in one place. He now had eight legions. He provided for grain and set out; in about fifteen days he reached the border of the Belgae (2.2).

Surprised by his sudden arrival, the Remi, the Belgae nearest to Gaul, sent two of their leading men, Iccius and Antebrogius: they put themselves and all they had under the protection of the Roman people, had not joined the others, and would give hostages and supply grain (2.3). Their capital later became Durocortorum (Reims), which the marker shows.

From the Remi Caesar learned what forces he faced. The Bellovaci could field a hundred thousand armed men and had promised sixty thousand; the Suessiones and the Nervii fifty thousand each, the Morini twenty-five thousand, the Atrebates fifteen thousand, the Atuatuci nineteen thousand, and the peoples called Germans about forty thousand (2.4). The Belgae claimed to be the only ones who had once kept even the Teutones and Cimbri out of their lands. The supreme command went to Galba, king of the Suessiones.

calc.src: According to Caesar the march to the border of the Belgae took “about fifteen days” (2.2). Ramsey and Raaflaub put the distance to the Matrona at about 235 km, which on pre-Roman roads may have been about a quarter longer; the calculator uses the later Roman roads to Reims.

s.t:
Caesar hurriedly crossed the Axona (Aisne), which flows on the edge of the land of the Remi, and camped on the far bank. Quintus Titurius Sabinus guarded the bridge with six cohorts; the camp was protected by a rampart twelve feet high and a ditch eighteen feet wide (2.5). Ramsey and Raaflaub place the camp near Berry-au-Bac, where excavations were also made under Napoleon III.

Eight miles away the Belgae attacked a town of the Remi called Bibrax; its commander, Iccius, sent word that he could hold out no longer. Caesar sent Numidian and Cretan archers and Balearic slingers, whereupon the Belgae gave up the siege and camped less than two miles from Caesar’s camp; judging by the fires, their camp stretched over more than eight miles (2.6–7). Caesar dug trenches on both sides of the hill so that he could not be outflanked. Between the two armies lay a marsh, and neither side wanted to be first to cross it.

The Belgae then tried to cross the Axona to take Sabinus’ fort; Caesar cut them down in the river with his cavalry and light infantry. Their plans having failed and their food running short, they decided to go home and to help whichever people Caesar attacked first. Caesar’s cavalry and three legions turned their departure into a rout (2.9–11).

s.n: Land of the Suessiones (Augusta Suessionum, Soissons)
s.t:
Next day Caesar marched into the land of the Suessiones and in one long march reached Noviodunum. He tried to take it straight from the march but failed because of the wide ditch and high wall. When he fortified his camp and began to build mantlets (vineae), a siege ramp and towers, the Gauls were frightened by siege works they had never seen, built so quickly, and surrendered (2.12–13). The site of the town is not certain; the marker shows the later capital of the Suessiones, Augusta Suessionum (Soissons).

From there he marched against the Bellovaci, who had gathered in their town called Bratuspantium. As he approached, the old men, then the women and children, held out their hands begging for mercy. The Aeduan Diviciacus also pleaded for them: the Bellovaci, he said, had always been friends of the Aedui and had been stirred up only by their leaders. Out of regard for the Aedui Caesar spared them, but demanded six hundred hostages (2.13–15). Then the Ambiani surrendered too.

Caesar learned that the Nervii, neighbours of the Ambiani, allowed no traders among them and admitted no wine or other luxuries, believing that these weakened the spirit and lessened courage. They were fierce and warlike men, reproached the other Belgae for surrendering, and declared that they would neither send envoys nor accept peace (2.15).

After three days’ march he learned from prisoners that the river Sabis (Sambre) was ten miles from his camp, that the Nervii stood on the far bank waiting for the Atrebates and the Veromandui, and that their women and those unfit for war had been gathered in a place protected by marshes (2.16). The Nervii knew that in the Roman marching column long baggage trains moved between the legions. They had no cavalry, so they had long hindered their neighbours’ horsemen with hedges of young trees bent down and interwoven; these hedges now also hampered the Romans (2.17).

s.n: The Sabis (Sambre) – site of the battle disputed
s.t:
The Romans began to build a camp on a hillside above the river; the Nervii were hiding in the woods on the far bank. When the first baggage wagons appeared, they burst out with their whole army, waded across the shallow river and reached the hillside so fast that Caesar had to do everything at once: hoist the flag, give the signal, recall the soldiers from the earthworks. The soldiers had no time to put on their helmets or take the covers off their shields (2.19–21). Where exactly along the Sambre the battle took place is disputed; the marker points to the river near Maubeuge.

On the left the ninth and tenth legions drove back the Atrebates, in the centre the eleventh and eighth the Veromandui; but on the right the twelfth and seventh legions were surrounded by the Nervii, the camp was taken, and the cavalry and camp followers fled. Caesar took a shield from a soldier at the rear, went into the front line, called the centurions by name and had the ranks opened out; the chief centurion of the twelfth legion, Publius Sextius Baculus, was badly wounded (2.25). Labienus captured the enemy camp and sent the tenth legion to help; the two legions escorting the baggage also arrived (2.26).

The Nervii fought standing on their dead. According to Caesar three of their six hundred councillors survived, and barely five hundred of their sixty thousand fighting men. He spared the survivors and forbade their neighbours to harm them (2.27–28).

s.n: Stronghold of the Atuatuci – site disputed (the marker shows Namur)
s.t:
The Atuatuci, who had set out to help the Nervii, turned back on hearing of the battle and, abandoning all their other towns, gathered in a single stronghold superbly protected by nature: high rocks and precipices on every side, with only one narrow approach, two hundred feet wide, closed by a double wall. According to Caesar they were descendants of the Cimbri and Teutones, left behind there by them (2.29). The site of the stronghold is disputed; the citadel of Namur is among the proposals, and the marker shows it.

When the Romans began to build a siege tower, the defenders laughed from the wall: how could such small men as the Romans move so great a tower up to the wall? When the tower began to move, they took fright and surrendered (2.30–31). They handed over most of their arms but hid about a third, and broke out at night; some four thousand were killed. Next day Caesar sold the whole population found in the town; the buyers reported 53,000 people (2.33).

Meanwhile Publius Crassus with one legion brought the maritime peoples – the Veneti, Unelli, Osismi, Coriosolites, Esuvii, Aulerci and Redones – under Roman control (2.34). The legions wintered in the lands of the Carnutes, Andes and Turones. On hearing the news the Senate decreed a thanksgiving of fifteen days, which had never before been granted to anyone (2.35).

Caesar sent the twelfth legion and part of the cavalry with Servius Galba into the lands of the Nantuates, Veragri and Seduni to open the road over the Alps, which traders could use only at great risk and paying heavy tolls (3.1). After a few successful engagements Galba settled in for the winter in a village of the Veragri called Octodurus (Martigny); a river divided the village in two, and he left one part to the Gauls.

A few days later the Gauls left the village at night, occupied the surrounding hills and attacked the half-finished camp. They fought for six hours; the Romans were running short of missiles and strength. Publius Sextius Baculus, who had been wounded in the battle against the Nervii, and the military tribune Gaius Volusenus advised Galba to break out; the sudden sortie routed the besiegers (3.2–6). Galba then did not want to stay in a valley short of grain: he burned the village and led the legion to winter in the province, among the Allobroges.

t: 56 BC: the Veneti and Aquitania
intro:
In 56 BC Caesar’s armies fought in several directions at once, as the third book of the Gallic War describes. The war was started by the coastal Veneti, who seized the officers Publius Crassus had sent for grain. Caesar had a fleet built at the mouth of the Liger (Loire) and defeated them at sea; meanwhile Quintus Titurius Sabinus fought the Unelli and the young Publius Crassus campaigned in Aquitania, and finally Caesar marched into the forests of the Morini and Menapii.

That spring Caesar also held political talks in Italy: from Cicero’s letters we know that he met Marcus Crassus at Ravenna and Pompey at Luca. The Gallic War does not mention this; Caesar only writes that he hurried to the army as soon as he could (3.9).

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017). The site of the sea battle with the Veneti and of Sabinus’ camp are not known exactly; the markers say so. The land line follows the later Roman road network; to the sea battle it follows the coastal sea route.

s.t:
Publius Crassus wintered with the seventh legion near the Ocean, among the Andes. As grain was scarce, he sent officers to the neighbouring peoples: Titus Terrasidius to the Esuvii, Marcus Trebius Gallus to the Coriosolites, Quintus Velanius and Titus Silius to the Veneti (3.7). The marker shows the later capital of the Andes, Iuliomagus (Angers).

The Veneti were the most powerful people of the coast: they had many ships, sailed to Britain in them and surpassed everyone in seamanship; they held the few harbours and took tolls from all who sailed there. They began it: they detained Silius and Velanius, hoping to get back the hostages they had given Crassus. Their neighbours followed their example and swore to resist together (3.8). From Italy Caesar ordered warships to be built on the rivers flowing into the Liger, and oarsmen, sailors and pilots to be raised in the province (3.9).

Caesar divided his army: he sent Labienus to the Treveri to keep the Belgae and the Germans in check; Crassus with twelve cohorts and many horsemen to Aquitania; Sabinus with three legions against the Unelli, Coriosolites and Lexovii; the young Decimus Brutus was given command of the fleet (3.11). He himself marched against the Veneti with the infantry.

The towns of the Veneti stood on the tips of spits and headlands: at high tide they could not be reached on foot, at low tide not by ship. When the Romans shut out the sea with dams and reached the walls, the inhabitants loaded their property onto their ships and moved to the nearest town; they did this for most of the summer (3.12). Their ships had flatter bottoms than the Roman ones, with high bows and sterns; they were built of oak, the cross-beams fastened with iron bolts an inch thick, the anchors let down on iron chains, and the sails made of hides; the Roman rams could not harm them (3.13). Caesar therefore saw that besieging the towns got him nowhere and waited for the fleet. The marker shows the later capital of the Veneti, Darioritum (Vannes).

s.n: The sea battle – traditionally Quiberon Bay; site not certain
s.t:
When the fleet arrived, about two hundred and twenty ships of the Veneti sailed out against it. The Romans could do nothing against the tall ships with their rams or their towers. One device, however, worked: with sharp sickles fixed to long poles they caught and cut the ropes binding the yards to the masts, and when the sail fell, the ship was helpless. After that the fight depended on the soldiers’ courage, and they fought in sight of Caesar and the whole army on the sea, which was plainly visible from the coastal hills (3.14).

When the Veneti tried to flee, a sudden calm fell and their ships could not move. The Romans took them one by one; the fighting lasted from the fourth hour until sunset, and only a few ships reached land (3.15). This ended the war with the Veneti: they had lost their young men, their leaders and their ships. Caesar decided to punish them severely so that the Gauls would respect the rights of envoys more in future: he had their council executed and sold the rest into slavery (3.16). Caesar does not name the site of the battle; tradition places it in Quiberon Bay.

s.n: Land of the Unelli (Cosedia, Coutances); site of Sabinus’ camp unknown
s.t:
Sabinus reached the land of the Unelli. Their leader, Viridovix, had gathered a large army from the rebel peoples; the Aulerci Eburovices and the Lexovii killed their councils, which had opposed the war, and joined him. Many criminals and robbers flocked there from all over Gaul, drawn by hope of plunder and love of war (3.17).

Sabinus camped in a good position and would not accept the daily challenge to battle, so that not only the enemy but his own soldiers began to think him a coward. Then he sent a clever Gaul, one of his auxiliaries, over to the enemy to say that Sabinus was afraid and would slip away the next night to help Caesar. The Gauls believed it; loaded with brushwood to fill the ditch, they ran up the slope to the camp and arrived out of breath. Sabinus broke out from two gates and routed them (3.18–19). According to Caesar this happened on the same day as the destruction of the Venetan fleet, and the surrounding peoples surrendered at once. Caesar remarks that the Gauls are quick and eager to start wars but have no stamina to bear defeat.

Publius Crassus reached Aquitania, which according to Caesar makes up a third of Gaul in extent and population. He knew he had to fight where a few years earlier the legate Lucius Valerius Praeconinus had been killed and his army routed, and from where the proconsul Lucius Manlius had fled leaving his baggage behind; so he prepared with great care. He collected grain, called up auxiliaries and cavalry, and summoned by name many proven soldiers from Tolosa, Carcaso and Narbo, the towns of the province bordering on Aquitania (3.20).

Tolosa (Toulouse) lay on the border of the province, and the campaign started from there. According to Ramsey and Raaflaub Crassus crossed the Garumna (Garonne) and entered Aquitanian land in the second half of July.

The Sotiates attacked Crassus on the march with a large army and their cavalry, in which their main strength lay; when their horsemen fled, their infantry, hidden in a valley, rushed out. After a long fight they were beaten, and Crassus besieged their town straight from the march. Against the Roman ramp and mantlets the defenders dug mines – according to Caesar the Aquitani were very skilled at this because they mine copper in many places – and finally surrendered (3.20–21). The marker shows the site given by Pleiades, modern Sos.

While the arms were being handed over, the leader of the Sotiates, Adiatuanus, tried to break out with six hundred devoted followers whom they called soldurii. Caesar explains the custom: these followers share everything with the lord to whom their friendship binds them; if he dies a violent death, they either die with him or kill themselves, and within living memory no one had refused (3.22). The sortie was driven back, yet Adiatuanus was granted the same terms of surrender.

Then the Vocates and Tarusates took up arms and called for help from Further Spain; as leaders they chose men who had fought for years with Quintus Sertorius, and they made camp in the Roman manner. Crassus attacked their camp of about fifty thousand; when the cavalry reported that the rear gate was weakly guarded, he sent four cohorts there by a roundabout way. The surprise attack decided the battle: according to Caesar barely a quarter of the enemy escaped. Upon this most of Aquitania surrendered and sent hostages (3.23–27).

s.h: The forests of the Morini and Menapii
s.t:
At the end of the summer Caesar marched against the Morini and Menapii, who had sent no envoys. They would not stand for open battle but withdrew into continuous forests and marshes and attacked the Romans from there while they were building camp (3.28). Caesar therefore had the forest cut down and the felled trees piled on both sides, turned towards the enemy, as a rampart. In a few days a large area was cleared and their cattle and baggage were reached, but the constant rain made it impossible to keep the soldiers under canvas any longer (3.29).

So Caesar burned their fields and villages and put the army into winter quarters among the Aulerci, the Lexovii and the other peoples that had lately rebelled. The marker shows the later capital of the Morini, Tarvenna (Thérouanne).

t: 55 BC: the Rhine and Britain
intro:
The fourth book of the Gallic War describes two ventures that caused a sensation in Rome: Caesar was the first to lead a Roman army across the Rhine, on a bridge built in ten days, and the first to cross to Britain. Before that he fought the Usipetes and Tencteri, who had crossed the Rhine; by Caesar’s own description this campaign ended in a bloody massacre.

Caesar also writes at length about the Germanic peoples: the Suebi, he says, are the largest and most warlike of the Germans; they have a hundred cantons, each of which sends a thousand armed men to war every year while the rest stay at home and work (4.1). The Usipetes and Tencteri too were fleeing from the pressure of the Suebi.

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017). The sites of the battle with the Usipetes, of the Rhine bridge and of the landing in Britain are disputed; the markers show the assumptions named in the text. The land line follows the later Roman road network, across the Channel the sea route.

s.t:
During the winter the Germanic Usipetes and Tencteri crossed the Rhine in great numbers, not far from the sea, where the river flows into it. They had been harassed for years by the Suebi, so they had wandered for three years in different parts of Germany before reaching the land of the Menapii. The Menapii had lands on both banks of the Rhine; after a feigned retreat the Germans came back in a single night, massacred them, seized their ships and crossed (4.4).

According to Caesar the Gauls are fickle and eager for change, so he set out for the army earlier than usual. He learned that some Gallic peoples had themselves invited the Germans and promised them everything; he kept quiet about what he knew, called together the Gallic leaders, demanded cavalry from them and set out against the Germans (4.5–7). According to Ramsey and Raaflaub the assembly probably took place at Samarobriva.

s.n: Defeat of the Usipetes and Tencteri – site disputed (the marker shows Kessel)
s.t:
Envoys of the Germans asked him either to give them land or to let them keep what they had won by arms; Caesar answered that there was no room for them in Gaul, but they could settle among the Ubii, who had asked him for help against the Suebi (4.7–8). They asked for three days’ delay; Caesar refused, because he understood that their cavalry had gone across the Mosa to plunder and they were only waiting for it (4.9).

During a one-day truce eight hundred German horsemen attacked Caesar’s five thousand cavalry and routed it; seventy-four horsemen fell, among them the Aquitanian Piso (4.12). Caesar regarded this as treachery. Next day, when the German leaders came to his camp in great numbers to apologise, he detained them and fell upon their leaderless camp in three lines. The Germans fled; the cavalry pursued the women and children; many of those who reached the confluence of the Mosa and the Rhine perished in the river. According to Caesar the enemy – women and children included – numbered 430,000, and not one Roman was killed (4.13–15).

According to Plutarch, Cato proposed in Rome that Caesar be handed over to the Germans for breaking the truce (Caesar 22). The site has long been disputed: Ramsey and Raaflaub think of the mouth of the Mosella (Koblenz), an archaeological interpretation presented in 2015 of Kessel in the Netherlands, on the Maas; the marker shows the latter.

s.n: The Rhine bridge – site disputed; often placed in the Neuwied basin
s.t:
Caesar decided to cross the Rhine: he wanted to show that the army of the Roman people could and dared to cross it, so that the Germans too would fear for their own lands. The Ubii offered boats, but Caesar judged this neither safe enough nor worthy of himself and the Roman people; he had a bridge built (4.16–17).

He gives a detailed description: two beams a foot and a half thick, sharpened at the bottom and measured to the depth of the river, were joined two feet apart and driven in by machines not vertically but leaning with the current; opposite them, forty feet downstream, two more beams were driven in the same way, leaning against the current. The pairs were joined by cross-beams two feet thick, and poles and wickerwork were laid on top; on the upstream side slanting buttresses and separate piles protected the bridge from tree trunks and boats floating down (4.17). The work was finished in ten days.

The Sugambri fled into the forests; Caesar burned their villages and cut their grain. When he learned that the Suebi were gathering in the middle of their land to await him there, he judged that he had achieved his aim: he spent eighteen days beyond the Rhine, returned to Gaul and had the bridge broken down (4.18–19). Caesar does not give the site of the bridge; it is often placed in the Neuwied basin between Koblenz and Andernach, as the marker shows.

s.n: Harbour of the Morini (Portus Itius? – Wissant)
s.t:
Although the summer was drawing to a close, Caesar wanted to cross to Britain, because he understood that in the Gallic wars his enemies had received help from there; even if there was no time for war, he thought it would be valuable to get to know the island, its peoples, harbours and landing places. Even the traders knew hardly anything of these (4.20). He sent Gaius Volusenus ahead with a warship to reconnoitre; he returned after five days but had not dared to land (4.21). He sent Commius, whom he had made king of the Atrebates, to the British peoples to win them over to the Roman people.

He marched to the land of the Morini, from where the crossing is shortest. He collected about eighty transports for two legions; the eighteen ships for the cavalry waited for a fair wind in another harbour eight miles away (4.22). In the fourth book Caesar does not name the harbour of departure; in the fifth he calls it Portus Itius. It is usually sought near Boulogne or Wissant; the marker shows Wissant, as in the map data.

Caesar set out about the third watch and reached the coast of Britain about the fourth hour; armed enemies stood everywhere on the high cliffs, from which missiles could be hurled down onto the shore. He waited until the ninth hour for the rest of the ships, then, with a favourable wind and tide, anchored about seven miles further on, off an open, level shore (4.23). The landing is usually placed near Deal.

The Britons sent ahead their cavalry and war chariots and tried to prevent the landing. The large ships could only stop in deep water; the soldiers, heavily armed, in an unknown place, had to jump down among the waves and fight. Caesar had the warships brought to the enemy’s open flank, and from there they drove them back with slings, arrows and artillery (4.24–25). Then the eagle-bearer of the tenth legion, after praying to the gods that his deed might bring the legion good fortune, cried: “Jump down, comrades, unless you want to betray the eagle to the enemy; I at least will have done my duty to the Republic and my general” – and he advanced towards the enemy with the eagle. The soldiers, urging one another on, leapt down after him (4.25). In the end the Britons were routed on the shore; without cavalry they could not be pursued (4.26).

img.c: The White Cliffs of Dover. Caesar says he first approached a steep, cliff-bound shore (BG 4.23), usually identified with Dover.

s.n: The camp on the shore (near Deal)
s.t:
The Britons sued for peace and gave hostages. On the fourth day, however, a storm arose and drove the eighteen cavalry ships back to the Continent, and that same night there was a full moon, when the Ocean tides are highest – according to Caesar the Romans did not know this. The warships drawn up on the beach were swamped, and the transports riding at anchor were battered by the storm (4.28–29). Seeing this, the Britons prepared for war again.

While the seventh legion was reaping grain, the Britons fell upon it from the woods. Here Caesar describes the war chariots: the warriors drive about, hurl missiles, and the noise of horses and wheels throws the ranks into confusion; driving in among the cavalry they jump down and fight on foot, while the drivers wait a little way off to take them up again if needed. Their practice is such that they can check their horses even on a steep slope, and run along the pole while driving (4.32–33). Caesar hurried to help.

After some days of storms the Britons attacked the camp too, but were defeated. Caesar demanded twice as many hostages and, as the equinox was near, did not want to risk winter sailing with damaged ships: he set sail after midnight, and the fleet reached the Continent safely (4.34–36). Two transports were carried further down by the current, and the Morini attacked their soldiers; they held out for four hours until the cavalry arrived (4.37). The Senate decreed a thanksgiving of twenty days (4.38).

t: 54 BC: Britain and Ambiorix
intro:
The first half of the fifth book of the Gallic War describes the second expedition to Britain: this time Caesar crossed with five legions and a large fleet and pushed beyond the Tamesis (Thames) into the land of Cassivellaunus. The second half tells of the Gallic rising against the winter camps: the Eburonian Ambiorix lured out and destroyed the army of Sabinus and Cotta by a ruse, and then the Nervii besieged the camp of Quintus Cicero – the orator’s younger brother – until Caesar relieved it.

We also know of the British expedition from Cicero’s letters: Quintus Cicero wrote to his brother from there, and Caesar too wrote to him from the British coast. In the Gallic War Caesar also describes the shape of the island, its inhabitants and their customs (5.12–14).

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017). The British sites, the winter camp of Sabinus and Cotta (Atuatuca) and Cicero’s camp cannot be identified with certainty; the markers show the assumptions named in the text. The march to relieve Cicero can also be computed with the legion calculator.

s.t:
During the winter Caesar had ships built: a little lower than usual, for quick loading, unloading and beaching, and a little broader, to carry horses and much baggage. About six hundred transports and twenty-eight warships were completed; he ordered them to Portus Itius, from where Britain is about thirty miles away (5.1–2). Meanwhile he marched with four legions and eight hundred horse to the Treveri, where Indutiomarus and the pro-Roman Cingetorix were contending for power; he demanded two hundred hostages, among them Indutiomarus’ son (5.3–4).

At the harbour the north-west wind, which blows there most of the time, held for twenty-five days. Caesar wanted to take the Gallic leaders with him because he did not trust them in his absence. The Aeduan Dumnorix tried every excuse to stay behind, and on the day of embarkation slipped away with his horsemen. Caesar sent the cavalry after him with orders to kill him if he resisted. Dumnorix resisted and, calling on his horsemen for help, kept crying that he was a free man and of a free people – and he was killed (5.6–7).

s.n: The first stronghold – often identified with Bigbury near Canterbury
s.t:
Labienus stayed on the Continent with three legions and two thousand horse; Caesar set sail at sunset with five legions and an equal number of horse. Together with the private vessels of individuals there were more than eight hundred ships in sight at once, so the Britons took fright and left the shore (5.8). Caesar landed about midday where he had found the best landing place the year before.

At night he marched twelve miles inland and met the Britons at a river; they withdrew to a place protected by woods and fortifications, which soldiers of the seventh legion took by forming a tortoise and throwing up a ramp (5.9). The place is often identified with the hillfort of Bigbury near Canterbury.

Next day it was reported that there had been a great storm in the night and the ships at anchor were damaged. About forty were lost; the rest Caesar had repaired within ten days, working day and night, by craftsmen from the legions and from the Continent, and he had all the ships hauled ashore and enclosed together with the camp in one fortification (5.10–11).

s.n: The crossing of the Tamesis – site unknown; the marker shows Londinium
s.t:
The Britons chose Cassivellaunus as their joint commander; his land was divided from the coastal peoples by the Tamesis, about eighty miles from the sea (5.11). With their war chariots and horsemen they constantly harassed the column; in one clash the military tribune Quintus Laberius Durus fell. When they fell upon the foragers, the legate Gaius Trebonius with three legions and all the cavalry routed them so thoroughly that their auxiliaries dispersed afterwards (5.15–17).

Caesar marched to the Tamesis, which could be forded on foot at one place only, and that with difficulty. The Britons stood on the far bank, which they had studded with sharp stakes, and stakes were also driven in under the water. The soldiers, up to their necks in water, attacked with such dash that the enemy could not stand and fled (5.18). We do not know the site of the crossing; the marker shows the later Londinium.

Cassivellaunus then dismissed his army and kept only about four thousand charioteers, with whom he watched the Romans along the roads and fell on the foragers (5.19).

s.n: Stronghold of Cassivellaunus – often linked with Wheathampstead near Verulamium
s.t:
The Trinovantes, perhaps the strongest people of Britain, sent envoys and asked for Mandubracius as king; Cassivellaunus had killed his father, and he had fled to Caesar in Gaul. Caesar asked for forty hostages and grain and sent Mandubracius to them (5.20). Other peoples submitted too and revealed that Cassivellaunus’ stronghold, protected by woods and marshes, was not far away. According to Caesar the Britons call a stronghold any dense wood they have surrounded with a rampart and ditch. He attacked it from two sides and took it, capturing many cattle (5.21). The site is often identified with Wheathampstead near Verulamium.

Cassivellaunus then sent word to four kings of Cantium – Cingetorix, Carvilius, Taximagulus and Segovax – to attack the naval camp; the Romans sallied out and drove them off. Upon this Cassivellaunus surrendered through the Atrebatian Commius. Since Caesar wanted to winter in Gaul because of sudden Gallic unrest, and little of the summer remained, he demanded hostages and fixed what tribute Britain should pay yearly to the Roman people (5.22). He then brought the army back safely in two crossings, in a calm (5.23).

s.h: Winter quarters in a year of drought
s.t:
The ships were beached, and Caesar held an assembly at Samarobriva. Because that year the drought had made the harvest in Gaul scanty, he spread the legions, contrary to his usual practice, among several peoples: Fabius went to the Morini, Quintus Cicero to the Nervii, Roscius to the Esuvii, Labienus to the Remi on the border of the Treveri; Crassus, Plancus and Trebonius stayed in the land of the Belgae. The legion most recently raised beyond the Padus, with five cohorts, was led by Quintus Titurius Sabinus and Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta into the land of the Eburones, who lived between the Mosa and the Rhine under Ambiorix and Catuvolcus (5.24). Caesar spread them so that they were at most a hundred miles apart, and stayed in Gaul until he had news that the camps were fortified.

Meanwhile the Carnutes killed Tasgetius, whom Caesar had made their king; Caesar sent Lucius Plancus to them with a legion (5.25).

s.n: Atuatuca – site of the winter camp unknown; the marker shows the later Roman Atuatuca (Tongeren)
s.h: The destruction of Sabinus and Cotta
s.t:
About fifteen days after the winter camps had been occupied, Ambiorix and Catuvolcus, urged on by the Treveran Indutiomarus, attacked the camp of Sabinus and Cotta; the Romans drove them back. Ambiorix then asked for a parley and said: the whole of Gaul would fall on all the Roman camps on one day, a great German army was approaching from beyond the Rhine; if the Romans withdrew to Cicero or Labienus, he promised them safe passage (5.26–27).

In the council of war Cotta and several tribunes and centurions held that the fortified camp must not be abandoned without Caesar’s orders; Sabinus argued the opposite and won after a dispute lasting until midnight. At dawn they marched out in a long column loaded with baggage (5.28–31). Two miles away, in a deep valley, the Eburones attacked them from both sides. The Romans formed a circle; Cotta did everything he could, Sabinus lost his head. When Sabinus went to parley with Ambiorix, he was surrounded and killed; Cotta fell fighting. The eagle-bearer, Lucius Petrosidius, threw the eagle inside the rampart and died in front of the camp. The survivors all killed themselves in the night; only a few made their way through the woods to Labienus (5.32–37).

Caesar names the camp in book 6: Atuatuca, almost in the middle of the land of the Eburones (6.32). Where it was we do not know; the marker shows the later Roman Atuatuca (Tongeren).

s.n: Cicero’s camp among the Nervii – site unknown (the marker shows Bagacum)
s.t:
After his victory Ambiorix also roused the Atuatuci and the Nervii, and they fell upon Quintus Cicero’s camp. In a single night, from the timber collected for the fortifications, the Romans raised about a hundred and twenty towers (5.40). The Nervii, in the way they had learned from prisoners, built a rampart and ditch around the camp and made towers and mantlets; on the seventh day, in a strong wind, they slung red-hot clay balls and fiery darts onto the thatched huts, and the camp went up in flames (5.42–43). In this siege two centurions, Titus Pullo and Lucius Vorenus, vied with each other: they sallied out one after the other and in the end saved each other’s lives (5.44).

Cicero’s messengers were caught one after another. At last a Nervian, Vertico, who had come over to him, sent a slave who, being a Gaul, passed without suspicion, with the letter tied to a javelin (5.45). Caesar received the news late in the day, ordered Crassus to Samarobriva to guard the baggage and winter supplies, and set out by forced marches with Fabius’ legion. He sent Cicero a letter written in Greek letters so that the enemy could not read it; a Gaul tied it to a javelin and threw it into the camp, where it was noticed only days later, but by then the fires of the approaching army could be seen (5.46–48).

About sixty thousand Gauls marched to meet Caesar. Caesar had barely seven thousand men, without baggage. He feigned fear, built a small camp, and when the enemy rushed the rampart he broke out from every gate and routed them (5.49–51). In Cicero’s legion barely one man in ten was left unwounded (5.52). At the news of the victory the Treveran Indutiomarus, who had planned to attack Labienus’ camp the next day, withdrew; at the end of the winter Labienus defeated him by a ruse, and he was killed at a ford (5.53, 5.58).

calc.src: According to Ramsey and Raaflaub Caesar marched by forced marches towards Cicero between 29 October and 2 November (5.46–48), fought the battle on 4–6 November and reached the camp on 6–7 November. The site of Cicero’s camp is unknown; the calculator computes to the marker (Bagacum).

t: 53 BC: vengeance for Ambiorix
intro:
The sixth book of the Gallic War covers the year after the destruction of Sabinus and Cotta. Caesar expected a larger rising, so he reinforced his army with three new legions and subdued in turn the Nervii, the Senones, the Carnutes and the Menapii; Labienus defeated the Treveri. Caesar crossed the Rhine a second time and then turned against Ambiorix and the Eburones, whom – in his own words – he meant to destroy completely.

In the middle of the book Caesar makes a long digression on the customs of the Gauls and the Germans (6.11–28): on the druids, Gallic society, the gods of the Germans and the strange animals of the Hercynian forest. This is the most famous ethnographic part of the Gallic War.

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017). The sites of the second Rhine bridge and of Atuatuca are not known for certain; the markers say so.

s.t:
During the winter Caesar raised new troops through his legates and also asked Pompey for a legion that he had sworn in as consul in Cisalpine Gaul. So before the end of winter he replaced, indeed doubled, the cohorts lost under Titurius with three legions, to show Gaul what resources Italy had (6.1). As the Treveri had drawn Germans and Ambiorix into their alliance, before spring he fell unexpectedly on the land of the Nervii with four legions and forced them to surrender (6.2–3).

The Senones, the Carnutes and the Treveri did not come to the spring assembly of Gaul; so Caesar moved the assembly to Lutetia, the town of the Parisii, which bordered on the Senones, and marched from there against the Senones. On the advice of the instigator of the revolt, Acco, they meant to take refuge in their towns, but at Caesar’s rapid arrival they surrendered; at the intercession of the Aedui he spared them, and the Carnutes likewise (6.3–4).

s.n: Land of the Menapii (Castellum Menapiorum, Cassel)
s.t: Ambiorix’s only ally whom, according to Caesar, he could trust were the Menapii, who had never sent envoys to Caesar and relied on their marshes and forests. Caesar sent the baggage with two legions to Labienus and marched himself with five legions without baggage against the Menapii. They gathered no army but fled into the forests and marshes. Caesar had bridges built in three columns, burned their villages and drove off their cattle and people, whereupon they asked for peace; Caesar took hostages and threatened to treat them as enemies if they received Ambiorix or his envoys (6.5–6). The marker shows the later centre of the Menapii, Castellum Menapiorum (Cassel).

s.n: Land of the Treveri (Augusta Treverorum, Trier)
s.t: Meanwhile the Treveri marched with a large army against Labienus, who was wintering with one legion on their border. When they learned that Caesar had sent him two legions, they camped by a river with steep banks and waited for the Germans to arrive. In a council of war, in the hearing of Gauls, Labienus said he would withdraw at dawn because he dared not face the Germans. Hearing this, the Treveri crossed the river and began to pursue him over narrow, difficult ground; Labienus then turned and attacked them. They fled at the first charge. Indutiomarus’ kinsmen fled to the Germans, and power was given to the pro-Roman Cingetorix (6.7–8). Caesar does not give the site of the battle; the marker shows the later capital of the Treveri, Augusta Treverorum (Trier).

s.n: The second Rhine bridge – “a little above” the first; site disputed
s.h: Across the Rhine a second time
s.t:
Caesar crossed the Rhine again for two reasons: the Germans had sent help to the Treveri, and he did not want Ambiorix to find refuge with them. A little above the place where he had taken the army across the year before, he had another bridge built; using the method already known, the soldiers finished it in a few days (6.9). The Ubii proved their loyalty and told him that the Suebi had withdrawn to a forest called Bacenis, of enormous extent, which separated them like a natural wall from the Cherusci. Because of the shortage of grain Caesar did not follow them into the forests (6.10, 6.29).

Here Caesar places his ethnographic digression. The druids oversee worship, sacrifices and law; their pupils study for as long as twenty years, and their teaching is not written down, because they do not want the knowledge to become common, nor the pupils to rely on writing and neglect their memory; they teach that the soul does not perish but passes after death from one body to another (6.13–14). The Gauls say they are all descended from father Dis (6.18). The Germans count as gods only those they can see and whose help they feel: the Sun, Fire and the Moon (6.21). Crossing the Hercynian forest takes a quick traveller nine days, and Caesar describes strange animals living there, among them the elk with jointless legs that sleeps leaning against a tree, and the urus, a little smaller than an elephant (6.25–28).

On his return he broke down the far end of the bridge for two hundred feet, and on the remaining part left a four-storey tower and a garrison of twelve cohorts (6.29).

s.n: Atuatuca – site unknown; the marker shows the later Roman Atuatuca (Tongeren)
s.h: The hunt for Ambiorix and Atuatuca
s.t:
Caesar set out against Ambiorix through the Arduenna forest, sending Lucius Minucius Basilus ahead with the cavalry. Basilus surprised Ambiorix at his house, but at the cost of a follower’s self-sacrifice Ambiorix got onto a horse and escaped. The other king of the Eburones, Catuvolcus, who because of his age could not bear the hardship of war or flight, poisoned himself with the juice of the yew (6.29–31).

Caesar left the baggage at Atuatuca, the fort where Titurius and Aurunculeius had wintered; he assigned the fourteenth legion and Quintus Cicero to guard it and promised to return on the seventh day. He divided the army into three and scoured the whole region (6.32–34). Meanwhile the news that the land of the Eburones was open to plunder crossed the Rhine: two thousand Sugambrian horsemen crossed thirty miles below the bridge in boats and on rafts. A prisoner told them that all the treasure was at Atuatuca with only a weak garrison, so they turned that way. On the seventh day Cicero sent five cohorts out for grain; just then the Germans reached the camp. The sick Publius Sextius Baculus, who had eaten nothing for five days, seized his arms and fought at the gate until he fainted. Some of the foragers broke through into the camp; two cohorts were lost (6.35–40, 6.44). After his return Caesar sent the army out again to lay waste the land of the Eburones (6.43).

We do not know the site of the fort; the marker shows the later Roman Atuatuca (Tongeren).

After losing the two cohorts, Caesar led the army to the town of the Remi, Durocortorum, and held an assembly of Gaul there about the conspiracy of the Senones and Carnutes. He condemned its leader, Acco, to death and had him executed after the custom of the ancestors; some who had fled for fear of trial were outlawed. He then sent two legions to winter on the border of the Treveri, two among the Lingones, and six in the land of the Senones, at Agedincum, and having provided for grain he set out for Italy to hold the assizes (6.44).

Acco’s execution, Caesar writes in the next book, caused great indignation among the Gallic nobles and contributed to the great rising of 52 BC (7.1).

t: 52 BC: Vercingetorix
intro:
The seventh book of the Gallic War tells of the greatest Gallic rising. At the beginning of 52 BC there were riots in Rome: Clodius was murdered, the Senate house burned down, and the Senate called the young men of Italy to arms. The Gallic nobles thought that Caesar would be detained by affairs in Rome and unable to reach his army (7.1). The rising began in the land of the Carnutes, at Cenabum, and the Arvernian Vercingetorix took the lead.

With a crossing of the mountains in winter and then rapid marches Caesar united his army, took Avaricum, but failed before Gergovia; after this even the Aedui, Rome’s old allies, defected. The war was decided by the siege of Alesia, where Caesar enclosed Vercingetorix with a double system of fortifications and held off the relief army.

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017); the Roman calendar was then more than a month ahead, so in Caesar’s text the rising begins “in winter”, by the Julian calendar in early January. The sites of Gergovia and Alesia have been identified by archaeological research (the plateau of Gergovie and Mont Auxois); the markers follow Pleiades.

s.t:
The Gallic nobles met in forests and remote places and complained about Acco’s death. The Carnutes undertook to start the war. On the appointed day, led by Cotuatus and Conconnetodumnus, they rushed into Cenabum and killed the Roman citizens trading there, among them Gaius Fufius Cita, whom Caesar had put in charge of the grain supply (7.2–3).

The news spread with incredible speed: the Gauls, writes Caesar, pass on every important event by shouting across fields and districts, and others take it up and pass it on. What happened at Cenabum at sunrise was heard in the land of the Arverni, about a hundred and sixty miles away, before the end of the first watch (7.3).

The Arvernian Vercingetorix, son of Celtillus – his father had held the greatest power in all Gaul and had been killed by his people for seeking kingship – called his dependants together and easily roused them. His uncle Gobannitio and the other nobles, unwilling to tempt fortune, drove him out of Gergovia. He, however, raised an army in the countryside from the poor and the outcasts, came back, drove out his opponents and was hailed king by his followers (7.4).

He sent envoys in every direction; the Senones, Parisii, Pictones, Cadurci, Turoni, Aulerci, Lemovices, Andes and the other peoples on the Ocean joined him and unanimously gave him the supreme command. According to Caesar he drove the hesitant to act by harsh punishments: for greater offences he had them put to death by fire and every kind of torture, for lesser ones he had their ears cut off or one eye put out and sent them home as a deterrent to others (7.4).

img.c: Gold stater of Vercingetorix inscribed (VERCI)NGETORIXS (Pionsat) and two bronze coins from Alesia (1st century BC; Saint-Germain-en-Laye, Musée d’Archéologie nationale). The head follows a Hellenistic model and is probably not a true portrait.

s.t:
Caesar learned of the rising in Italy. He saw that the legions could not come to him through the Gauls, nor could he safely reach the legions. The Cadurci under Lucterius threatened the province, so he first went to Narbo, calmed the frightened inhabitants and posted garrisons on the borders of the province (7.5–7). According to Ramsey and Raaflaub he covered about 1,030 km from Ravenna to Narbo in thirteen days.

He then set out for the border of the Arverni with troops gathered in the land of the Helvii. The Cevennes, which separate them, had covered the road with snow six feet deep in the hardest season of the year; the soldiers dug it clear with great effort, and Caesar appeared unexpectedly in the land of the Arverni, who had believed the mountain protected them like a wall. Vercingetorix then turned back from the land of the Bituriges to defend his own people (7.8). Caesar now left the troops to Decimus Brutus and two days later went to Vienna, where the cavalry was waiting (7.9).

s.n: Land of the Lingones (Andematunnum, Langres) – site of the winter camp unknown
s.h: Night and day to the legions
s.t: From Vienna Caesar hurried with the cavalry, marching day and night without a break, through the land of the Aedui to the Lingones, where two legions were wintering, so that if the Aedui too were plotting against him, he could forestall them by speed. From there he sent word to the other legions and gathered them all in one place before the Arverni could learn of his arrival (7.9). According to Ramsey and Raaflaub the army was united at Agedincum, where two legions guarded the baggage.

f: Col. Vienna|Colonia Iulia Augusta Florentia Vienna
calc.src: According to Ramsey and Raaflaub Caesar left Vienna on 26 March and reached the two legions wintering among the Lingones on 29 March: about 3 days, with cavalry, travelling night and day (7.9). The calculator uses a forced march but with a night’s rest.

s.t:
From Agedincum Caesar took Vellaunodunum of the Senones, Cenabum of the Carnutes, which he plundered and burned for the massacre, and then Noviodunum of the Bituriges (7.11–13). Vercingetorix then announced a new plan: the Romans must be cut off from food, so every village and town that could not be defended must be burned. In a single day more than twenty towns of the Bituriges went up in flames; Avaricum, perhaps the finest town in Gaul, was spared at the request of the Bituriges, since the river and marsh protected it on almost every side (7.14–15).

Caesar besieged it. The army went hungry and was without grain for days, but when Caesar offered to give up the siege, the soldiers begged him not to (7.17). Caesar also describes the Gallic wall: beams laid lengthwise with stones filling the spaces, in alternating layers, so that the stone protected against fire and the timber against the battering ram (7.23). In twenty-five days they raised a ramp three hundred and thirty feet wide and eighty feet high (7.24). On a rainy day, when the guards were less watchful, the legions took the town by storm. Because of the massacre at Cenabum the soldiers spared neither the old, nor women, nor children: of about forty thousand people barely eight hundred reached Vercingetorix (7.27–28).

img.c: A reconstruction of the murus gallicus, the Gallic wall construction Caesar describes at Avaricum (BG 7.23), in the Celtic Museum at Manching.

s.t:
Caesar sent Labienus with four legions against the Senones and Parisii and led six himself towards Gergovia along the Elaver (Allier). Vercingetorix marched along the far bank and broke down the bridges. So Caesar hid two legions in a wooded place and divided the rest so that they looked like the usual number of legions, and when the Gauls had moved on, he had the bridge rebuilt on the old piles and crossed (7.34–35).

Gergovia lay on a very high mountain, difficult of access on every side (7.36). Caesar seized a hill opposite and linked two camps with a trench. Meanwhile Litaviccus stirred up revolt among the Aedui, and only Caesar’s quick intervention prevented the Aeduan troops from going over (7.37–41). One day, when the Gauls were fortifying one side of the town, Caesar drew their attention away with feints – dressing the pack animals up as cavalry – and the legions took the Gallic camps beneath the wall (7.44–46). The soldiers, however, did not hear or did not obey the signal to withdraw and pressed on to the wall; the centurion Lucius Fabius climbed onto it. A Gallic counter-attack threw them back. The centurion Marcus Petronius sacrificed himself at the gate so that his men could escape. Caesar lost forty-six centurions and nearly seven hundred soldiers (7.47–51). Next day he rebuked the soldiers for setting their own judgement above their general’s (7.52), and then withdrew.

img.c: The Gergovia plateau at sunset, with the Vercingetorix monument.

s.h: The defection of the Aedui and Labienus
s.t:
After Gergovia the Aedui defected too. At Noviodunum (Nevers) on the Liger, where Caesar kept the hostages, the grain, the war chest and the horses, they killed the garrison and the traders, took the hostages to Bibracte and set the town on fire (7.55). Caesar crossed the flooded Liger at a ford, the water up to the soldiers’ shoulders, and went into the land of the Senones (7.56).

Meanwhile Labienus marched from Agedincum towards Lutetia, which lay on an island in the Sequana. The Aulercan Camulogenus barred his way at the marshes; Labienus crossed by boat at Metlosedum (Melun) and marched on the right bank of the Sequana towards Lutetia, which the Gauls set on fire. By a ruse at night – noisy boats going upstream, a silent crossing downstream – he took the army across to the far bank and defeated the Gauls in battle; Camulogenus fell (7.57–62). He then returned to Agedincum and joined Caesar.

An assembly of Gaul was held at Bibracte; Vercingetorix was unanimously chosen commander-in-chief. The Remi, the Lingones and the Treveri took no part (7.63).

When Caesar was marching through the border of the Lingones towards the Sequani to help the province, Vercingetorix’s cavalry attacked the column; Caesar’s German horsemen drove it off, and Vercingetorix withdrew to Alesia, a town of the Mandubii (7.66–68). The town stood on top of a hill between two rivers; Caesar’s siege works had a circuit of eleven miles, with twenty-three forts (7.69).

Vercingetorix sent away his cavalry to bring a relief army from all Gaul, and distributed grain for thirty days (7.71). Caesar had a ditch dug twenty feet wide with vertical sides, behind it two water-filled ditches and a rampart twelve feet high with towers; in front he laid out sharpened branches called “gravestones” (cippi), stakes hidden in slanting pits which the soldiers called “lilies”, and pieces of wood fitted with iron hooks (stimuli). He built the same works facing outwards, fourteen miles long, against the relief army (7.72–74).

According to Caesar the relief army had eight thousand horse and about a quarter of a million foot, led by Commius, Viridomarus, Eporedorix and Vercassivellaunus (7.75–76). Food ran short in the town; Critognatus proposed that they keep themselves alive on the bodies of those unfit to fight; finally the Mandubii were driven out with their wives and children, but Caesar would not take them in (7.77–78). After several days of fighting, in the last battle the Gauls broke through at the weak northern part of the camp; Caesar, recognisable by the distinctive colour of the cloak he usually wore in battle, led the help himself, the cavalry took the Gauls in the rear, and seventy-four standards were captured (7.79–88). Next day Vercingetorix surrendered and the arms were handed over. Except for the Aedui and the Arverni, every one of Caesar’s soldiers received one captive as booty (7.89). Caesar wintered at Bibracte; the Senate decreed a thanksgiving of twenty days (7.90).

img.c: A reconstruction of the rampart of the Roman siege line (contravallation) at Alesia.

t: 51 BC: the last resistance
intro:
The eighth and last book of the Gallic War was not written by Caesar but by his officer Aulus Hirtius, after Caesar’s death; in a preface addressed to Balbus he explains that he is completing Caesar’s unfinished accounts. After Alesia the great Gallic coalition broke up, but some peoples fought on: the Bituriges, the Carnutes, the Bellovaci, and finally the last bands arming at Uxellodunum in the land of the Cadurci.

According to Hirtius, even in his winter campaigns Caesar forestalled those plotting by speed, and he wanted the Gauls to see that they could not resist one by one. After Uxellodunum he made a cruel example so that there would be peace for the rest of his time – until the end of his governorship.

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017); the Roman calendar was then almost a month ahead. The places are the map’s DARE points or from Pleiades (Uxellodunum: Puy d’Issolud).

s.t: Caesar was wintering at Bibracte, but when he learned that several Gallic peoples were preparing for war at the same time, so as to split up the Romans, in midwinter he fell unexpectedly on the land of the Bituriges with two legions. The unsuspecting inhabitants working in the fields were captured before they could flee to the towns; the Bituriges surrendered. According to Hirtius he returned to Bibracte on the fortieth day, and as a reward for their winter labours the soldiers received two hundred sesterces each and the centurions two thousand (8.2–4).

img.c: Marble bust of Cicero, mid-1st century AD (Rome, Capitoline Museums).

s.t: When the Bituriges complained that the Carnutes had attacked them, Caesar, after eighteen days’ rest, set out against the Carnutes with the fourteenth and sixth legions. They had sheltered from the cold in the houses of ruined Cenabum and in huts thrown up in haste, but at Caesar’s approach they scattered. Because of the frost Caesar quartered the soldiers in Cenabum and sent out the cavalry and auxiliaries to pursue the scattered Carnutes (8.4–5).

The Remi reported that the Bellovaci, who surpassed all Gauls and Belgae in military glory, were raising an army with their neighbours under Correus and the Atrebatian Commius. Caesar marched against them with four legions; the Gauls camped on a height protected by a marsh, and Caesar built a fortified camp facing them (8.6–10). After long skirmishing the Gauls withdrew at night: to hide their departure they set fire to bundles of brushwood and straw in front of their lines and escaped behind the smoke and flames (8.15–16).

Correus then laid an ambush for the Roman foragers in a wooded place with six thousand picked foot and a thousand horse. The Romans got the upper hand; according to Hirtius neither wounds nor persuasion could make Correus surrender, and he fell fighting (8.17–19). The Bellovaci then surrendered; Caesar reproached them for having wanted war more than the others but spared them (8.21–22). Commius fled to the Germans; Hirtius relates that Labienus had earlier tried to have him treacherously killed, and that Commius had then sworn never again to come into the sight of a Roman (8.23).

s.h: Lemonum and the bridge on the Liger
s.t: Caesar then laid waste the land of Ambiorix and sent Labienus to the Treveri. Meanwhile Gaius Caninius Rebilus received a letter from Duratius, the pro-Roman leader of the Pictones: the Andan Dumnacus was besieging him with a large army in the town of Lemonum. Caninius set out to help him, and then Gaius Fabius too (8.24–27). Dumnacus gave up the siege and marched towards the Liger to cross by the bridge; Fabius’ cavalry caught up with him, and when the legions arrived, more than twelve thousand of his men fell in the battle according to Hirtius (8.27–29). After this the Carnutes and the Aremorican peoples of the coast submitted as well (8.31).

The Senonian Drappes and the Cadurcan Lucterius, who were preparing to attack the province, withdrew into a town of the Cadurci called Uxellodunum, protected on every side by steep cliffs, with a river flowing below. Caninius invested it; Drappes was captured while escorting a grain convoy (8.32–36). Caesar, so that the Gauls should not think that perseverance could achieve anything, hurried there himself with the cavalry (8.39).

The town’s water came from the river and from a spring rising beneath the wall. Caesar cut off the river with archers and slingers, raised a ramp sixty feet high and a ten-storey tower against the spring, and secretly had mines dug. The defenders rolled burning barrels onto the ramp, but when the mines reached the veins of the spring and the water dried up, they thought this the will of the gods and surrendered (8.40–43).

According to Hirtius, Caesar knew that his clemency was known to all and did not need to fear that severity would be put down to cruelty; so he had the hands cut off all who had borne arms, but left them alive so that their punishment should be before everyone’s eyes. Drappes starved himself to death; Lucterius was handed over to Caesar by the Arvernian Epasnactus (8.44). Archaeologists have identified the site with the plateau of Puy d’Issolud, where the mines around the spring have also been found.

img.c: Delos: the Terrace of the Lions.

s.h: Nemetocenna: the end of the war
s.t:
Caesar then went to Aquitania, where he had never been in person; there every people sent envoys and hostages. He distributed the legions to winter quarters and wintered himself in the land of the Belgae, at Nemetocenna (modern Arras) (8.46). The Atrebatian Commius badly wounded his old enemy Gaius Volusenus in a cavalry fight, and then surrendered to Marcus Antonius on condition that he should never have to come into the sight of a Roman (8.48).

In 50 BC Caesar treated Gaul gently so that there should be no war in the last year of his governorship (8.49). He travelled to Italy to support Antonius’ election as augur, and the towns everywhere received him with ceremony (8.50–51). In Rome, meanwhile, there was debate about whether Caesar and Pompey should give up their armies at the same time; the Senate asked each of them for a legion for a Parthian war, but the consul Marcellus handed them over to Pompey (8.52–55). The eighth book ends here; the story continues in Caesar’s Civil War.

t: 49 BC: Italy and Spain
intro:
The Civil War, after the first two books of Caesar’s second great account, the Civil War (Bellum civile). In January 49 BC the Senate passed its final decree against Caesar, and the tribunes who stood by him, Marcus Antonius and Quintus Cassius, fled to him at Ravenna. Caesar set out with the thirteenth legion; in two months all Italy was his, and Pompey crossed from Brundisium to Greece.

Caesar then did not follow Pompey but turned west: he left the siege of Massilia to his legates, and in Spain, at Ilerda, he forced Pompey’s legates Afranius and Petreius to surrender by manoeuvre, almost without a battle. In the same year Curio fell in Africa. In the Civil War Caesar argues his own case: he stresses that he repeatedly offered peace and showed clemency to prisoners.

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017); the Roman calendar was then almost two months ahead, so “10 January” was in reality in late November. Caesar does not mention the Rubicon; the crossing is described by Suetonius and Plutarch.

s.d: 23–25 November 50 BC (10–12 January 49 BC in the Roman calendar)
s.t:
The consuls only with great difficulty allowed Caesar’s letters to be read in the Senate. Pompey, Scipio, Cato and the consul Lentulus took a hard line; the Senate ordered Caesar to disband his army by a set date or be regarded as an enemy of the state. When the tribunes protested, the Senate passed the final decree that the magistrates should see to it that the state came to no harm; Antonius and Cassius fled to Caesar at Ravenna (1.1–5).

Before his soldiers Caesar listed the wrongs done by his opponents and asked them to defend their general’s honour; the soldiers of the thirteenth legion cried out that they were ready to defend their general and the tribunes. With this legion Caesar marched to Ariminum, where he met the tribunes (1.7–8). Caesar does not mention the boundary river, the Rubicon; according to Suetonius it was at the crossing that he said “the die is cast” (Caesar 32).

img.c: Silver denarius of Caesar from 49–48 BC: an elephant tramples a serpent, below CAESAR; struck by the mint travelling with the army (found in England).

s.t:
Caesar took Pisaurum, Fanum, Ancona and Auximum one after another; panic broke out in Rome, and the consul Lentulus fled (1.11–14). Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus held Corfinium with about twenty cohorts. Caesar invested the town with the twelfth and thirteenth legions. Domitius secretly planned to flee, but his soldiers found out, seized him and handed him over to Caesar (1.16–20).

Caesar protected the senators, knights and tribunes brought before him from the insults of his soldiers and let them go; according to Caesar he spoke only a few words to them, reproaching them for having been ungrateful for his favours. Domitius’ soldiers he took into his own army under oath (1.22–23). This was the first great occasion on which he could stress his clemency (clementia).

From Corfinium Caesar hurried with six legions to Brundisium, where Pompey had gone with the consuls and most of his army; the consuls had already crossed to Dyrrachium with part of the army. Caesar wanted to block the harbour mouth: on both sides of the shore, where the water was shallow, he had moles built, and in the deeper part he joined rafts thirty feet square, anchored at their four corners, covered them with earth and raised towers on them (1.25). Pompey built towers on large merchant ships to hinder the work.

After nine days the ships that had carried the consuls returned. Pompey embarked quietly at night, having barricaded the streets between the houses and blocked them with trenches and sharpened stakes; the townspeople signalled to Caesar’s soldiers from the rooftops. The Romans got in with ladders, but apart from two ships full of men Pompey’s fleet escaped (1.27–28). Without a fleet Caesar could not follow, so he decided first to take Spain, Pompey’s strongest province (1.29).

calc.src: According to Cicero’s letters and Caesar, Caesar left Corfinium on 21 February by the Roman calendar (2 January Julian) and reached Brundisium on 9 March (18 January): about 16½ days with two rest days; about 460 km according to Ramsey and Raaflaub (1.25; Cicero, Ad Atticum IX.13A).

s.t:
In Rome Caesar told the Senate that he had always sought the lawful way, and asked for envoys to be sent to Pompey, but no one would go (1.32–33). He then set out for Spain. The people of Massilia shut their gates against him and sided with Pompey; soon Domitius, whom Caesar had released at Corfinium, arrived and took over the defence of the town (1.34–36).

At Arelate Caesar had twelve warships built, in thirty days from the felling of the timber; he gave the fleet to Decimus Brutus and the siege on land to Gaius Trebonius with three legions (1.36). Brutus’ smaller fleet, manned with picked soldiers, grappled the enemy ships and defeated the Massiliots (1.56–58), and then won a second sea battle too (2.3–7). Trebonius built a ramp, later a six-storey brick tower and a covered siege gallery; the town finally surrendered when Caesar returned from Spain. Domitius escaped by ship (2.1–22).
