Pompey’s legates in Spain, Lucius Afranius and Marcus Petreius, were encamped with five legions at Ilerda on the river Sicoris (Segre); the third legate, Marcus Varro, held the further province (1.38). Caesar arrived with nine hundred horse. In a five-hour fight for a hill both sides claimed victory (1.43–47). Then a storm and flood swept away both bridges over the Sicoris and cut Caesar’s army off from supplies; the price of grain soared, and in Rome Afranius’ victory was celebrated (1.48–53).

Caesar then had boats built of the kind he had seen in Britain: wickerwork on a light frame covered with hides; he had them carried twenty-two miles on wagons, crossed, and built a bridge in two days (1.54). He had channels dug from the Sicoris to make a ford. Afranius and Petreius wanted to withdraw towards the Iberus (Ebro) and Celtiberia; Caesar’s soldiers crossed by the ford and cut them off by a difficult roundabout route. Caesar did not want a battle: he cut the enemy off from water. The soldiers of the two camps began to fraternise; Petreius then had the Caesarians found in his camp massacred and made his men take a new oath (1.59–76). Finally Afranius and Petreius surrendered. Caesar’s condition was that the army be disbanded: those with homes in Spain were released at once, the rest at the river Varus (1.84–87). Then Varro surrendered too, and Corduba and Gades went over to Caesar (2.17–21).

s.n: Utica and the Bagradas (the line shows Curio’s route from Sicily)
s.t:
Gaius Scribonius Curio, who had supported Caesar as tribune, crossed from Sicily to Africa with two legions and five hundred horse; Publius Attius Varus held the province there for Pompey. He landed at Anquillaria and marched towards Utica; he camped at the old Castra Cornelia, where Scipio Africanus had once encamped, and defeated Varus (2.23–35).

He then heard that King Juba of Numidia was approaching, but believed that only his general Saburra was coming with a small force. At the river Bagradas Saburra lured him onto the plain by a feigned retreat, where the king’s army surrounded the exhausted Romans. When Curio saw that all was lost, he declared that having lost the army entrusted to him by Caesar he would not return to Caesar’s sight, and he fell fighting. Of the survivors few reached the ships; most of those who surrendered to Varus were put to death by Juba (2.37–44).

t: 48 BC: Dyrrachium and Pharsalus
intro:
The third book of the Civil War tells of the decisive campaign against Pompey. Caesar became consul for 48 BC and in winter, in spite of Pompey’s fleet, crossed to Epirus. At Dyrrachium he was defeated in months of siege warfare fought with lines of earthworks, but he withdrew to Thessaly and won a decisive victory at Pharsalus. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered.

In this book too Caesar stresses his own moderation and his opponents’ overconfidence: he describes how Pompey’s men argued before the battle over the offices they would hold after victory, and how in Pompey’s camp tables were found laid for a victory feast.

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017); the Roman calendar was then about two months ahead: the battle of Pharsalus was on 9 August in the Roman calendar but in reality on 7 June. The exact site of the battlefield of Pharsalus is disputed; the marker shows the town.

s.d: 6 November 49 BC (4 January 48 BC in the Roman calendar)
s.t:
As dictator Caesar held the consular elections and was elected consul with Publius Servilius, since the laws allowed re-election after ten years (3.1). He stayed eleven days in Rome and then went to Brundisium. Twelve legions and all the cavalry had gathered there, but there were only enough ships to carry barely fifteen thousand legionaries and five hundred horse; the legions had been thinned by the Gallic wars, the long march from Spain and the unhealthy autumn in Apulia (3.2).

Pompey had spent a year gathering his forces: he raised nine legions of Roman citizens, his fleet and cavalry were far larger, and he had grain collected from Greece, Asia and Egypt (3.3–5). On 4 January by the Roman calendar Caesar set sail with seven legions (3.6).

s.n: Oricum (Orikum) – the landing was at Palaeste by the Ceraunian rocks
s.t:
Next day Caesar landed among the Ceraunian rocks near Palaeste, in a quiet bay, without losing a single ship. Pompey’s admiral, Bibulus, was at Corcyra; when he caught the returning ships, he took thirty and burned them with their crews, furious at his own negligence (3.6–8).

That same night Caesar marched on Oricum; the townspeople would not fight against a Roman consul and opened the gates. Apollonia received him too, and soon other towns submitted (3.11–12). Caesar sent Vibullius Rufus to Pompey with peace proposals, but Pompey hurried to Dyrrachium by forced marches and got there before Caesar (3.10–13).

For most of the winter the two armies faced each other on either bank of the river Apsus. Caesar waited in vain for Marcus Antonius and Quintus Fufius Calenus to cross from Brundisium with the remaining legions; Pompey’s fleet guarded the sea (3.13–25). At last they set out with a south wind; the Pompeians chased them, but the wind changed, Antonius’ ships put in safely at the harbour of Nymphaeum near Lissus, and several of the pursuing ships were wrecked on the rocks (3.26–27).

Antonius brought four legions and eight hundred horse. Pompey tried to prevent the two armies from uniting, but Caesar marched to Antonius and joined forces with him (3.29–30).

By a long and difficult detour Caesar got between Pompey and Dyrrachium; Pompey encamped by the sea on a height called Petra, where his ships could supply him (3.41–42). Caesar then began a strange undertaking: he built forts from hill to hill and started to enclose Pompey’s larger army with a line of earthworks. Pompey answered with an inner line of twenty-four forts, fifteen miles in circuit (3.43–44). For lack of grain Caesar’s soldiers baked bread from a root called chara mixed with milk; when the Pompeians mocked their hunger, they threw such loaves over to them (3.48).

One day there was fighting at six places; in the defence of one fort, according to Caesar, a hundred and twenty holes were counted in the shield of the centurion Cassius Scaeva (some manuscripts give two hundred and thirty); Caesar rewarded him with two hundred thousand sesterces and promoted him to chief centurion (3.53). Finally Pompey broke out with sixty cohorts at the unfinished southern end of the lines by the sea. Caesar’s counter-attack failed: he lost nine hundred and sixty soldiers, thirty-two tribunes and centurions, and thirty-two standards (3.62–71). According to Suetonius and Plutarch Caesar then remarked that the enemy would have won that day if they had had a commander who knew how to win. Caesar addressed his soldiers and withdrew towards Apollonia (3.73–75).

Caesar sent the baggage ahead at night, crossed the river Genusus, and on the fourth day Pompey gave up the pursuit (3.75–77). At Apollonia he left the wounded, paid the troops, left garrisons at Apollonia, Lissus and Oricum, and set out for Thessaly to join Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus, who was facing Pompey’s father-in-law Scipio in Macedonia (3.78–79).

Gomphi, the first town of Thessaly, shut its gates against him on hearing of the defeat at Dyrrachium. Caesar took it in a single afternoon and let his soldiers plunder it; neighbouring Metropolis, hearing this, opened its gates without a fight, and all Thessaly except Larisa submitted (3.80–81).

s.n: Pharsalus (Farsala) – exact site of the battlefield disputed
s.d: 7 June 48 BC (9 August in the Roman calendar)
s.t:
Pompey joined forces with Scipio. In their camp, according to Caesar, they were already disputing the priesthoods and consulships to be shared out after the victory (3.82–83). Pompey had about a hundred and ten cohorts, some forty-five thousand men, and seven thousand horse; Caesar eighty cohorts, about twenty-two thousand men, and a thousand horse (3.84–89). As Pompey meant to outflank his right wing with the cavalry, Caesar took one cohort from the third line of each legion, formed a fourth line of six cohorts and hid it behind his right wing (3.89).

The battle was begun by the former chief centurion Crastinus, who charged first with a hundred and twenty volunteers, crying that he would fight that day so that Caesar, alive or dead, would be grateful to him; he fell in the fighting (3.91, 3.99). When Pompey’s cavalry charged the right wing, the cohorts of the fourth line rushed at them so fiercely that they fled, and then took the Pompeian left in the rear (3.93). Pompey withdrew to his camp and then fled. In his camp Caesar’s soldiers found arbours, silver plate set out and tents laid with fresh turf (3.96).

According to Caesar he lost about two hundred soldiers and thirty centurions; he puts the enemy dead at about fifteen thousand and those who surrendered at more than twenty-four thousand, and took a hundred and eighty standards and nine eagles (3.99). The site of the battlefield – north or south of the river Enipeus – is disputed by scholars.

Pompey fled through Larisa to the sea and sailed by way of Amphipolis, Mytilene and Cyprus to Egypt. There the boy king Ptolemy stood with his army at Pelusium against his sister Cleopatra. Pompey asked to be received as a former friend of the king’s father. The king’s advisers, however, feared that Pompey might win over the army, or that they would draw Caesar’s anger upon themselves; they sent Achillas, the king’s general, and Lucius Septimius, once an officer of Pompey’s, to fetch him in a small boat, and as he was about to land, they killed him (3.96–104). According to Ramsey and Raaflaub this was on 28 September by the Roman calendar, in reality on 25 July.

A few days later Caesar arrived at Alexandria from Rhodes with two legions and eight hundred horse, and there learned of Pompey’s death (3.106). The sequel is shown in the walk on the Alexandrian War.

img.c: Marble portrait of Pompey, made c. AD 30–50 (Copenhagen, Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek).

t: 48–47 BC: the Alexandrian War
intro:
Caesar arrived at Alexandria with a small army while pursuing Pompey, and for months had to defend himself in one quarter of the city against the Egyptian royal army and the population. The war begins in the last chapters of the Civil War and is continued in the Alexandrian War, whose author is uncertain; in antiquity it was attributed to Hirtius or Oppius.

After street fighting in the city, struggles around the island of Pharos and the causeway linking it to the harbour (the Heptastadion), an attack on the water supply and naval battles, Caesar defeated King Ptolemy in the Nile delta, after joining the relief army of Mithridates of Pergamum.

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017). The battle by the Nile took place on one of the branches of the delta; its exact site is unknown.

s.t:
Caesar arrived with about three thousand two hundred legionaries and eight hundred horse. When he landed, the royal soldiers grumbled because he had the consular fasces carried before him, which they thought an insult to the king’s majesty (3.106). Because of the Etesian winds he could not sail away (3.107). He decided that, in the name of the Roman people and as consul, he would settle the dispute between Ptolemy and his sister Cleopatra, and ordered both to disband their armies.

The king’s guardian, the eunuch Pothinus, summoned Achillas with the royal army – about twenty thousand men and two thousand horse – to Alexandria. Caesar held part of the city, and since he could not defend the whole harbour, he had the Egyptian ships burned and then seized the island of Pharos with its lighthouse so that he could be supplied from the sea (3.108–112). He had Pothinus executed; with this – he writes – the Alexandrian War began.

img.c: Bronze coin of Cleopatra VII, Alexandria, 51–31 BC (Harvard, Arthur M. Sackler Museum).

s.n: Alexandria – Pharos island and the causeway
s.t:
Ptolemy’s younger sister Arsinoë had Achillas killed and put the eunuch Ganymedes at the head of the army. The Alexandrians led seawater through the channels into the cisterns of the quarter held by Caesar; Caesar’s soldiers dug wells and in a single night found plenty of fresh water (Alexandrian War 4–9). According to the author Alexandria was almost fireproof, because the houses were built of stone without timber or beams.

In sea fights the Rhodian Euphranor distinguished himself (10–16). Caesar took the town on the island of Pharos, but when he tried to seize the causeway as well, the Alexandrians attacked his soldiers in the rear. So many crowded onto Caesar’s ship that it sank; Caesar escaped by swimming to the ships further off. In this fight about four hundred legionaries and slightly more sailors and rowers perished (17–21).

The Alexandrians asked Caesar to release King Ptolemy, because they were weary of the rule of Arsinoë and Ganymedes; Caesar let him go, but the king at once made war on him (23–24). Meanwhile Mithridates of Pergamum, whom Caesar had sent to Syria and Cilicia for troops, reached Egypt overland with a large army and took Pelusium by storm (26). He also won against the king’s forces and pressed on along the Nile towards Alexandria.

s.n: The battle by the Nile – in the delta, exact site unknown
s.t:
When the king had marched off with his army against Mithridates, Caesar set out from Alexandria by ship at night to join Mithridates. The king’s camp lay on a height, protected on one side by the Nile and on the other by a marsh. Caesar’s soldiers got up at a neglected, steep point and came upon the enemy’s rear; the camp was taken and many fell. The king fled to a ship, but the overloaded ship sank and he drowned in the river (28–31).

Caesar at once hurried with the cavalry to Alexandria, where the inhabitants met him as suppliants carrying their sacred emblems and surrendered. Caesar entrusted the kingdom to Cleopatra and her younger brother, the younger Ptolemy, removed Arsinoë, and left Roman legions in Egypt (32–33). He then set out overland for Syria with the sixth legion.

t: 47 BC: Zela
intro:
After the Alexandrian War Caesar did not return at once to Rome but settled the eastern provinces. His most urgent task was Pharnaces, king of the Bosporus and son of the great Mithridates, who had taken advantage of Pompey’s fall to defeat Caesar’s legate Domitius Calvinus and seize Pontus. The second part of the Alexandrian War describes the journey through Syria, Cilicia and Cappadocia to Zela.

The battle of Zela was decided in a few hours at the end of a campaign of less than five days. According to Suetonius and Plutarch Caesar then wrote the famous three words in a letter: “I came, I saw, I conquered” (veni, vidi, vici); the Alexandrian War does not mention it.

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017).

s.t: When Caesar reached Syria from Egypt he heard that matters in Rome were going badly, but he decided first to settle the provinces he passed through, so as not to leave internal quarrels behind him (Alexandrian War 65). According to Ramsey and Raaflaub he reached Antioch on 3 April. He entrusted Syria to his kinsman Sextus Caesar and went by ship to Cilicia (66).

At Tarsus, the most famous and strongest town of Cilicia, he held an assembly of the towns of the province. He then marched by forced marches through Cappadocia, spent two days at Mazaca and came to Comana, where he gave the priesthood of the ancient and much revered shrine of Bellona to the Bithynian Lycomedes. He confirmed Ariobarzanes on the throne of Cappadocia (66).

On the way Deiotarus, tetrarch of Gallograecia and king of Lesser Armenia, who had fought on Pompey’s side, came to him in the dress of a defendant and begged pardon. Caesar forgave him but warned him that his services did not absolve him of his faults; he gave him back his royal dress and ordered him to join with his legion and cavalry (67–68).

From Mazaca Caesar marched towards Pontus. The author writes frankly about his army: the veteran sixth legion, which he had brought from Alexandria, numbered less than a thousand men because of so much fighting and marching; to this were added Deiotarus’ legion and two others that had taken part in Domitius’ battle (69). According to Ramsey and Raaflaub he reached Sebasteia on 13 May, where he gathered the four legions.

Envoys of Pharnaces brought a golden crown and claimed that the king had never fought against Caesar. Caesar replied that Pharnaces must leave Pontus, release the prisoners and restore what he had taken from Romans and their allies. Pharnaces made promises and played for time, knowing that Caesar was being called back to Rome (69–71).

s.d: 20–21 May 47 BC (1–2 August in the Roman calendar)
s.t:
Zela was a fortified town of Pontus, on an artificial mound. Three miles from it Pharnaces stood on a hill, at the place where his father Mithridates had once defeated Triarius and the Romans in a fortunate battle (72). Caesar camped five miles away and then at night, leaving the baggage behind, seized with the legions the hill that Mithridates had once used; a valley about a mile wide separated the two camps (73).

At dawn Pharnaces drew up his line. Caesar at first thought it a show, but the king came down into the valley and attacked uphill, up the steep slope, against the Romans who were building the rampart; according to the author he was encouraged by the old good fortune of the place, by omens and by the small number of the Romans (74). Caesar recalled the soldiers from their work; the scythed chariots threw the ranks into confusion, but missiles stopped them. The decision came on the right wing, where the sixth legion stood; the enemy was driven down the hill, the centre and left also prevailed, the camp was taken, and Pharnaces fled with a few horsemen (75–76).

According to the author Caesar was incredibly pleased to have finished so great a war so quickly. He gave the booty to the soldiers, sent the sixth legion to Italy for rewards and honours, and left two legions in Pontus (77).

calc.src: According to Ramsey and Raaflaub Caesar left Mazaca on 7 May, reached Sebasteia on 13 May and Zela on 20 May: about 13 days, including the gathering of the legions. The source does not give the exact numbers; the sixth legion had fewer than a thousand men (69).

t: 47–46 BC: Africa and Thapsus
intro:
After Pharsalus the Pompeians gathered in Africa: Metellus Scipio, Labienus, Afranius, Petreius and Cato, with King Juba of Numidia as their ally, whose cavalry and war elephants were a formidable force. Caesar crossed from Sicily at the beginning of winter with a small army; for months he was in a difficult position around Ruspina, until reinforcements arrived.

The author of the African War is unknown; from the text he was probably one of Caesar’s officers who saw much of the campaign himself. He often writes about the soldiers’ daily life and stresses Caesar’s skill and care.

Dates are Julian (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017); the Roman calendar was then almost three months ahead: the battle of Thapsus was on 6 April in the Roman calendar but in reality on 7 February. Caesar himself ended this confusion by introducing the Julian calendar from 1 January 45 BC.

s.t: Caesar arrived at Lilybaeum by long marches and wanted to embark at once, although he had only one legion of recruits and barely six hundred horse there. He had his tent pitched right by the shore so that everyone could see he did not mean to wait a single day (African War 1). Finally he embarked with six legions and two thousand horse, and since he did not know where a safe harbour would be, he gave the ship captains no written orders about their destination (2).

Part of the fleet was scattered; Caesar reached the neighbourhood of Hadrumetum with few men; Gaius Considius held it with two legions. Caesar tried to bring him to talks, but his envoy was killed; not wanting to waste time on the town, he marched on (3–5). According to Suetonius he stumbled on landing but turned the bad omen round by saying: “I hold you, Africa!” (Caesar 59); the African War does not mention this.

Caesar encamped at Ruspina and then at Leptis; the scattered transports slowly came in (6–11). On 17 October he went foraging with thirty cohorts, four hundred horse and a hundred and fifty archers, when he was surrounded by the huge army of Labienus and the Pacidei brothers, mostly cavalry with light infantry mixed among them (12–14).

Labienus rode bareheaded in the front line and mocked Caesar’s recruits: “Well, recruit, how bold you are! Has he fooled you too with his talk?” – whereupon a veteran, a former soldier of the tenth legion, showed that he was no recruit and brought down Labienus’ horse with his javelin (16). Caesar extended his line as far as possible and had every second cohort face about, so that with a line facing two ways he broke out of the ring and withdrew to Ruspina (17–18). He then surrounded Ruspina with fortifications and waited for reinforcements.

Scipio arrived, then Juba too; after the arrival of the thirteenth and fourteenth, later the ninth and tenth legions Caesar moved onto the hills and camped near Uzita. For weeks there were mutual offers of battle, building of earthworks and cavalry skirmishes (24–66). To accustom his soldiers and horses to the elephants, Caesar had elephants brought from Italy: the soldiers learned where the animal was vulnerable, and the horses got used to their smell and noise (72).

s.d: 5–7 February 46 BC (4–6 April in the Roman calendar)
s.t:
Caesar marched by night from Aggar to Thapsus and invested the town, which Vergilius held. Scipio followed and tried to reach the town over a narrow strip of land between a lagoon and the sea, but Caesar had already built a fort there with three cohorts; so Scipio marched round the lagoon and took up position near Caesar’s camp (79–80). Caesar drew up his army in three lines and placed cohorts of the fifth legion on both wings against the elephants (81).

Caesar was still hesitating, but on the right wing a trumpeter sounded the charge without orders, and the cohorts surged forward; Caesar, seeing that the soldiers could not be held back, gave the watchword “Good Luck!”, mounted and charged himself (82). The missiles of the slingers and archers terrified the elephants, which turned and trampled their own ranks; a soldier of the fifth legion stabbed at an elephant trampling a fallen comrade until it fled (83–84). Caesar’s veterans – in spite of Caesar’s pleas – cut down the fugitives even when they laid down their arms and surrendered (85). According to the author the enemy lost about ten thousand men, Caesar about fifty; sixty-four elephants were captured (86).

Marcus Cato commanded at Utica. At the news of the defeat the fleeing horsemen plundered the neighbourhood; Cato gave money to the fugitives so that they could sail away. When he saw that the inhabitants did not want to fight on, he ran himself through with his sword; the doctors bandaged the wound, but he tore it open and died. Out of gratitude the people of Utica gave him a splendid funeral (88). Caesar entered a few days later; he imposed heavy fines on the Roman traders who had supported Pompey (89–90).

img.c: Bronze bust found at Volubilis (1st century AD, Rabat), usually identified as Cato the Younger.

s.h: Zama: the end of Juba and Petreius
s.t:
Juba fled with Petreius to Zama, his royal town, but the inhabitants shut the gates against him and sent envoys to Caesar (91–92). After a banquet in a country villa the king and Petreius fought each other with swords so as to die honourably: Juba killed Petreius and then had a slave kill him (94). Afranius and Faustus Sulla were captured and killed (95). Scipio, fleeing by sea, was overtaken near Hippo Regius by the fleet of Publius Sittius; he ran himself through with his sword (96).

At Zama Caesar sold the king’s property, made Numidia a province and then sailed back by way of Utica and Sardinia; he reached Rome on 26 May by the Julian reckoning (97–98). He then celebrated four triumphs: over Gaul, Egypt, Pontus and Africa.

img.c: Silver denarius of King Juba I of Numidia inscribed REX IVBA, with a Neo-Punic legend on the reverse (60–46 BC).

t: 46–45 BC: Spain and Munda
intro:
The last campaign of the Civil War took place in Spain. Pompey’s sons, Gnaeus and Sextus, with Labienus and Attius Varus, raised a large army in the further province, in the towns of Baetica. Caesar arrived from Rome at the end of 46 BC after a rapid journey; the winter campaign was filled with sieges, cruel reprisals against towns and skirmishes, and was decided at Munda, perhaps Caesar’s hardest battle.

The Spanish War is the least polished of the accounts attached to Caesar’s name; its author is unknown, probably an officer who took part in the campaign; its style is uneven, and the text breaks off in the middle of Caesar’s speech at Hispalis. Even so, many details are known only from it.

From 1 January 45 BC Caesar’s new Julian calendar was in force, so the dates of the campaign are also Julian dates (Ramsey and Raaflaub 2017). The site of Munda is disputed; the marker shows one of the proposed sites, as in the map data.

s.t: Caesar was in Rome as dictator when he heard that Gnaeus Pompey was winning over the towns of Spain one after another and that the legates he had left there could not cope. He set out in great haste (Spanish War 1–2). According to Strabo and Suetonius he travelled from Rome to Obulco in twenty-seven days; Ramsey and Raaflaub reckon this at about 2,100 km, some 78 km a day. This was the journey of Caesar and a small escort, not of an army; the legion calculator computes for armies, so a comparison here would not be meaningful.

Caesar first sent troops to relieve Ulia and then marched against Corduba; they fought for days over the bridge across the Baetis (Guadalquivir), with heavy losses on both sides (3–5). He then set out at night against Ategua, one of the strongest Pompeian places, and besieged it; Gnaeus Pompey camped nearby but could not relieve it (6–9).

During the siege the Pompeian garrison massacred the pro-Caesarian inhabitants and threw them from the walls (15). The town finally surrendered on 19 February, and the soldiers hailed Caesar as imperator (19). Pompey then had seventy-four citizens suspected of favouring Caesar executed at Ucubi (21).

s.n: Munda – site disputed (the marker shows Cerro de las Camorras)
s.t:
After weeks of skirmishing Pompey camped beside the town of Munda on a height and drew up his army on the slope; in front lay level ground and a stream. According to the author Pompey had thirteen legions, six thousand light infantry and almost as many auxiliaries; Caesar eighty cohorts and eight thousand horse (27–30).

The battle was hard; on the right wing the tenth legion pressed the enemy, whereupon Pompey moved a legion over to his left, but this weakened his line; the cavalry broke in too, and the Pompeian army fled (30–31). According to the author the Pompeians lost more than thirty thousand men, among them Labienus and Attius Varus; on Caesar’s side there were about a thousand dead and five hundred wounded; thirteen eagles were captured (31). According to Plutarch Caesar said afterwards that he had often fought for victory, but now for the first time for his life (Caesar 56).

Caesar invested those who had fled into Munda; the soldiers built a rampart from the bodies of the dead, their shields and javelins, and set the severed heads on sword points facing the town (32).

After Munda Caesar marched to Corduba. Fighting broke out in the town between the Pompeian fugitives and the inhabitants; the pro-Caesarians let Caesar’s soldiers in. Scapula, a Pompeian partisan who had led the revolt, killed himself on a pyre. According to the author twenty-two thousand people perished, many of them also outside the walls (33–34).

s.h: Hispalis: the end of the war
s.t:
Caesar marched against Hispalis; Lusitanian troops had seized the town, but Caesar retook it (35–36). Gnaeus Pompey, wounded, fled to Carteia and put to sea from there with twenty ships; Caesar’s admiral Didius pursued him and burned his ships. Pompey hid in a cave, where he was found and killed; his head was taken to Hispalis and put on public display (37–39). According to Ramsey and Raaflaub this happened near Lauro on 9 April. Sextus Pompey escaped.

Caesar held an assembly at Hispalis and made a speech to the inhabitants: he listed what he had done for Spain as quaestor, praetor and consul, and reproached them for their ingratitude. The text of the Spanish War breaks off in the middle of his speech (42). Caesar returned to Rome in the autumn and in October celebrated a triumph over Spain; barely half a year later, on the Ides of March 44 BC, he was murdered.

img.c: Silver denarius of Caesar from early 44 BC, with his wreathed head and CAESAR DICT PERPETVO (“dictator in perpetuity”).

t: Hannibal’s march from Spain to Italy (218 BC)
intro:
In the spring of 218 BC the Carthaginian general Hannibal set out from New Carthage (Carthago Nova, today Cartagena) in the Iberian peninsula to attack Rome overland, across the Alps; this began the Second Punic War. His march is described in most detail by the Greek historian Polybius (Histories, book III), who in his own words questioned eyewitnesses still living and went over the Alpine route himself (3.48). Livy (book XXI) differs from him in part; where it matters, we note it.

Polybius gives distances in stades; he writes that the stretch between Emporium and the Rhone had been carefully measured by the Romans and marked with milestones every eight stades (3.39.8). We have reckoned the km values with a stade of about 185 m. The main uncertainty: Polybius’ description does not settle which pass Hannibal used to cross the Alps; scholars propose several. On the Alpine stretch the line therefore shows only one of the roads of the later Roman network, for orientation. The numbers in brackets give Polybius’ book, chapter and section.

s.t:
Hannibal wintered at New Carthage. During the winter he provided for the defence of Africa and Spain: he sent Iberian troops to Africa, brought Africans to Spain, and put his brother Hasdrubal in charge of Spain. In early spring he led the troops out of their winter quarters (3.33–34), with about ninety thousand foot and twelve thousand horse (3.35.1).

Polybius sets out the distances of the march: from New Carthage to the Ebro 2,600 stades, from there to Emporium 1,600, from Emporium to Narbo about 600, from Narbo to the crossing of the Rhone about 1,600, from there along the river to the foot of the Alpine pass 1,400, and across the Alps to the plain of the Po about 1,200 stades; about nine thousand stades in all (3.39). That is about 1,650 km.

img.c: Remains of the Carthaginian city wall of Carthago Nova (Cartagena), 3rd century BC.

s.n: The Ebro (the marker shows Dertosa, Tortosa)
s.t: The Ebro was the boundary fixed in the Roman–Carthaginian agreement of 226 BC. Hannibal crossed it and quickly, but at the cost of severe fighting and losses, subdued the Ilergetes, Bargusii, Aerenosii and Andosini as far as the Pyrenees (3.35.2–3). According to Polybius the road from New Carthage to the Ebro was 2,600 stades (about 480 km). The text does not say where he crossed the river; the marker shows Dertosa only for orientation.

He put Hanno in charge of the conquered region with ten thousand foot and a thousand horse, and left with him the heavy baggage of the army. With the rest of the army, now lightened of its baggage – about fifty thousand foot and nine thousand horse – he set out through the Pyrenees towards the Rhone (3.35.4–7). From the Ebro to Emporium, at the coastal end of the Pyrenees, it was 1,600 stades (about 300 km). According to Livy, at the Pyrenees Hannibal sent home several thousand Iberian soldiers who did not want to leave their country (Liv. 21.23).

From Emporium to Narbo it was about 600 stades, and from there to the crossing of the Rhone about 1,600 stades (3.39.8). Polybius notes that by his time the Romans had carefully measured this stretch and marked it with milestones every eight stades – this is the later Via Domitia. Hannibal marched “keeping the Sardinian Sea on his right” and reached the Rhone unexpectedly (3.41.7).

s.n: The Rhone crossing (site disputed; the marker shows Avennio, Avignon)
s.h: Crossing the Rhone; the elephants on rafts
s.t:
Hannibal crossed the Rhone where the river still flows in a single stream, about four days’ march from the sea (3.42.1). The site cannot be fixed exactly; the marker shows only the stretch that comes into question. He bought up the canoes and boats of the local people and had new ones built of timber. On the third night he sent Hanno son of Bomilcar with a detachment about 200 stades upstream, where an island divides the river; they crossed there on rafts and fell on the rear of the Gauls gathered on the far bank, while the main army crossed in boats, with the horses swimming behind them (3.42–43).

The hardest task was getting the thirty-seven elephants across (3.42.11). From pairs of rafts lashed together, about fifty feet wide, they built a jetty about two hundred feet long, covered with earth, running from the bank into the water, so that the animals would think it was dry land; from its end the detachable rafts were towed across by boats. Some frightened elephants jumped into the water; their drivers drowned, but the elephants got across holding their trunks above the water (3.46).

Meanwhile the consul Publius Cornelius Scipio had arrived by sea at Massalia; by the time he reached the crossing with his army, Hannibal had left it three days earlier (3.41, 3.49.1).

After four days’ march Hannibal came to the district called the “Island”: a fertile, populous area between the Rhone and another river, which Polybius compares to the Nile delta, with mountains on its third side. In the manuscripts the other river is called Skaras; most scholars think of the Isère (3.49.5–7). The marker therefore shows only the neighbourhood of the confluence of the Rhone and the Isère.

Here two brothers were disputing the kingship; Hannibal helped the elder, who in return gave the army corn, new weapons, warm clothing and footwear, and escorted them as far as the mountains (3.49.8–13). From here, after ten days’ march, about 800 stades along the river, the ascent into the Alps began (3.50.1).

s.n: The Alps – the pass is unknown (the marker shows the Mont Genèvre pass, one of the proposed routes)
s.t:
At the beginning of the Alpine ascent the Allobroges occupied the heights above the pass and attacked the column in a narrow defile; many horses and pack animals fell to their deaths before Hannibal drove them off from higher ground (3.50–51). Later the natives living near the pass came to meet him with olive branches and wreaths, feigning friendship; they provided guides, but two days later they attacked the army in a steep defile, rolling down rocks and throwing stones. Hannibal spent that night by a strong, bare rock (in Polybius’ word a “white rock”) (3.52–53).

On the ninth day he reached the top of the pass, where he rested two days to gather the stragglers. As the setting of the Pleiades was already near – in Polybius’ time this fell at the end of October or the beginning of November –, there was already snow on the summits; Hannibal showed his dispirited soldiers the plain of Italy spread out below (3.53.9–54.3).

Which pass he crossed cannot be decided from Polybius’ description; scholars argue, among others, for the Col de la Traversette, the Mont Cenis, the Col du Clapier, the Little St Bernard and the Mont Genèvre. The marker shows one of these, not a known site.

s.n: The plain of the Po: the city of the Taurini (probably the later Augusta Taurinorum, Turin)
s.t:
On the way down a landslip had carried away the path for about one and a half stades. The detour had to be abandoned because of fresh snow; Hannibal had the path widened along the cliff. In one day it was made passable for the pack animals and the horses, with the Numidians working in relays; but getting the elephants across took three days, and by then the animals were almost dead from hunger (3.54.4–55.8). Three days later he reached the plain (3.56.1).

Polybius’ summary: the march from New Carthage had taken five months, the crossing of the Alps fifteen days. Hannibal came down into the plain of the Po, in the territory of the Insubres; according to his own inscribed column on the Lacinian promontory (near Croton), twelve thousand African and eight thousand Iberian foot and no more than six thousand horse survived (3.56.1–4). He had left the Rhone with thirty-eight thousand foot and more than eight thousand horse; he lost about half his army in the crossing of the Alps (3.60.5).

After a rest he attacked the Taurini, who were at odds with the Insubres and had rejected his alliance; he took their chief city in three days (3.60.8–9). According to Livy, all authors agree that Hannibal came down into the land of the Taurini (Liv. 21.38).

s.n: The Ticinus (the marker shows Ticinum, Pavia)
s.t: Publius Scipio, with part of the army that had sailed back from Massalia, crossed the Po, had a bridge built over the Ticinus, and advanced against Hannibal. The cavalry of the two armies met; the Numidian horsemen outflanked the Romans, and the Roman cavalry broke and fled. Scipio was severely wounded and withdrew across the Po (3.64–66). In another place Polybius writes that the wounded consul was saved by his son, then only about seventeen or eighteen – the later Scipio Africanus, who defeated Hannibal at Zama (10.3). The exact site of the battle is not known.

s.n: The Trebia (the marker shows Placentia, Piacenza)
s.t:
The second consul, Tiberius Sempronius Longus, marched up from Sicily and joined Scipio. The battle took place around the winter solstice, on a cold, snowy day: the Roman soldiers left the camp without breakfast and had to wade through the swollen Trebia, which was breast-high (3.72.3–4). Hannibal’s Numidian horsemen got into the Romans’ rear; the Roman wings were pressed back to the river. About ten thousand Romans broke through in close order and withdrew to Placentia; most of the rest perished. The cold and snow killed all of Hannibal’s elephants but one, and many men and horses too (3.73–74).

The following year Hannibal crossed the Apennines into Etruria and won another great victory at Lake Trasimene; in 216 BC he destroyed the Roman army at Cannae.

t: Scipio Africanus’ campaigns in Spain and Africa (210–202 BC)
intro:
In the Second Punic War, while Hannibal was fighting in Italy, Rome also suffered severe defeats in Spain: in 211 Publius Scipio and Gnaeus Scipio fell there. In 210 BC Publius Cornelius Scipio, son of the fallen general and only 24 years old, received an extraordinary command in Spain. In a few years he drove the Carthaginians out, then carried the war into Africa, and in 202 BC defeated Hannibal at Zama. This earned him the name Africanus.

Livy is detailed, but less accurate in military matters; scholars often consider the partly lost Polybius more reliable, who used the account of Scipio’s friend Laelius. Some dates (the fall of New Carthage in 210 or 209) are disputed, and the sites of several battles are uncertain. The numbers in brackets are Livy’s books and chapters.

s.t: Since no one came forward for the Spanish command, the assembly elected the young Scipio, who had until then been only an aedile. With 10,000 infantry, 1,000 cavalry and 30 ships he sailed from Ostia to Spain and landed at the Greek city of Emporiae; from there he marched by land to Tarraco (26.18–20).

At Tarraco he received the envoys of the Spanish allies and over the winter planned his bold venture: the three Carthaginian armies were camped far from one another and from New Carthage, the Carthaginians’ capital, treasury and arsenal in Spain, which was defended only by a weak garrison (26.41–42; Polybius 10.7–9).

Scipio arrived by land and with the fleet at the same time. He had learned from fishermen that the lagoon bordering the city on the north became fordable at ebb tide in the afternoons. While the main forces assaulted the walls from the isthmus, five hundred men waded across the shallow water to the undefended north wall; Scipio proclaimed that Neptune was showing them the way. The city was taken in a single day; besides the booty, the Spanish hostages fell into Scipio’s hands, and he generously sent them home (26.42–51; Polybius 10.8–19).

At Baecula Scipio attacked Hasdrubal Barca, Hannibal’s brother, who was camped on a height; climbing up on both flanks, he defeated him. But Hasdrubal got away with most of his army and his money, and set off over the Alps to Italy to help his brother – he fell there at the Metaurus in 207 (27.17–20). This Spanish victory was thus only a half success.

s.h: Ilipa: Spain is lost to Carthage
s.t: At Ilipa he faced the great army of Hasdrubal son of Gisgo and Mago. For days Scipio drew up in the same order, with the Roman legions in the centre; then on the decisive morning he reversed it, placing the legions on the wings and the Spanish allies in the centre, and attacked early, while the enemy were still hungry. The Carthaginian army broke up (28.12–16). With this Carthaginian rule in Spain came to an end; with Gades, the whole peninsula passed into Roman hands.

Scipio became consul in 205 and, despite the opposition of the senate, received Sicily with permission to cross to Africa. He organised an army of volunteers and legions made up of survivors of Cannae. In 204 he crossed from Lilybaeum to Africa with a large fleet, according to Livy about four hundred transports (29.24–26).

s.h: The burned camps and the Great Plains
s.t: He landed at the Fair Promontory and camped before Utica. Early in 203, feigning negotiations, he set fire at night to the camps of the Numidian king Syphax and Hasdrubal son of Gisgo, built of reeds and timber; according to Livy forty thousand perished (30.3–6) – certainly an exaggeration. Shortly after, on the Great Plains, he defeated their reorganised army; Syphax was captured (30.8–12). Carthage then recalled Hannibal from Italy.

s.n: Zama (the site of the battle is disputed; according to Livy near Naraggara)
s.t:
Before the battle the two generals met in person; Hannibal offered peace, but Scipio refused (30.29–31). Livy places the Roman camp near Naraggara (30.29), Polybius at a place called Margaron; the name ‘battle of Zama’ is later. Hannibal opened the battle with elephants, but the Romans left lanes in their ranks and the animals ran through them. In the end the cavalry of Laelius and Masinissa attacked Hannibal’s army in the rear (30.32–35).

According to Livy more than twenty thousand Carthaginians and allies fell, as many were captured, and about two thousand of the victors fell (30.35). Hannibal fled to Hadrumetum and himself advised peace. In 201 Carthage gave up Spain and its fleet and paid an indemnity for fifty years; Scipio held a triumph in Rome and took the name Africanus (30.37–45).

t: Marius’ war against the Cimbri and Teutones (105–101 BC)
intro:
At the end of the 2nd century BC the Cimbri and Teutones (with the Ambrones and Tigurini), who had migrated from the North Sea region, wandered for years through Gaul and the Alpine lands and defeated one Roman army after another; in 105 BC at Arausio Rome suffered one of its worst defeats. Gaius Marius, victor of the Jugurthine war, was therefore elected consul five times in a row between 104 and 100. In 102 BC Marius destroyed the Teutones and Ambrones at Aquae Sextiae, and in 101, together with Catulus, the Cimbri near Vercellae.

Our main source is Plutarch’s Life of Marius, which partly used the memoirs of Sulla (Catulus’ officer and later Marius’ enemy); it therefore disputes Marius’ merits. The figures (hundreds of thousands dead) are certainly exaggerated, and some sites (Marius’ camp on the Rhône, the ‘Raudine Plain’ at Vercellae) are disputed. The numbers in brackets are Plutarch’s chapters.

s.t: In 105 BC at Arausio on the Rhône the Cimbri destroyed two rival Roman armies, those of the proconsul Q. Servilius Caepio and the consul Cn. Mallius Maximus. According to the summary of Livy 80,000 soldiers and 40,000 camp followers fell (Per. 67). The panic in Rome was great; according to Plutarch this is why the people re-elected the absent Marius consul (11–12).

s.h: Marius’ canal and the Rhône camp
s.t: The Cimbri unexpectedly marched off towards Spain, so Marius could train his army for two years; he made the soldiers carry their own baggage (‘Marius’ mules’). To secure supplies from the sea he had a canal dug at the silted mouth of the Rhône, called after him Fossa Mariana (15). He pitched a strong camp by the Rhône and would not let his soldiers out to fight, so that they should get used to the sight of the enemy; the Teutones and Ambrones took six days to march past the camp, mockingly asking whether the Romans had any messages for their wives in Rome (18). The site of the camp is not known.

s.h: Aquae Sextiae: the destruction of the Ambrones and Teutones
s.t:
Marius followed the barbarians and at Aquae Sextiae pitched camp on a height poorly supplied with water. On the first day servants and soldiers who went down to the river for water clashed with the Ambrones, who were bathing and feasting; the Ligurian auxiliaries began the fight, and the Romans drove them beyond the river (19–20).

Two days later the Teutones attacked the hill. Claudius Marcellus with 3,000 men, lying in ambush, fell on their rear, and their army broke up. According to Plutarch more than a hundred thousand were killed or captured; the people of Massilia are said to have fenced their vineyards with the bones, and the soil was extraordinarily fertile for years from the bodies (20–21).

s.n: The valley of the Athesis (Adige), around Tridentum (Trento)
s.t: Meanwhile the Cimbri were heading over the Alps towards Italy. According to Plutarch they slid down the snowy slopes on their shields. The consul Q. Lutatius Catulus tried to hold them along the Athesis (Adige); the barbarians blocked the river with trees and rocks, and the Roman soldiers fled. Catulus took the eagle and went before them, so that the flight should be not a disgrace but a retreat led by the commander. The Cimbri overran the Po plain (23).

s.n: Vercellae (Vercelli; the site of the Raudine Plain is disputed)
s.t: Marius joined Catulus’ army. Boiorix, king of the Cimbri, asked when and where they should fight; they agreed on the third day and the plain of Vercellae, suitable both for the Roman cavalry and for the great mass of the Cimbri (25). According to Plutarch, following Sulla, Marius fought with 32,000 men and Catulus with 20,300; in the thick dust and the midday heat, which exhausted the northern warriors, the Cimbri were defeated. Their front ranks were chained together; their women, standing on the wagons, killed the fugitives, their children and themselves (25–27). According to Plutarch more than sixty thousand were captured and twice as many fell.

Marius and Catulus held a joint triumph. But they quarrelled over the glory: Catulus’ soldiers claimed that they had fought the decisive part of the battle and taken most of the captured standards (27). According to Plutarch the people called Marius the third founder of Rome (27). In 100 Marius became consul for the sixth time; his later career ended in civil war.

t: The revolt of Spartacus (73–71 BC)
intro:
In 73 BC some seventy or eighty gladiators escaped from a gladiatorial school at Capua; their leader became the Thracian Spartacus, with the Gauls Crixus and Oenomaus beside him. Masses of slaves and poor free men joined the fugitives, and for two years they marched up and down the length of Italy, defeating one praetorian and consular army after another. The revolt was finally crushed by M. Licinius Crassus in 71 BC.

The main sources, Plutarch and Appian, differ in many details (for example in the numbers of the rebels and their route); some of the sites are known only approximately. Spartacus’ aim – to escape from Italy, or to attack Rome – is contradictory in the sources too. The numbers in brackets are chapters of the source (Plut. = Life of Crassus, App. = Civil Wars book 1).

s.h: Escape from the school at Capua
s.t: In Lentulus Batiatus’ gladiatorial school at Capua mostly Gauls and Thracians were kept. According to Plutarch two hundred planned to escape; the plan was discovered, but seventy-eight broke out with kitchen knives and spits, capturing wagons carrying weapons on the way. Their leader became the Thracian Spartacus, whom Plutarch describes as brave, strong and cultured, more Greek than barbarian (Plut. 8).

The fugitives withdrew to Vesuvius. The praetor C. Clodius (Glaber) surrounded the mountain with 3,000 men, blocking its one steep path. The rebels wove ladders from the wild vines growing on the summit, let themselves down the cliff on them, and attacking from behind took the Roman camp (Plut. 9). They then defeated the army of the praetor P. Varinius too; Spartacus captured Varinius’ lictors and horse (Plut. 9; App. 116).

In 72 the senate sent both consuls against the rebels. Crixus, separated from the main army with his 30,000 men, was defeated at Mount Garganus by the army of the consul L. Gellius and fell (App. 117; in Plutarch a detached band of 3,000 fights against Gellius). According to Appian Spartacus made 300 Roman prisoners fight one another as gladiators in Crixus’ honour.

s.h: North towards the Alps – and back
s.t: Spartacus, having defeated the two consuls one after the other, marched north, so that by leaving Italy each man could return home to Thrace or Gaul. At Mutina he defeated the ten-thousand-strong army of C. Cassius Longinus, governor of Cisalpine Gaul (Plut. 9). But then – according to the sources because of the will of the army, which wanted plunder – he did not cross the Alps but turned back south. According to Appian he had 120,000 infantry and for a while considered attacking Rome (App. 117).

The senate entrusted the war to the wealthy Crassus, with six legions. He sent his legate Mummius with two legions after Spartacus with orders not to give battle; Mummius attacked nevertheless and was routed. From the fugitives Crassus chose 500 men and decimated them: every tenth man was executed – an ancient punishment long out of use (Plut. 10; according to Appian it was carried out on the whole army, App. 118).

s.n: Rhegium (Reggio Calabria) and the Bruttian peninsula
s.h: The pirates’ betrayal and Crassus’ trench
s.t: Spartacus marched through Lucania to the sea and made a bargain with Cilician pirates to carry 2,000 of his men to Sicily, where he could have kindled a new slave revolt; but the pirates took the money and sailed away. Crassus then had a trench and wall 300 stades long and 15 feet deep and wide built across the neck of the peninsula from sea to sea, to shut the rebels in. On a snowy, stormy night Spartacus filled part of the trench with earth, timber and branches and got across with a third of his army (Plut. 10).

s.n: The area of the river Silarus (Sele) (site of the battle uncertain)
s.t: Crassus hurried to finish the war before Pompey and Lucullus arrived. Part of the rebels broke away and were defeated at the Lucanian lake. Spartacus withdrew into the mountains of Petelia, then at last accepted battle; according to Plutarch before the fight he killed his horse, saying that if he won he would have many fine horses from the enemy, and if he lost he would not need one. He fought his way towards Crassus, killed two centurions, and fell surrounded, fighting; his body was never found (Plut. 11; App. 120). Scholars usually place the battle in the upper valley of the Silarus (Sele); its exact site is not known.

s.n: The Via Appia from Capua to Rome
s.h: Six thousand crosses along the Via Appia
s.t: According to Appian the 6,000 rebels captured in the battle were crucified along the Via Appia from Capua to Rome (App. 120). The five thousand who fled north were destroyed by Pompey, returning from Spain, who wrote to the senate that Crassus had won the battle but he had ended the war (Plut. 11). Crassus received only a lesser triumph (ovatio); the rivalry of the two generals shaped the politics of the following decades too.

t: Crassus’ Parthian campaign and the defeat at Carrhae (55–53 BC)
intro:
Marcus Licinius Crassus, the richest man in Rome and, with Pompey and Caesar, a member of the triumvirate, received the governorship of Syria as consul in 55 BC. He longed for military glory like his two partners and started a war against the Parthian Empire, which had not attacked Rome. In 53 BC near Carrhae (Harran) the horse archers and armoured cavalry of the Parthian general Surena destroyed his army; Crassus died during truce negotiations.

Plutarch’s Life of Crassus is very detailed and reports many ill omens and dramatic scenes; his source was probably a survivor, perhaps from Cassius’ circle. The exact site of the battle is not known. The numbers in brackets are Plutarch’s chapters.

s.h: Ateius’ curse at the city gate
s.t: According to Plutarch Crassus hoped for conquests beyond the Parthians as far as Bactria and India. Many disapproved of his starting a war against a people that had done Rome no harm. The tribune Ateius first tried to have him arrested, then ran to the city gate, poured incense and libations on a brazier, and calling on strange and dreadful deities cursed Crassus (16).
At Brundisium he did not wait for better weather: although the sea was still stormy he put out, and lost many ships. With the rest of the army he marched by land through Galatia to Syria (17).

s.h: The first campaign and winter quarters
s.t: In 54 he crossed the Euphrates and took several Greek cities of Mesopotamia without resistance; Zenodotia, where a hundred of his soldiers were killed, he stormed and plundered. He left 7,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry as garrisons, then withdrew to Syria for the winter (17). According to Plutarch he spent the winter more like a businessman than a general: he had the treasures of the temple of the goddess at Hierapolis weighed on scales. Here his son Publius joined him with a thousand Gallic horsemen from Caesar’s army (17).

s.h: The crossing at Zeugma – ill omens
s.t: Artavasdes, king of Armenia, arrived with six thousand horsemen and advised him to attack through Armenia, across the mountains, where the Parthian cavalry would be ineffective; Crassus refused (19). At Zeugma, where a bridge of boats crossed the Euphrates, extraordinary thunder and a storm broke out, and the wind carried away part of the bridge; the first eagle turned back of its own accord, and the soldiers were given lentils and salt – the food of funerals (19). Crassus set out with seven legions, nearly four thousand horsemen and as many light-armed troops (20).

s.n: The river Balissus (Balikh) (exact site of the battle not known)
s.h: The battle: the death of Publius
s.t:
Ariamnes, an Arab chieftain and according to Plutarch an agent of the Parthians, persuaded Crassus to leave the river and pursue the ‘fleeing’ enemy across the desert. At the river Balissus Surena’s army appeared: after his concealed armoured cavalry, his horse archers surrounded the Romans drawn up in a square and shot them with volleys of arrows constantly replenished from camels (21–25).

Publius broke out with the Gallic cavalry to relieve the pressure, but was lured into a trap; the Gauls crept under the armoured horses and slit their bellies, but in the end were worn down. Publius had his armour-bearer kill him; his head was shown to his father on a spear (25–26). Crassus then encouraged his soldiers: the grief was his, not theirs (26).

At night, on the advice of Cassius and Octavius, the army abandoned the camp and fled to Carrhae, leaving behind about four thousand wounded; in the morning the Parthians massacred the wounded (27–28). From Carrhae Crassus set out towards the Armenian mountains with another treacherous guide; Cassius escaped to Syria with five hundred horsemen (29).

With Octavius’ troops they were near Sinnaca, already at the foot of the hills, when Surena invited Crassus to a parley. The soldiers forced him to go; according to Plutarch Crassus said that if he died, they should tell that the enemy’s deceit, not the treachery of his fellow citizens, had killed him. At the parley a scuffle broke out and Crassus was killed; according to some a Parthian named Pomaxathres killed him and cut off his head and right hand (30–31). According to Plutarch twenty thousand Romans fell in the whole campaign and ten thousand were taken prisoner (31).

s.h: The Bacchae at the court of Orodes
s.t: Meanwhile Orodes, king of Parthia, made peace in Armenia with Artavasdes and married his son Pacorus to the Armenian king’s sister. After the banquet the actor Jason of Tralles performed from Euripides’ Bacchae; then Sillaces threw Crassus’ head into the hall, and Jason, holding the head, sang the song of the play in the role of Agave (33). Plutarch does not name the place; the point stands symbolically at the Armenian capital. The standards lost at Carrhae were recovered only by Augustus, through diplomacy, in 20 BC.

t: Cicero’s journey to the province of Cilicia and back (51–50 BC)
intro:
In 51 BC Cicero, the orator and former consul, was given the governorship of the province of Cilicia for a year, against his will. We know his journey almost day by day from his letters – mainly those to his friend Atticus: their dates show where he was and when. It is one of the most precisely dated journeys of antiquity, so several of its stretches can be compared with the calculator.

Note: the dates are those of the Roman calendar. At this time, before Caesar’s calendar reform, the Roman calendar did not follow the seasons exactly, so a “July” date did not necessarily fall in the real midsummer. In the calculator comparisons we use the date unchanged; the warnings about the season should therefore be read with reservation. The references in brackets are to the letters (Att. = to Atticus, Fam. = to his friends).

s.t: Under a new law that obliged former magistrates to govern provinces, Cicero was assigned Cilicia in March 51 BC – according to his letters he very much did not want to go. He left Rome in early May; on the way he wrote to Atticus from Minturnae, Pompeii and the neighbourhood of Trebula (Att. 5.1–3).

img.c: Marble bust of Cicero, mid-1st century AD (Rome, Capitoline Museums).

s.t: At Brundisium he waited for almost two weeks: in his letters he complains that he has to wait for his legate Pomptinus (Att. 5.8; Fam. 3.3–4).

s.n: Actium (the marker shows the later Nicopolis)
s.t: “We reached Actium on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of [July]” – he writes to Atticus (Att. 5.9.1), that is on 15 June. From here he did not sail round the Peloponnese, but went on overland towards Athens. Twenty years later, in 31 BC, Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra off Actium; Nicopolis was founded in memory of the victory, and this is what the marker shows.

He arrived in Athens on 24 June and set off again from the Piraeus on 6 July; he himself writes that he spent “just ten days” in the city (Att. 5.10–11). In Athens, where he had studied philosophy as a young man, he met philosophers and looked at the city’s buildings.

He left the Piraeus on 6 July and travelled from island to island on open coastal boats: on 8 July Ceos, on the 9th Gyaros, on the 10th Syros, on the 11th Delos. In a letter to Atticus he remarks that a sea voyage is a serious business even in July, and that they reached Delos from Athens on the sixth day; in the open, undecked Rhodian boats they could only make slow progress from island to island (Att. 5.12). This shows well how a Roman official travelled across the Aegean.

calc.src: According to the letters he left the Piraeus on 6 July and reached Delos on 11 July by way of Ceos, Gyaros and Syros (commentary on Fam. 15.4; Att. 5.12). The date is that of the Roman calendar; the real season may have differed.

img.c: Delos: the Terrace of the Lions.

s.t: On 22 July he landed at Ephesus, the capital of the province of Asia, where he was received with great celebration; Atticus congratulated him by letter on the reception (Att. 5.13). He stayed four days, then set off overland on 26 July.
“I arrived at Tralles on 27 July” – he writes to his predecessor, Appius Claudius Pulcher (Fam. 3.5). The road between Ephesus and Tralles is 32 Roman miles.

On 31 July he reached Laodicea, the first city of his province. “From this day you can start crossing off the days of my year” – he writes to Atticus (Att. 5.15). His year of office should in principle have begun on 1 July, but he entered the province only now, so his year ran until 30 July. In his letters he complains that his predecessor had plundered and ruined the province.

f: Ephesus| Arsinoeia| Arsinoe|Aya Soluḳ|Aya Soluq|Ayāsulūk|Ayā Sulūk|Arsinoē
calc.src: Cicero left Ephesus on 26 July, reached Tralles on the 27th and Laodicea on the 31st – about five days (Att. 5.13–15; Fam. 3.5). The date is that of the Roman calendar.

img.c: Ruins of Laodicea on the Lycus: the “Syria Street”.

s.t: From 5 to 9 August he held assizes at Apamea, from 10 to 14 August at Synnada, then set off to the army towards Iconium (Att. 5.16; Fam. 15.4).

At Iconium he took over the army, then camped at Cybistra on the borders of Cappadocia, fearing that the Parthians – who two years earlier had destroyed Crassus’ army at Carrhae – would invade Syria and Cilicia (Att. 5.18; Fam. 15.2).

In the autumn he led a campaign against the inhabitants of the Amanus mountains, where his soldiers hailed him as imperator. He then besieged the mountain fortress of Pindenissus: “on the morning of the Saturnalia the people of Pindenissus surrendered to me, on the fifty-seventh day after we began the siege” (Att. 5.20), that is on 17 December. The site of Pindenissus is not known exactly, so it is not marked on the map. At the end of the year he was at Tarsus, from where he asked the Senate in official letters for a thanksgiving (supplicatio), which was voted.

After a year, on 30 July 50 BC, he handed the province over to his quaestor, Caelius Caldus, and set out for home. In early August he was in the harbour of Side in Pamphylia (Att. 6.6; Fam. 3.12). From here he sailed back to Greece by way of Rhodes and Ephesus.
On 14 October he landed at the Piraeus (Att. 6.9). The journey back was slow: it took several months to get from Cilicia to Athens.

On 2 November he was at Patrae, where he had to leave behind his sick secretary and confidant, the freedman Tiro; he wrote him several touching letters on the way (Fam. 16). On 7 November he was at Leucas and Actium, and from 9 to 22 November on Corcyra (Corfu), where he waited because of the weather.

On 24 November he reached Brundisium (Att. 7.2). He arrived at Rome only in early January – just as the civil war broke out between Caesar and Pompey. He never held the triumph he hoped for his victory in the Amanus.

calc.src: Cicero waited on Corcyra until 22 November and reached Brundisium on 24 November (Att. 7.2; Fam. 16.9). The date is that of the Roman calendar; for the calculator it falls in the closed winter sailing season, so winter sailing is allowed.

t: Horace’s journey from Rome to Brundisium (38 or 37 BC)
intro:
In the fifth poem of the first book of his Satires the poet Horace describes how he travelled from Rome to Brundisium on the Via Appia. The party was led by his patron Maecenas and by Cocceius Nerva, who were going on Octavian’s behalf to negotiate with Mark Antony – Horace says only that they were envoys on important business, “used to reconciling estranged friends”. On the way Virgil, Varius and Plotius joined them too.

The poem is not a political report but a humorous travel diary: bad inns, gnats, stomach trouble, inflamed eyes, a kitchen that almost burned down and a girl who did not come. But it gives the place names and events exactly, so the journey can be followed well. Scholars put the year at 38 or 37 BC (the time of the negotiations before the agreement of Tarentum); the poem itself gives no date. The line numbers refer to Satires 1.5.

s.t: “Having left mighty Rome” – so the poem begins. Horace first set out in the company of the Greek rhetorician Heliodorus, whom he calls “by far the most learned of the Greeks” (1–3).
For the first night Aricia received them “in a modest lodging” (1–2). Aricia lay on the Via Appia, about 16 miles from Rome, at the foot of the Alban Hills.

s.h: Forum Appii and the canal boat
s.t:
From Aricia they went to Forum Appii, “stuffed with boatmen and spiteful innkeepers”. This stage they “lazily” divided into two days, which brisker travellers do in one – “the Appian Way is less tiring to the slow” (3–6). Because of the bad water Horace “declared war on his stomach” and watched hungrily as his companions dined (7–9).

From Forum Appii they travelled by night through the Pomptine Marshes on a canal, in a boat towed by a mule. Boatmen and passengers quarrelled, gnats and frogs kept them from sleeping, the drunken boatman and a passenger sang of their distant sweethearts; at last the boatman tethered the mule to graze and fell asleep. At dawn an angry passenger beat the mule and the boatman with a cudgel; only at the fourth hour (about 10 a.m.) did they land (9–23).

calc.src: According to Horace they divided the road from Rome to Forum Appii into two days; brisker travellers do it in one (5–6). The date is an estimate (spring 37 BC): the poem does not give the season. The calculator uses the daily pace of a marching column on foot; the travellers may partly have ridden in carriages or on mules, and so could be faster.

s.t: At the spring of the goddess Feronia they washed their faces and hands, and after eating they “crawled” three miles up to Anxur, built “on rocks gleaming white far and wide” (24–26). Here they awaited Maecenas and Cocceius, who were coming as envoys on important business (27–29). Here Horace smeared black ointment on his inflamed eyes; meanwhile Maecenas, Cocceius and Fonteius Capito, Antony’s confidant, arrived (30–33).

img.c: The terraces of the so-called sanctuary of Jupiter Anxur above Tarracina.

s.t: They “gladly” left Fundi, where Aufidius Luscus, the “praetor”, received them – Horace laughs at the little town’s magistrate, who came to meet them in a bordered toga, a broad-striped tunic and with a pan of coals (34–36).

Tired, they stayed in “the city of the Mamurrae” (Formiae): Murena provided lodging, Capito his kitchen (37–38). Mamurra, Caesar’s rich and notorious prefect, came from here; Catullus too wrote mocking poems about him.

The next day at Sinuessa Plotius, Varius and Virgil joined them; according to Horace “the earth has borne no purer souls”, and he values nothing more than a dear friend (39–44). From here a little farmhouse near the Campanian bridge received them, where the local officials provided firewood and salt (45–46).
At Capua the mules were unloaded early. Maecenas went to play ball, Horace and Virgil to sleep, for ball games are bad for sore eyes and weak stomachs (47–49).

From here Cocceius’ well-stocked villa received them, above the inns of Caudium (50–51). At dinner a battle of wits between two buffoons, Sarmentus and Messius Cicirrus, entertained the company, “so that we gaily prolonged that supper” (51–70).

From here they went straight on to Beneventum, where the bustling innkeeper almost burned down while roasting lean thrushes: the fire got loose in the old kitchen and the flames shot up to the roof. Hungry guests and frightened slaves scrambled to save the dinner and put out the fire (71–76).

After Beneventum the well-known mountains of Apulia came into view, scorched by the Atabulus (the hot south wind) (77–78). Here the party left the Via Appia. They stayed at a farmhouse near Trivicum, where the smoke of damp branches on the fire brought tears to their eyes; Horace waited in vain until midnight for a girl who had promised to come (79–85).

s.n: The little town “whose name won’t fit the verse” (Equus Tuticus according to the ancient commentator; the marker shows Aequum Tuticum)
s.t: From here they covered twenty-four miles by carriage to a little town whose name “cannot be spoken in verse”, but is easy to describe by signs: here water, elsewhere the cheapest of things, is sold, but the bread is so good that the wise traveller carries it on his shoulders (86–91). According to the ancient commentator (scholiast) this was Equus Tuticus; the identification is not certain.

At Canusium – founded, according to tradition, by the valiant Diomedes – the bread is gritty, and a jug of water is worth no more (91–92). Here Varius left them, sadly taking leave of his weeping friends (93).
They reached Rubi tired, for they had covered a long stretch, and the rain had spoiled it too (94–95).
The next day the weather was better, but the road worse, as far as the walls of Barium, rich in fish (96–97).

Gnatia, built according to Horace “under the anger of the nymphs”, gave them laughter and jokes: the locals wanted them to believe that on the sacred threshold incense melts without fire. “Let the Jew Apella believe it, not I,” writes Horace; he had learned that the gods live untroubled and do not busy themselves with the wonders of nature (97–103).
“Brundisium is the end of a long journey and of my paper” – so the poem ends (104). Brundisium was the end of the Via Appia and the main port for ships leaving for Greece.

t: Antony’s Parthian campaign and retreat (36 BC)
intro:
Mark Antony, master of the eastern half of the Roman empire, attacked the Parthian Empire in 36 BC with a great army, to avenge Crassus’ defeat and recover the lost standards. He marched not through Mesopotamia but from the north, through Armenia, against Media Atropatene (today’s Iranian Azerbaijan), an ally of the Parthians. His siege train was destroyed in a raid, the siege of the capital failed, and during a retreat lasting months a large part of his army perished.

Our main source is Plutarch’s Life of Antony, which probably used the account of a participant, Q. Dellius; Plutarch attributes the failure partly to Antony’s love for Cleopatra. Many of the sites are uncertain; even the site of the besieged capital, Phraata (Praaspa), is disputed. The numbers in brackets are Plutarch’s chapters.

s.t: The Parthian king Phraates had killed his father Orodes, and many Parthian nobles fled; Monaeses deserted to Antony, who gave him three Syrian cities. Antony then sent Monaeses back to deceive Phraates with a show of peace, and demanded the return of the standards taken from Crassus (37). According to Cassius Dio the army gathered at Zeugma in spring (49.25). Antony sent Cleopatra back to Egypt (37).

Antony marched through Arabia and Armenia to the place where his army and the troops of the allied kings were assembling; the largest contingent was provided by Artavasdes, king of Armenia, six thousand horse and seven thousand foot. According to Plutarch the review counted 60,000 Roman infantry, 10,000 Iberian and Celtic horse and 30,000 men of other nations; this power, according to Plutarch, terrified even the Indians beyond Bactria (37). According to Strabo and Plutarch the march from Zeugma to Atropatene was 8,000 stades (38).

s.n: Media Atropatene (site of the raid unknown; symbolic point)
s.t: His siege engines were carried on three hundred wagons, including a battering ram eighty feet long. Antony left the slow train behind under the command of Oppius Statianus with a strong guard, and hurried ahead himself. Phraates’ cavalry surprised the train: Statianus and ten thousand of his men were killed, the engines destroyed, and king Polemon of Pontus taken prisoner. Artavasdes, king of Armenia, then withdrew with his army (38–39).

Antony besieged Phraata, the capital of the Median king, where the king’s wife and children were. Lacking siege engines he had a mound raised, without success. With ten legions and cavalry he set out on a foraging expedition and routed the Parthians, but killed few of the enemy. When some of his soldiers fled from a sortie of the defenders, he had them decimated (39). As autumn and winter approached, Phraates promised peace, but only on condition that the Romans withdrew (40). Scholars look for the city near Maragheh or Takht-e Soleyman; the point follows one proposal in the database.

s.n: The river Araxes (Aras), the border of Media and Armenia (symbolic point)
s.t:
On the advice of a Mardian guide Antony retreated through the mountains instead of across the plain. The Parthians attacked ceaselessly; once the legionaries formed a ‘tortoise’ (testudo) with their shields and beat off the arrows. Hunger and dysentery took their toll; the soldiers ate poisonous herbs, and one night the army plundered its own baggage (41–48).

On the twenty-seventh day they reached the river Araxes, the border of Media and Armenia. The review showed that twenty thousand infantry and four thousand cavalry had perished, more than half by disease. According to Plutarch they had beaten the Parthians in eighteen battles, but to no effect (49–50).

s.n: Leuke Kome (the coast between Berytus and Sidon; site uncertain)
s.t: Antony did not dare to punish Artavasdes, as the army was exhausted. He hurried on, and on the snowy winter roads of Armenia eight thousand more men died. With a few soldiers he went down to the coast, to a place called Leuke Kome between Berytus and Sidon, and waited there for Cleopatra; according to Plutarch in his impatience he passed the time drinking and often ran down to the shore to see whether she was coming. Cleopatra brought clothing and money for the soldiers (51). Two years later Antony seized Artavasdes by a trick and led him in chains in a triumph at Alexandria (50).

t: Ovid’s exile: the journey from Rome to Tomis (AD 8–9)
intro:
In AD 8 Augustus banished Ovid, the most famous poet of his time, to Tomis on the Black Sea (today Constanța, Romania). Ovid himself names the cause only thus: “a poem and a mistake” (carmen et error, Tristia 2.207); the poem was the Art of Love, and about the mistake he reveals nothing. Formally it was not exile (exilium) but relegation (relegatio): he kept his property and his citizenship.

In the poems he wrote in exile (Tristia, Epistulae ex Ponto) Ovid relates some stages of the journey and his life at Tomis. This is a literary walk: the lines were not written as a travel account, and the exact route is unknown in several places. At sea the line consists of straight stretches and shows only the direction; the numbers in brackets give book, poem and lines.

s.t: One of the most famous poems of the first book of the Tristia recalls the last night in Rome: “When the sad image of that night comes over me, which was my last in Rome…” (1.3.1–2). It describes the hurried preparations, the weeping wife and friends, the house fallen silent, and the Capitol, which he looked at for the last time in the moonlight; at dawn he left.

s.n: Brundisium (Brindisi) – the probable port of departure
s.h: A stormy winter on the Adriatic
s.t: The poems do not name the port from which he set out; most commentators think of Brundisium. According to Tristia 1.11 he wrote the poems of the book on the way: “the Adriatic saw me writing in the middle of its waters in icy December” (1.11.3–4) – that is, he crossed in winter, in Vegetius’ closed sailing season. In several poems he describes the storm, the mountainous waves and the fear of death (1.2, 1.4, 1.11).

s.n: Lechaeum, the western harbour of Corinth
s.t: Across the Adriatic and the Gulf of Corinth he came to the “two-sea” Isthmus, the Isthmus of Corinth (1.11.5). According to the commentators he landed here and went across the isthmus to the eastern harbour, Cenchreae. The line shows the probable direction of the voyage.

“I have, and pray that I may always have, the protection of golden-haired Minerva, and my bark draws her name from an emblazoned helmet” – so begins Tristia 1.10. Ovid first knew the ship “at Corinthian Cenchreae”, and praises her speed: with wind or oar she outstrips other ships (1.10.1–10).

The ship passed through the Cyclades to the “sea of Aeolian Helle”, the Hellespont; there, however, she did not sail into the strait but turned to the left, away from “Hector’s city”, Troy, and put into the harbour of Imbros (1.10.15–18).

From Imbros, with a light breeze, the ship reached the “Zerynthian shore”, the Thracian Samos, that is Samothrace (1.10.19–20). According to the commentators Tristia 1.10 was written here. From here the ship turned back through the Hellespont: she passed Dardania and Lampsacus, went through the strait between Sestos and Abydos to Cyzicus and Byzantium, at the entrance of the Pontus. Ovid prays that the ship, along the western shore of the Black Sea – past Apollonia, Anchialus, Mesembria, Odessus, the city of Bacchus and the settlers of Alcathous –, may at last reach “the Milesian city”, Tomis, where the anger of the god has sent him (1.10.23–50).

s.n: Tempyra – site uncertain, on the Thracian coast opposite Samothrace
s.t: “From here ’tis but a short leap for one who seeks Tempyra on the opposite coast: thus far only did my bark attend her master. For it was my resolve to pick my way on foot through the Bistonian land” (1.10.21–23). So Ovid crossed from Samothrace to the Thracian coast and went on towards Tomis by land. No poem describes the stages of this journey; from here the line shows only the probable direction found on the map’s road network.

Tomis was a Greek colony of Miletus; in one poem Ovid tells the mythical origin of the name: here Medea cut up her brother Absyrtus (Tristia 3.9). Tristia 3.10 describes winter at Tomis: the Hister (Danube) freezes, Sarmatian horsemen and wagons cross on the ice, the wine freezes in the shape of the jar and is served in pieces. He complains that he hardly hears a Greek or Latin word, surrounded by Getae and Sarmatians.

According to one of the Epistulae ex Ponto he even wrote a poem in the Getic language in praise of Augustus (4.13.19–20). Ovid was never allowed to return to Rome; he died at Tomis in AD 17 or 18. His statue stands on the main square of today’s Constanța.

img.c: Statue of Ovid in Constanța, ancient Tomis (Ettore Ferrari, 1887).

t: Germanicus’ journey in the East (AD 18–19)
intro:
After the German campaigns the emperor Tiberius sent his adopted son Germanicus with an extraordinary supreme command to the eastern provinces. Germanicus travelled with his wife Agrippina, and combined his journey with visits to famous places of the Greek world – according to Tacitus he was led by a desire to see ancient and celebrated places. The journey led through the Greek islands, the Bosporus, Asia Minor and Armenia to Syria, then to Egypt, and in the autumn of 19 Germanicus died unexpectedly near Antioch.

Tacitus gives the places and the order, but hardly any days. At sea the line consists of straight stretches and shows only the probable direction; the Egyptian journey went along the Nile.

s.t:
Germanicus visited his brother Drusus in Dalmatia, then came to Nicopolis along the Illyrian coast, after a stormy voyage in the Adriatic and Ionian seas. He entered on his second consulship here, together with Tiberius; he stayed a few days so that the fleet could be repaired (Ann. 2.53).
