Meanwhile he viewed the bay of Actium, the victory monuments set up by Augustus and Antony’s camp. Tacitus notes that this was especially moving for him, as Augustus was the brother of his grandmother Octavia, and Antony his grandfather (2.53).

At Athens, out of respect for the ancient allied city, Germanicus appeared with only a single lictor. The Athenians received him with the most elaborate honours, recalling their ancient deeds and sayings to give their flattery more dignity (2.53). The line shows the probable route through the Gulf of Corinth; Tacitus does not describe it.

From Athens he went by way of Euboea to Lesbos, where Agrippina gave birth to their last child, Julia (Julia Livilla) (2.54). The exact place on the island is not known; the marker shows Mytilene, the island’s capital.

s.h: Perinthus, Byzantium and the mouth of the Pontus
s.t: From there he went along the edges of Asia to the Thracian cities of Perinthus and Byzantium, then through the straits of the Propontis to the mouth of the Pontus (Black Sea), out of a desire to get to know ancient and famous places. On the way he relieved provinces exhausted by internal strife or by the wrongdoing of officials (2.54).

On the way back he wanted to go to Samothrace to learn about the mysteries held on the island, but the north winds drove him off. So he visited Ilium, and everything there worthy of reverence for the changes of fortune and for the origin of the Romans (2.54). The Romans traced their descent from Troy through Aeneas.

s.n: Claros, the oracle of Apollo (near Colophon)
s.t: Along the coast of Asia he went to Colophon to consult the oracle of Apollo at Claros. Tacitus describes how here it is not a priestess but a priest chosen from certain families – usually from Miletus – who prophesies: he hears only the number and names of the enquirers, goes down into a cave, drinks from a secret spring, and though usually unlettered answers the unspoken questions in verse. Rumour had it that in ambiguous words he foretold Germanicus’ early death (2.54).

Meanwhile Cn. Calpurnius Piso, the new governor of Syria, was hurrying after Germanicus, and gave an insulting speech at Athens. Near Rhodes a storm caught him and drove him onto the rocks; Germanicus – though he knew how hostile Piso was to him – sent warships to rescue him. Piso nevertheless stayed barely a day, and hurried on ahead to Syria to win over the legions (2.55).

Germanicus went to Armenia, where there was a dispute over the throne. At Artaxata, with the approval of the nobles and before a great crowd, he crowned as king Zeno, son of Polemo of Pontus, who had followed Armenian customs from his youth. The people hailed him as Artaxias, after the name of the city (2.56). Meanwhile Cappadocia and Commagene became Roman provinces. Tacitus does not describe the route by which he reached Armenia; the line shows only the direction.

s.n: Cyrrhus (Nebi Uri), winter quarters of the Tenth Legion
s.t: In Syria, at Cyrrhus, in the winter quarters of the Tenth Legion, he met Piso. Both controlled their expressions, but parted in open hatred. From then on Piso rarely appeared at Germanicus’ tribunal, and when he did, he opposed him rudely (2.57). The marker shows the ruined city of Cyrrhus; the exact site of the camp is not known.

In 19 Germanicus went to Egypt to see its antiquities, although officially he was dealing with the province’s affairs. He opened the granaries and so lowered the price of grain. He went about without guards, in sandals and Greek dress, as Scipio once had in Sicily (2.59).

Tiberius mildly rebuked his dress and bearing, but sharply criticised his entering Alexandria without permission: Augustus had forbidden senators and leading knights to go to Egypt without permission, since whoever held the province could starve Italy (2.59). The line starts from Antioch; the exact route is not known.

From Canopus, founded according to tradition by Spartans and named after Menelaus’ helmsman, Germanicus sailed up the Nile. At the ruins of Thebes an aged priest read him the hieroglyphic inscriptions: they told of the power and army of the old kings and of the tribute of subject peoples (2.60).

s.h: Memnon’s statue and the empire’s former limit
s.t: Germanicus saw the stone statue of Memnon, which gives a human sound when touched by the rays of the rising sun; the pyramids rising like mountains among the sand; the lakes dug to receive the Nile’s floods; and stretches of the river of immeasurable depth. Finally he reached Elephantine and Syene, once the limits of the Roman empire – which now extends to the Red Sea (2.61).

On returning from Egypt Germanicus found that Piso had cancelled all his arrangements. Soon afterwards he fell ill. In the house were found human remains, spells, curses and lead tablets inscribed with Germanicus’ name – so the illness was attributed to Piso’s poison or sorcery (2.69). On his deathbed Germanicus asked his friends for vengeance, and Agrippina to restrain her anger (2.71–72).

He died at Epidaphne near Antioch, aged 33 or 34; the traditional date is 10 October. Before cremation his body was displayed in the forum of Antioch; whether it showed signs of poison remained disputed. According to Tacitus many compared him with Alexander the Great, who also died young in a foreign land (2.72–73).

img.c: Marble bust of Germanicus (Los Angeles, J. Paul Getty Museum).

s.t: With the ashes and her children, Agrippina sailed over the wintry sea without stopping, spent a few days at Corcyra, then arrived at Brundisium. The harbour, the walls and the rooftops were covered by a great crowd; when Agrippina stepped off the ship with two of her children and the urn, a single groan was heard (Ann. 3.1). The sea voyage took place in the winter period dangerous for sailing; the line shows only the direction.

img.c: Benjamin West’s painting (1768, Yale University Art Gallery): Agrippina lands at Brundisium with the ashes of Germanicus (Tacitus, Annals 3.1).

t: The Pannonian–Dalmatian revolt and Tiberius’ war (AD 6–9)
intro:
In AD 6, when Tiberius was preparing to attack Maroboduus, king of the Marcomanni, the Pannonian and Dalmatian peoples of Illyricum rose in revolt. The rising was led by two leaders of the same name: Bato of the Dalmatian Daesitiates and Bato of the Breuci on the Sava, with Pinnes beside them. According to Velleius the revolt kept all Italy in fear; Tiberius suppressed it in three years of hard war. It was one of Rome’s most difficult wars under Augustus, and its theatre included the south of today’s Transdanubia, the land between the Drava and the Sava, and Bosnia.

Velleius Paterculus was an eyewitness as an officer of Tiberius, but he idolised his commander; Cassius Dio wrote two centuries later, in more detail but sometimes confusingly. Some of the sites (the Volcaean marshes, the river Bathinus, Arduba) are uncertain; the text says so. The numbers in brackets give book and chapter of the sources.

s.h: The campaign against Maroboduus – and the news of the revolt
s.t: Tiberius set out from Carnuntum, on the Danube in Noricum (later Pannonia), against the kingdom of Maroboduus, while Sentius Saturninus approached from the Rhine; the two armies were a few days’ march from the Marcomanni. Then came the news that all Pannonia and Dalmatia had revolted. Tiberius quickly made peace with Maroboduus on favourable terms and turned back (Velleius 2.109–110).

s.h: The outbreak of the Dalmatian revolt
s.t: According to Dio the Dalmatians were embittered by heavy tribute; when the governor Valerius Messallinus levied troops for Tiberius’ campaign, the young men rose under Bato of the Daesitiates. Bato attacked Salona, the seat of the province, but was wounded by a stone; his men ravaged the coast as far as Apollonia (Dio 55.29). According to Velleius the rebels numbered 800,000, with 200,000 infantry and 9,000 cavalry (2.110) – the figure is certainly exaggerated.

The Breuci on the Sava, led by the other Bato, marched against Sirmium. Caecina Severus, governor of Moesia, defeated them near the Drava, but suffered heavy losses and had to return to Moesia, which had been invaded by Dacians and Sarmatians (Dio 55.29–30).

s.h: The two Batos on Mount Alma
s.t: The two Batos joined forces and took up position on Mount Alma (in Syrmia, near Sirmium); here the Thracian king Rhoemetalces, an ally of Rome, defeated them. The rebels then withdrew to their mountain strongholds, from which they ravaged the country (Dio 55.30).

There was panic in Rome: according to Velleius Augustus declared in the senate that unless they took care, the enemy could be in sight of Rome within ten days; levies were ordered, and freedmen were enrolled too (Velleius 2.111). Tiberius made Siscia on the Sava his base. In 7 Germanicus was also sent there; according to Dio Augustus suspected that Tiberius was deliberately prolonging the war (Dio 55.31).

According to Velleius ten legions, more than seventy cohorts, fourteen alae and more than ten thousand veterans were assembled at once – too large, in Tiberius’ view, to move effectively together, so he divided it (2.113).

s.n: The Volcaean marshes (site uncertain; shown near Cibalae)
s.h: The battle at the Volcaean marshes
s.t: The five legions of Caecina Severus and Plautius Silvanus were marching from Moesia to join Tiberius when the two Batos attacked them at the Volcaean marshes. The auxiliaries fled and the legions too were thrown into confusion, but in the end the courage of the legionaries turned the battle (Velleius 2.112; Dio 55.32). The marshes are sought between the Drava and the Sava, in the area of Cibalae.

s.n: The river Bathinus (perhaps the Bosna; site uncertain)
s.t: Famine and disease exhausted the rebels. The Breucian Bato betrayed and handed over Pinnes, receiving rule over the Breuci in return; but the Daesitiate Bato captured and executed him. Plautius Silvanus subdued the Breuci (Dio 55.34). According to Velleius the Pannonians laid down their arms at the river Bathinus (2.114). The river is usually identified with today’s Bosna.

s.h: Germanicus in Dalmatia: Splonum and Raetinium
s.t: In 9 the war was fought in the mountains of Dalmatia. Germanicus took Splonum when Pusio, a German horseman, brought down part of the wall with a stone. At Raetinium the defenders themselves set fire to their outer wall and houses; the Romans who broke in were trapped between the flames and the missiles and suffered heavy losses, and the defenders abandoned the citadel at night (Dio 56.11). Tiberius took Seretium, which he had failed to capture earlier, then divided the army into three (Dio 56.12).

Bato shut himself up in the rocky, well-supplied fortress of Andetrium near Salona. Here Tiberius himself was put almost in a state of siege, as his supplies were cut off; in the end, at the soldiers’ clamour, he ordered an assault. The defenders rolled stones and wagons down on the climbers, but a detachment sent round attacked them from behind, and the fortress surrendered (Dio 56.12–14). Meanwhile Germanicus took Arduba, where the women, with their children, threw themselves into the fire or the river rather than surrender (Dio 56.15).

Bato negotiated through his son Sceuas, then came before Tiberius and pleaded for everything but his own life. When Tiberius asked why they had rebelled, he answered: “You are to blame, for you send as guardians of your flocks not dogs or shepherds, but wolves” (Dio 56.16). According to Suetonius Tiberius assigned him a residence at Ravenna (Tiberius 20).

s.h: Triumph – and the news from Teutoburg
s.t: The senate voted Augustus and Tiberius the title imperator and a triumph, and two triumphal arches in Pannonia; Germanicus received triumphal ornaments. But after the decrees came the news of the destruction of Varus’ three legions in Germany, and the celebrations were called off (Dio 56.17). According to Velleius the grievous news came barely five days after the end of the Pannonian–Dalmatian war (2.117). Tiberius held his Pannonian triumph only in 12 (Suetonius, Tiberius 20). The sequel can be seen in the walk “Varus and Germanicus”.

t: The defeat of Varus and the campaigns of Germanicus (AD 9–16)
intro:
In the autumn of AD 9 the Germanic tribes, led by Arminius, a chief of the Cherusci who held Roman equestrian rank, destroyed three Roman legions – the XVII, XVIII and XIX –, three cavalry alae and six cohorts (Velleius 2.117) in the forests of Germania. The army’s commander, Publius Quinctilius Varus, took his own life. After the defeat Rome gave up the conquest of Germania beyond the Rhine. Six years later Germanicus, Tiberius’ adopted son, led campaigns of revenge into the region, visited the battlefield and buried the dead.

The events are described by Cassius Dio (56.18–24), Velleius Paterculus (2.117–120) and Tacitus (Annals, books 1–2); none of them gives an exact location. Kalkriese near Osnabrück, where thousands of Roman finds have been excavated since 1987, is today generally held to be one site of the battle; but this is disputed, and some scholars assign the finds to Germanicus’ campaign of 15. Most places beyond the Rhine (Varus’ summer camp, Idistaviso, the Angrivarian wall) cannot be located exactly; the walk notes this at every stop. Beyond the Rhine the line consists of straight stretches and shows only the probable direction.

s.t: Vetera was one of the main legionary bases on the lower Rhine, from which roads led along the Lippe valley into the interior of Germania. From here comes the tombstone of Marcus Caelius, a centurion of the XVIII legion who, according to the inscription, “fell in the Varian war”; the stone also records that his bones may be buried here too, if they are found. It is one of the rare direct, contemporary memorials of the defeat.

s.n: Haltern on the Lippe (Aliso? – the identification is disputed)
s.t: In the time of Augustus several Roman camps and settlements were built along the Lippe; the largest known of them is Haltern, abandoned around AD 9. It is often identified with Aliso, the fort which, according to Dio and Velleius, alone held out after the defeat: its defenders under Lucius Caedicius repeatedly drove off the Germans with their archers, and then, when food ran short, broke out on a stormy night; at the third outpost they were discovered because of the cries of the women and children, but the strongest reached the Rhine (Dio 56.22). The identification of Haltern with Aliso is not certain.

s.n: Varus’ summer camp by the Weser (Visurgis) – site unknown (the marker shows the Minden area)
s.h: The summer camp by the Visurgis
s.t:
According to Dio, Varus governed the province as though the Germans were slaves, and exacted money from them. The Germanic leaders did not revolt openly, but feigned friendship and drew Varus into the land of the Cherusci, towards the Visurgis (Weser); Varus distributed his soldiers among the communities to guard them, to hunt robbers and to escort supply trains (56.18–19).

The leaders of the conspiracy were Arminius and his father Segimerus, Varus’ constant companions. According to Velleius and Tacitus another Cheruscan noble, Segestes, warned Varus and advised him to arrest them – Varus would not listen (Velleius 2.118; Tac. Ann. 1.55).

s.n: Kalkriese (one probable site of the battle)
s.t:
The revolt broke out among a distant tribe, so that Varus would march against them through land thought to be friendly. The Germanic leaders escorted him, then left him on the pretext of gathering allies; the communities killed the soldiers stationed with them and attacked Varus in the dense forests (Dio 56.19).

The Romans marched with many wagons and pack animals, women, children and servants, as in peacetime; they had to fell trees and build roads and bridges. Violent rain and wind broke up the column, and the Germans first shot from the thickets at a distance, then closed in. On the first night they camped on a wooded hill and burned most of the wagons. The next day they reached open country, but had to enter the woods again, where cavalry and infantry collided with one another and with the trees. On the fourth day another downpour soaked their shields, bows and javelins; Varus and the senior officers, already wounded, took their own lives, after which resistance collapsed (Dio 56.20–22).

At Kalkriese, in a narrow passage between the Kalkrieser Berg and a great bog, thousands of Roman finds have been excavated since 1987: coins, weapons, the face mask of a cavalry helmet and a turf rampart that the Germans may have built. The latest coins date from the time of Augustus; several bear the countermark VAR. The connection of the site with Varus’ battle is widely accepted, but disputed.

img.c: Face mask of a Roman cavalry helmet, one of the most famous finds from the Kalkriese battlefield (Museum und Park Kalkriese).

s.h: Augustus: “Varus, give me back my legions!”
s.t: According to Dio, on hearing the news Augustus tore his garments and feared that the Germans would invade Gaul and Italy; he drafted soldiers by lot and sent them to Germania with Tiberius. He sent his German bodyguard away to islands, and the unarmed Germans and Gauls had to leave Rome (56.23). According to Suetonius he left his hair and beard uncut for months, and sometimes, beating his head against a door, he cried: “Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!” (Aug. 23). The XVII, XVIII and XIX legions were never raised again.

In AD 15 Germanicus attacked across the Rhine. Lucius Stertinius found the lost eagle of the XIX legion among the Bructeri; the army ravaged the country between the Amisia (Ems) and the Lupia (Lippe), not far from the Teutoburg forest, where Varus and his legions lay unburied (Tac. Ann. 1.60).

Germanicus visited the battlefield. First Varus’ first camp came into view, with its wide circuit and its central space showing the work of three legions; then a half-ruined rampart and shallow ditch, where only the decimated remnant had made a stand. In the middle of the field lay the whitening bones of the dead, as they had fled or stood their ground; skulls were nailed to tree trunks, and in the nearby groves stood barbarian altars on which the tribunes and first-rank centurions had been sacrificed. Survivors showed where the legates fell, where the eagles were lost, where Varus received his first wound and where he ended his life. Six years after the defeat the army buried the bones of the three legions; Germanicus himself laid the first turf of the mound (Ann. 1.61–62).

On the way back his legate Caecina got into serious difficulty at the “long bridges” (pontes longi), a causeway across a marsh, because of an attack by Arminius (Ann. 1.63–68); some scholars connect the Kalkriese finds with this battle.

In AD 16 Germanicus decided to carry the army into Germania by sea: he had a thousand ships built and assembled them at the island of the Batavi (Ann. 2.6). Through the canal of his father Drusus and the lakes they sailed out to the Ocean and then to the river Amisia (Ann. 2.8). The exact route and the landing place are not known; the line shows the direction only for orientation.

s.n: Idistaviso by the Weser – site unknown
s.t: By the Visurgis (Weser) Arminius gathered his allies on a plain called Idistaviso, between the river and the hills. The Romans won a great victory; on the battlefield Germanicus set up a trophy with the names of the conquered peoples (Ann. 2.16–18). Shortly afterwards there was another battle by a rampart of the Angrivarii, which Germanicus also won (Ann. 2.19–22). Neither site can be identified with certainty.

Towards the end of summer he sent some of the legions to winter quarters overland and carried the rest back by ship down the Amisia to the Ocean. On the calm sea a storm suddenly broke out: it scattered the fleet, many ships sank or were driven to distant islands, horses and baggage had to be thrown overboard; some ships were carried as far as Britain. Germanicus’ trireme alone ran ashore on the coast of the Chauci (Ann. 2.23–24). In the same year the second lost eagle was recovered from the Marsi (Ann. 2.25).

Tiberius recalled Germanicus. On 26 May AD 17 he celebrated a triumph over the Cherusci, Chatti, Angrivarii and the other peoples living as far as the Elbe; according to Strabo, Arminius’ wife Thusnelda and her little son were led in the procession (Ann. 2.41; Strabo 7.1.4). But the conquest of Germania was not resumed; the frontier remained the Rhine. Arminius was killed around AD 21 by his own kinsmen (Ann. 2.88). The third lost eagle, according to Dio, was recovered only under Claudius, in AD 41 (60.8).

img.c: Dupondius of Caligula in honour of his father Germanicus (AD 37–41): SIGNIS RECEPT(IS) DEVICTIS GERM(ANIS) – “the standards recovered, the Germans defeated”.

y: The conquest of Britain and Boudica (43–61)
t: Claudius’ invasion of Britain (AD 43) and the revolt of Boudica (60/61)
intro:
After Caesar’s two landings in Britain (55 and 54 BC) there was no Roman campaign on the island for almost a hundred years. In AD 43 the emperor Claudius, who longed for military glory, launched the conquest with four legions under Aulus Plautius. Seventeen years later, in 60 or 61, Boudica, widowed queen of the Iceni, led a great revolt; the rebels burned Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before the governor Suetonius Paulinus defeated them.

The invasion was described by Cassius Dio, the revolt by Tacitus (whose father-in-law Agricola was present as a tribune) and Dio. The sources do not name the landing place (Richborough or the south coast), the river battle (traditionally the Medway) or the site of Boudica’s last battle (perhaps Mancetter); the points are therefore conjectures. The numbers in brackets give book and chapter of the sources.

s.n: Gesoriacum (Boulogne; the port is not named in the sources)
s.t: Aulus Plautius’ soldiers did not want to campaign ‘outside the inhabited world’. Claudius sent them his favourite, the freedman Narcissus; when he mounted the commander’s platform, the soldiers mocked him with the shout “Io Saturnalia!” – at the Saturnalia slaves wore their masters’ clothes – and then followed Plautius after all. Because of the delay they set out late (Dio 60.19.1–3). Dio does not name the port of departure; Gesoriacum (Boulogne) was later the main port of the British fleet.

s.n: Rutupiae (Richborough; the landing site is disputed)
s.t: The army crossed in three divisions, so that the landing could not be prevented. The Britons had not expected them, so they landed unopposed; the enemy withdrew into marshes and forests (Dio 60.19.4–5). At Richborough an early Roman defensive ditch and later the remains of a huge monumental arch were found, so many look for the landing here; others on the south coast, near Chichester.

s.n: The river battle (traditionally the Medway, near Durobrivae/Rochester)
s.t: Plautius first defeated Caratacus, then his brother Togodumnus. At a river the Britons were camped carelessly on the far bank; Plautius sent across Celtic (Germanic) auxiliaries, who swam over in full armour and wounded the horses of the chariots. After them Vespasian, the future emperor, and his brother Sabinus crossed. The battle continued the next day; Hosidius Geta, who was almost captured, won a decisive victory and received triumphal honours although he was not a consul (Dio 60.20). Dio does not name the river; it is traditionally identified with the Medway.

The Britons fell back to the Thames, and in the marshes the Romans suffered losses. Togodumnus died, and British resistance stiffened; Plautius halted and – as had been arranged – sent for Claudius (Dio 60.20.5–21.2). Claudius travelled down the Tiber to Ostia, from there along the coast to Massilia, then by land and river to the coast, and crossed to Britain with elephants. He crossed the Thames, defeated the gathered Britons and took Camulodunum, the capital of Cunobelinus. He spent only sixteen days in Britain (Dio 60.21.2–5, 23.1). At Camulodunum a veteran colony and the temple of the deified Claudius were later built.

The senate voted Claudius and his son the name Britannicus, a triumph, an annual festival and two arches, one in Rome and one in Gaul. Claudius returned after six months’ absence; in his triumph he climbed the steps of the Capitol on his knees (Dio 60.22–23). According to the inscription of his arch in Rome he received the surrender of eleven British kings without loss.

The governor Suetonius Paulinus attacked the island of Mona, the refuge of the druids and fugitives. The infantry crossed in flat-bottomed boats, the cavalry swimming. On the shore stood armed men, among them women in black, with dishevelled hair, brandishing torches like Furies, and the druids, raising their hands to the sky, poured out curses; the soldiers stood frozen for a moment, then broke through. The sacred groves were cut down (Tacitus, Ann. 14.29–30). Then came the news of the revolt.

Prasutagus, king of the Iceni, in his will named the emperor and his two daughters as heirs, hoping thus to protect his kingdom. But Roman officials plundered it: his wife Boudica was flogged and his daughters raped. The Iceni and their neighbours the Trinovantes rose in revolt (Ann. 14.31). The veteran colony of Camulodunum – where the hated temple of Claudius stood – had no wall; the defenders held out for two days in the temple, then fell. Petillius Cerialis, coming to the rescue with the Ninth Legion, had his infantry massacred and escaped with his cavalry (Ann. 14.32).

Suetonius hurried through hostile country to Londinium, which, according to Tacitus, was not a colony but a busy centre of merchants and goods. Because his army was small he decided to sacrifice the town; despite the pleas of the inhabitants he withdrew, taking with him only those who could follow. The rebels destroyed Londinium, then Verulamium too; according to Tacitus seventy thousand Roman citizens and allies died (Ann. 14.33). In London and St Albans the red-and-black layer of the burning can be traced archaeologically.

s.n: Boudica’s last battle (site unknown; shown at Manduessedum, on Watling Street)
s.t: Suetonius, with the Fourteenth Legion, part of the Twentieth and auxiliaries, about ten thousand men in all, chose a position in the mouth of a narrow valley, with a wood behind him. Behind the huge mass of the Britons their women watched the battle from wagons. According to Tacitus Boudica drove along the ranks in a chariot with her daughters. The Romans charged in wedge formation; the fugitives were hindered by the line of wagons. According to Tacitus about eighty thousand Britons fell, and four hundred Romans. Boudica took poison; Poenius Postumus, camp prefect, who had not led his legion into battle, fell on his sword (Ann. 14.34–37). The site of the battle is unknown; Mancetter is one frequent suggestion.

t: Corbulo’s campaigns in Armenia and the coronation of Tiridates (AD 54–66)
intro:
Armenia was a buffer state between Rome and the Parthian Empire. Around 52/53 the Parthian king Vologaeses I placed his brother Tiridates on the Armenian throne. In 54 the emperor Nero entrusted the war in the East to the disciplined, hard Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo. Corbulo took Artaxata and Tigranocerta; later his substitute Caesennius Paetus suffered a humiliating defeat at Rhandeia, but Corbulo’s superior force finally led to a compromise: Tiridates kept Armenia, but received his crown in Rome from Nero.

Tacitus admired Corbulo and partly used Corbulo’s own memoirs; his account therefore favours Corbulo, not Paetus. Several sites of the operations (Volandum, Rhandeia, Corbulo’s crossing of the Euphrates) cannot be identified with certainty. The numbers in brackets are book and chapter of Tacitus’ Annals.

s.n: The border of Cappadocia and Armenia (symbolic point at Satala)
s.h: Disciplining the army and the winter
s.t: Corbulo found the Syrian legions softened by long peace: according to Tacitus there were veterans who had never stood guard or seen a rampart or ditch, and lived without helmets or breastplates, like traders. He discharged the old and sick, raised recruits, and kept the whole army under canvas through a hard winter in Armenia; frost took the limbs of some, and sentries were found frozen at their posts. Deserters he had executed without mercy (13.35). Satala later became a legionary fortress; the point is symbolic.

In the spring of 58 Corbulo invaded Armenia, while his allies, the Iberian king and the king of Commagene, attacked from other directions. Negotiations began with Tiridates but led nowhere. Corbulo took the fortress of Volandum and the surrounding forts in a single day, then marched against Artaxata; Tiridates did not dare to give battle. The city opened its gates; since it could not be held, after the inhabitants had left it was set on fire and razed (13.37–41).

s.n: Tigranocerta (site disputed; shown by the database at Silvan)
s.t: Corbulo marched towards Tigranocerta in the summer heat, struggling with a lack of food. His envoys reported that the city gates stood open and the inhabitants awaited his orders; they sent him a golden crown, which Corbulo received graciously, and the city was not harmed, so that it should obey the more willingly (14.24). Nero then made Tigranes, a Cappadocian royal scion, king of Armenia; Corbulo became governor of Syria (14.26). The site of Tigranocerta is disputed; the point shows one proposal in the database.

s.n: Rhandeia on the river Arsanias (Murat) (site uncertain; symbolic point)
s.t: The Parthians attacked Tigranes; Corbulo stayed to defend Syria and asked for another general for Armenia. Caesennius Paetus invaded Armenia boastfully with two legions, then scattered his forces, and at Rhandeia on the river Arsanias Vologaeses besieged him in his winter camp. Corbulo set out to help him late; meanwhile Paetus surrendered on humiliating terms: the Romans had to build a bridge over the river for the enemy, leave Armenia, and the Parthians took everything from the camp. Tacitus’ account attributes this to Paetus’ cowardice (15.6–15).

s.n: The Euphrates (site of the meeting unknown; symbolic point at Melitene)
s.t: Earlier Corbulo had bridged the Euphrates with boats under the eyes of the Parthians: he set towers and catapults on the boats, which drove off the horsemen on the far bank (15.9). Now Paetus’ retreating army met Corbulo’s troops at the Euphrates; according to Tacitus Corbulo’s soldiers received their comrades in tears, who were returning with the shame of submission (15.16).

In 63 Corbulo marched into Armenia again with extraordinary powers, along the road once taken by Lucullus. Vologaeses and Tiridates asked for negotiations; Rhandeia, where Paetus’ army had been disgraced, was chosen as the meeting place. A few days later, before the two armies, Tiridates approached a statue of Nero, took the royal diadem from his head and laid it at the statue’s feet; he promised to take it back in Rome from Nero’s hand (15.24–29).

According to Dio Tiridates came to Rome with a great retinue on a land journey lasting nine months. In the Forum, before an enormous crowd, he knelt before Nero, who placed the diadem on his head; the doors of the temple of Janus were closed as a sign of peace (Dio 63.1–6; Suetonius, Nero 13). The next year Nero summoned Corbulo to Greece and forced him to suicide at Cenchreae; according to Dio his last word was: “I deserved it” (Dio 63.17).

t: The first journey of the Apostle Paul (c. AD 46–48)
intro:
The journeys of the Apostle Paul are described in the Acts of the Apostles, which tradition ascribes to Luke, Paul’s companion. The book gives many ports, routes and lengths of stay, but not a single year; scholars reckon the chronology of Paul’s journeys mainly from an inscription at Delphi, according to which Gallio, whom Paul met at Corinth, was proconsul of Achaia in AD 51–52. The years given here are therefore only approximate, and they are disputed among scholars.

On the first journey Barnabas and Saul (Paul) set out from Antioch in Syria; they went to the island of Cyprus and then to the south of Asia Minor, to Pamphylia, Pisidia and Lycaonia, and returned the same way. The numbers in brackets give chapter and verse; the line is the probable route found on the map’s road network and sea routes.

s.t: The capital of Syria, one of the largest cities of the empire, was the place where, according to the text, the disciples were first called Christians (11:26). From among the prophets and teachers of the church at Antioch the community set apart Barnabas and Saul; after fasting and prayer they laid their hands on them and sent them off (13:1–3).
Antioch lay some 25–30 km from the sea, on the river Orontes; its port was Seleucia Pieria. From here they sailed across to Cyprus (13:4). Barnabas himself was a native of Cyprus (4:36).
In Salamis, the port city of eastern Cyprus, they proclaimed the word in the synagogues of the Jews; John (Mark) was their helper (13:5).

They went through the whole island as far as Paphos, the seat of the province. Here the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, summoned them to hear the word; but a magician and false prophet called Bar-Jesus (Elymas) tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Saul, “who is also called Paul”, according to the text struck the magician blind, and the proconsul believed (13:6–12). From here on the book calls him Paul, and from here on he leads the group.

From Paphos they sailed to Perga in Pamphylia. Here John (Mark) left them and returned to Jerusalem (13:13) – later this became the cause of the quarrel between Paul and Barnabas (15:37–39). Perga lay a few kilometres from the sea; the text does not say where they landed.

From Perga they went over the Taurus mountains to Pisidian Antioch, a Roman colony since Augustus. On the sabbath, in the synagogue, Paul gave a long address on the history of Israel and on Jesus (13:14–41). On the next sabbath almost the whole city gathered; some of the Jews turned against them, and Paul and Barnabas declared that they would turn to the Gentiles (13:44–48). In the end, by stirring up the devout women of rank and the leading men of the city, their opponents drove them out of the district, and they “shook off the dust of their feet” (13:50–51).

At Iconium they stayed “a long time” (14:3). The people of the city were divided: some sided with the Jews, others with the apostles. When they learned of a plan to mistreat and stone them, they fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe (14:1–6).

At Lystra Paul healed a man lame from birth. The crowd shouted in the Lycaonian language that the gods had come down to them in human form; they called Barnabas Zeus and Paul – because he was the chief speaker – Hermes. The priest of the temple of Zeus before the city brought oxen and garlands to sacrifice to them; the apostles tore their clothes and could scarcely restrain the crowd (14:8–18).

Not long after, Jews who had come from Antioch and Iconium turned the crowd against Paul: they stoned him and, thinking he was dead, dragged him out of the city. But Paul got up, and the next day went with Barnabas to Derbe (14:19–20). According to the text Timothy, Paul’s later companion, also came from Lystra (16:1).

Derbe was the farthest point of the first journey; here they made many disciples (14:21). A road also led from Derbe over the Taurus into Cilicia, towards Paul’s home town of Tarsus, but they turned back and went through the same cities in reverse.

On the way back they strengthened the disciples at Lystra, Iconium and Pisidian Antioch – “through many afflictions we must enter into the Kingdom of God” – and appointed elders in every church (14:21–23). Through Pisidia and Pamphylia they came to Perga, spoke the word there, and then went down to Attalia, the port of Pamphylia (14:24–25).

From Attalia they sailed back to Antioch, gathered the church and reported how God had “opened a door of faith to the nations”; they stayed there “no little time” (14:26–28).

Then followed the council at Jerusalem (chapter 15), which decided that Christians from among the Gentiles need not be circumcised.

t: The Jewish War: the campaigns of Cestius, Vespasian and Titus (AD 66–74)
intro:
In AD 66 a revolt against Roman rule broke out in the province of Judaea. Vespasian and his son Titus suppressed it in 67–70, and in 70 Jerusalem was destroyed together with the Temple; the last fortress, Masada, fell in 73 or 74. The war was a turning point in Jewish history, and also part of the rise of the Flavian dynasty: Vespasian was proclaimed emperor in 69, in the middle of the war.

Our main source is Flavius Josephus, who was first the rebels’ commander in Galilee, was captured at the fall of Jotapata, and then, alongside Vespasian and Titus, witnessed the siege of Jerusalem; he wrote his work in Rome under Flavian patronage. His account is therefore partly self-justification and spares the Romans; his figures (especially of the dead) are often exaggerated. The dates follow J. Lendering’s conversion (Livius.org); the numbers in brackets are book and paragraph of the work.

s.t: According to Josephus the war began in the twelfth year of Nero, in the month of Artemisius. At Caesarea, the seat of the province, Jews and Greeks clashed over a plot beside a synagogue. The governor Gessius Florus gave no justice, then demanded 17 talents from the Temple treasury in Jerusalem; he had his soldiers massacre the protesters (2.284–308). Tacitus too saw the bad government of the procurators as the cause of the revolt.

In the Temple the sacrifice for the emperor was stopped – this meant open rebellion. In early August the rebels attacked the Antonia fortress, then the royal palace; the Roman garrison was massacred after being promised free withdrawal. Meanwhile Menahem at the head of rebels took Masada (2.408–456; dates: Livius.org).

Cestius Gallus, governor of Syria, marched down from Antioch with the Twelfth Legion (Fulminata) and auxiliaries via Ptolemais and Caesarea; during the Feast of Tabernacles he found Lydda empty and burned it. He attacked the walls of Jerusalem but unexpectedly withdrew. On the slopes of the Beth Horon pass the rebels attacked the column; the Romans fled with heavy losses, abandoning their siege engines (2.499–555). After this victory the revolt spread across all Judaea, and Josephus was made commander in Galilee.

Nero entrusted the war to the experienced general Vespasian. He gathered the troops at Antioch and marched to Ptolemais together with king Agrippa’s army; his son Titus brought the Fifteenth Legion (Apollinaris) from Alexandria, so that with the Fifth (Macedonica) and the Tenth (Fretensis) three legions were assembled. According to Josephus, with the troops of the allied kings the army numbered about 60,000 (3.29–69).

Advancing into Galilee Vespasian burned Gabara, then surrounded Jotapata, which Josephus had entered from Tiberias. The siege lasted 47 days; Josephus describes in detail the ruses of the defence, the battering ram and the earthwork. The town was taken on 1 July through betrayal (3.141–339).

Josephus hid in a cave with forty companions; when they chose suicide instead, they drew lots, and Josephus was among the last left, then surrendered. Brought before Vespasian, he foretold that he and his son would be emperors; Vespasian therefore spared him, but kept him in chains (3.340–408). Suetonius also mentions this prophecy.

s.h: Tarichaeae and the battle on the lake
s.t: Tiberias opened its gates; Tarichaeae, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, was stormed by Titus with cavalry. Those who fled onto the lake were pursued by the Romans on rafts and slaughtered in their boats; according to Josephus the water of the lake was mixed with blood and its shores were filled with wreckage and corpses. Of the prisoners Vespasian had 1,200 old men killed, sent 6,000 strong young men to Nero to dig the Corinth canal, and sold 30,400 into slavery (3.443–542).

Across the lake, Gamala stood on a ridge shaped like a camel’s hump and was, according to Josephus, even harder to take than Jotapata. The defenders repulsed the first assault, and Vespasian himself was in danger; in the second assault the Romans took the town. According to Josephus many threw themselves into the ravine, and only two women survived (4.1–83). The ruins of Gamla were identified in 1968 and excavated from 1976; arrowheads and sling stones of the siege were found at the wall.

The last town of Galilee to resist was Gischala. Titus called on it to surrender; the rebel leader, John of Gischala, asked for a delay because of the Sabbath and fled at night with his followers to Jerusalem, where he became one of the leaders of the factional fighting. The town surrendered (4.84–120). Vespasian wintered at Caesarea.

In the spring of 68 Vespasian took Gadara, then entered the Jordan valley; in early June he reached Jericho (4.413–450). Here Josephus describes the Jordan valley and the Dead Sea (Lake Asphaltitis). Then came the news of Nero’s death; Vespasian suspended operations and watched events in Rome (4.491–502). On 1 July 69 he was proclaimed emperor at Alexandria, and a few days later in Judaea; Josephus, his prophecy fulfilled, was set free (4.616–629).

s.h: The siege of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Temple
s.t:
Titus began the siege with four legions just before Passover; the city was weakened by the infighting of the factions (John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora, Eleazar) and by famine. The first wall was taken on 7 May, the Antonia fortress on 5 July; the Romans walled the city in. Beneath the walls Josephus, as interpreter, called on the defenders to surrender (5.99–6.68).

On the 10th of Lous (10 August) the Temple burned; according to Josephus Titus wanted to spare it, but a soldier threw fire into it. On 8 September the upper city fell too, and the city was razed. Josephus mentions 1,100,000 dead and 97,000 prisoners – the number of the dead is certainly exaggerated (6.250–420).

After the victory Titus held games at Caesarea Philippi and other Syrian cities, where many of the prisoners were thrown to wild beasts or forced to fight one another (7.23–24, 37–40). He then sailed to Rome by way of Alexandria.

In 71 Vespasian and Titus held a joint triumph in Rome. Josephus describes the procession as an eyewitness: the portable stages showing scenes of the war, the treasures of the Jerusalem Temple – the golden table, the seven-branched lampstand and the book of the Law – and at the end of the procession Simon bar Giora was executed (7.123–157). Vespasian placed the spoils in the Temple of Peace; the scene can still be seen on the relief of the Arch of Titus. The sea route line is only symbolic.

The last fortress, Herod’s rock castle above the Dead Sea, was held by sicarii under Eleazar ben Yair. The governor Flavius Silva surrounded it with the Tenth Legion and had a huge ramp built against the rock. When the wall fell, according to Josephus the defenders, after a speech by Eleazar, killed their families and one another; 960 dead remained, and only two women and five children survived, who told what had happened (7.252–406). The year is uncertain; because of coins found on the rock, 74 is thought more likely. The ramp and the Roman camps can still be seen today.

img.c: Masada from the air: Herod’s rock fortress above the Dead Sea.

y: The year of the four emperors (69)
t: The year of the four emperors: the war of the Rhine and Danube legions in Italy (AD 69)
intro:
After Nero’s death (June 68) four emperors succeeded one another within a year. Galba was murdered in Rome on 15 January 69, and the praetorians raised Otho to the throne; meanwhile the German legions had already proclaimed Vitellius emperor at the beginning of January. Vitellius’ army crossed the Alps in two columns and in April defeated Otho at Bedriacum, who killed himself. In July the eastern legions proclaimed Vespasian; at the head of the Danube legions Antonius Primus burst into Italy with a rapid attack, won at Cremona in October and in December took Rome, where Vitellius was killed.

Tacitus’ Histories are the main source; Tacitus was then young, but he could talk with many eyewitnesses. The two battles of Bedriacum were fought between Bedriacum and Cremona; the battlefields and some dates are disputed (the dates here follow Fyfe’s summary). The walk also shows the council of war at Poetovio (Ptuj), with its link to the Pannonian legions. The numbers in brackets are book and chapter of the Histories.

s.t: On 1 January the legions of Upper Germany refused the oath to Galba; the next day Fabius Valens rode with cavalry into Colonia Agrippina and proclaimed Aulus Vitellius, governor of Lower Germany, emperor, and the army of Upper Germany joined him (1.56–57). Tacitus portrays Vitellius as a lazy glutton, carried to the throne by his generals Valens and Caecina. The campaign against Italy was led by two columns: Caecina over the Great St Bernard, Valens through Gaul and over the Mont Genèvre (1.61).

In March Caecina crossed the Alps and assaulted Placentia, defended by Otho’s general Spurinna. In the fighting the splendid amphitheatre outside the walls burned down; the assault was repulsed and Caecina withdrew to Cremona (2.17–23).

On 6 April at Locus Castorum (12 miles from Cremona) Otho’s troops defeated Caecina; then Valens too arrived at Cremona (2.24–30). Otho’s generals, Suetonius Paulinus and Marius Celsus, advised waiting until the Danube legions arrived, but Otho chose a quick decision, and himself stayed at Brixellum (2.31–33).

The Othonian army marched from Bedriacum towards Cremona and met the enemy in marching column, hampered by baggage and wagons, on a plain full of vineyards. The Batavians decided the fight; the Othonians fled to Bedriacum and surrendered the next day (2.39–45).

His soldiers begged Otho to continue the fight, since the Danube legions were on their way. But Otho said he did not want more citizen blood shed; he took his leave, settled his affairs, slept peacefully for a night, then at dawn stabbed himself in the heart with a dagger. Some of his soldiers killed themselves beside his pyre (2.46–49). In Tacitus’ view his death was nobler than his life. He had reigned three months.

s.n: Poetovio (Ptuj), camp of the Thirteenth Legion Gemina
s.h: The council of war at Poetovio
s.t: On 1 July Vespasian was proclaimed emperor at Alexandria, on the 3rd in Judaea; the Danube legions – among them the Thirteenth, humiliated at Bedriacum and forced by Vitellius to build amphitheatres – joined him (2.79–86). The Flavian leaders held a council of war in the winter camp of the Thirteenth Legion Gemina at Poetovio. Antonius Primus, commander of the Seventh Legion Galbiana – according to Tacitus a bold, eloquent but restless man – demanded that they should not wait for Mucianus’ eastern army but invade Italy at once, while Vitellius’ forces were scattered (3.1–3). His proposal was accepted.

Antonius marched through Aquileia and Patavium to Verona and fortified it; here the Pannonian and Moesian legions arrived too (3.6–10). Vitellius’ general Caecina was camped at Hostilia on the river Tartarus; he attempted treachery and tried to bring his army over to Vespasian, but his soldiers imprisoned him and set off by forced march for Cremona (3.13–14). The Ravenna fleet also went over to Vespasian.

s.n: Cremona – the second battle and the destruction of the city
s.h: The second battle of Bedriacum and the sack of Cremona
s.t:
Antonius went to meet the Vitellian army. The battle between Bedriacum and Cremona began in the daytime and went on into the moonlit night; at sunrise the soldiers of the Third Legion Gallica, in the eastern custom, saluted the rising sun, which the Vitellians took to mean that Mucianus’ army had arrived, and they wavered (3.15–25). Tacitus describes a harrowing scene: in the dark a soldier killed his own father, who was fighting on the other side (3.25).

The defeated fled into Cremona. The city surrendered, but Antonius’ soldiers plundered it for four days and set it on fire; according to Tacitus forty thousand armed men broke in, and the city burned to the ground except for the temples (3.26–34).

Antonius advanced via Ariminum to Fanum Fortunae. Vitellius blocked the Apennine pass at Mevania, but then returned to Rome. Valens was captured and beheaded at Urbinum; his head was thrown into the Vitellian camp at Narnia, which then surrendered. Antonius crossed the mountains, camped at Carsulae, then pushed on to Ocriculum (3.41–63, 3.78).

On 17 December Vitellius tried to abdicate, but the soldiers and the crowd would not let him. Vespasian’s brother Flavius Sabinus fled to the Capitol, where the Vitellians besieged him; on 19 December the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus burned, Sabinus was killed, and the young Domitian escaped (3.68–74). Tacitus calls this the most shameful deed of the Roman people (3.72).

The Flavian army forced its way into the city along the Via Flaminia and other roads and took it after street fighting; the people watched the fighting like a show. Vitellius was found in the palace, dragged with a rope round his neck through the Forum, and killed on the Gemonian stairs (3.82–85). With the victory the rule of the Flavian dynasty began.

t: The second journey of the Apostle Paul (c. AD 49–52)
intro:
On the second journey Paul set out from Antioch with Silas and, cutting across Asia Minor by land, reached Europe for the first time: Macedonia and Achaea. The stay at Corinth is the only point that another source dates: an inscription at Delphi puts the proconsulship of Gallio in AD 51–52; the other years are reckoned back from it, and are therefore only approximate.

From the departure from Troas part of the text speaks in the first person plural (“we”), as if the writer himself had taken part in the journey. The numbers in brackets give chapter and verse. On land the line is the probable route found on the map’s road network; at sea, where the text moves from port to port, the line consists of straight stretches through the named ports, islands and capes – it shows only the probable direction, not the ship’s exact course.

s.t: Paul suggested to Barnabas that they visit the brothers again in the cities where they had been on the first journey. Barnabas wanted to take John (Mark) with them, but Paul did not, because he had left them in Pamphylia; the dispute was so sharp that they parted. Barnabas sailed to Cyprus with Mark, while Paul chose Silas and set out through Syria and Cilicia (15:36–41).

Through Syria and Cilicia – the text does not name the route; the line shows the road through Tarsus and the Cilician Gates – they came to Derbe and then to Lystra. Here Timothy joined them, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, well spoken of by the brothers (16:1–3). In the cities they delivered the decisions of the council at Jerusalem (16:4).

s.h: Troas: the vision of the Macedonian
s.t:
Then they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia. According to the text the Holy Spirit forbade them to speak the word in the province of Asia; they tried to go into Bithynia, but “the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them”; so they passed through Mysia and came to Troas, the port city at the entrance of the Dardanelles (16:6–8). The text does not give the route exactly; the line shows only the probable direction.

At Troas Paul saw a vision in the night: a man of Macedonia stood before him and begged him, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.” From this sentence on the text speaks in the first person plural: “immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia” (16:9–10).

From Troas they sailed straight to the island of Samothrace, and the next day reached Neapolis (Kavála) (16:11). That is about two days at sea. On the third journey they covered the same stretch in the opposite direction, from Philippi to Troas, in five days (20:6) – the difference shows well how much the direction of the wind and the season mattered. In the northern Aegean northerly winds (the Etesians) prevail in summer, which favour sailing southwards.

Philippi was, according to the text, the first city of that part of Macedonia and a Roman colony (16:12) – veterans were settled here in 42 BC, after the battle of Philippi. On the sabbath, outside the city gate by the river, where people used to pray, they met Lydia, a seller of purple from Thyatira, who was baptised and received them into her house (16:13–15).

A slave girl possessed by a spirit of divination, who brought her masters much gain by fortune-telling, followed them crying out for many days; Paul drove the spirit out of her. Her masters dragged Paul and Silas into the marketplace before the magistrates, who had them beaten with rods and thrown into prison. At night an earthquake shook the prison and the doors opened; the jailer was about to kill himself, but Paul stopped him, and the jailer was baptised with his household. The next day it came out that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens who had been beaten without trial; so the magistrates themselves begged them to leave the city (16:16–40).

Through Amphipolis and Apollonia – along the Via Egnatia – they went to Thessalonica, the seat of the province of Macedonia. For three sabbaths Paul reasoned in the synagogue (17:1–3). His opponents gathered a mob, attacked the house of Jason, where Paul was staying, and not finding him, dragged Jason and some brothers before the rulers of the city (17:5–9). The text calls these officials politarchs; this title is confirmed by inscriptions from Thessalonica.

The brothers sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. The Beroeans were, according to the text, “more noble” than those of Thessalonica: they received the word readily and examined the Scriptures daily. When the Jews of Thessalonica came after them there too, the brothers sent Paul off to the sea; Silas and Timothy stayed in Beroea (17:10–14).

Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens (17:15). The text does not say whether he went by ship or by land – only that the brothers sent him to the sea –, so the line here shows only the overland direction.

Paul was provoked to see the city full of idols. He reasoned in the synagogue and daily in the agora; Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him and took him to the Areopagus to explain his new teaching. He began his speech by saying that in the city he had seen an altar with the inscription “To an unknown god”. When he spoke of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, while others said, “We want to hear you again concerning this.” A few joined him, among them Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris (17:16–34).

At Corinth, the seat of the province of Achaea, Paul stayed with Aquila and Priscilla: this Jewish couple had recently come from Italy, because the emperor Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. They practised the same trade as Paul: they were tentmakers, and they worked together (18:1–3). Paul stayed in the city a year and a half (18:11).

When Gallio was proconsul of Achaea, some of the Jews brought Paul before the tribunal. But Gallio would not take up the case: if it were a matter of crime he would hear them, but he would not be a judge of words, names and the Jewish law (18:12–17). Gallio, the elder brother of the philosopher Seneca, was proconsul in AD 51–52 according to an inscription at Delphi; this is the only firm external anchor in the chronology of Paul’s journeys.

img.c: Fragment of the Gallio inscription at Delphi (Delphi Museum): Claudius’ letter mentions Gallio’s proconsulship of Achaea, which dates Paul’s stay in Corinth.

s.t: Corinth had two harbours; in the eastern one, Cenchreae on the Saronic Gulf, Paul had his hair cut because of a vow, and then sailed for Syria with Aquila and Priscilla (18:18).

At Ephesus Paul reasoned in the synagogue; they asked him to stay longer, but he declined, promising only to return if God willed. He left Aquila and Priscilla there and sailed on himself (18:19–21). On the third journey he did return, and spent more than two years here.

He landed at Caesarea, the seat and great harbour of the province of Judaea; he “went up and greeted the assembly” – the phrase probably refers to the church at Jerusalem – and then went down to Antioch (18:22).

The second journey ended at Antioch. The text does not say whether he went from Caesarea by sea or by land; the line shows the coastal road. Paul stayed here “some time”, then set out on his third journey (18:22–23).

t: Agricola’s campaigns in Britain (AD 77/78–83/84)
intro:
Gnaeus Julius Agricola was governor of Britain for seven years under Vespasian, Titus and Domitian. His campaigns extended Roman rule over northern Wales and northern England, then pushed deep into today’s Scotland, where he defeated the Caledonian tribes at the battle of Mons Graupius. He was the first Roman commander whose fleet sailed round Britain and proved it to be an island.

His biography was written in 98 by his son-in-law, the historian Tacitus. The work is laudatory: it presents Agricola as a victim of the cruel Domitian, and is therefore partial. Tacitus numbers the summers and gives no years; according to scholars the first summer was 77 or 78. In Scotland he names only estuaries and one mountain, so the points are symbolic; the archaeology of Roman marching camps and forts helps, but none can be tied with certainty to a particular year of Agricola. The numbers in brackets are chapters of the Agricola.

s.t: As a young man Agricola had already served in Britain as a tribune under Suetonius Paulinus at the time of Boudicca’s revolt (5), and later commanded the Twentieth Legion (7). As governor he arrived in midsummer; the soldiers thought there would be no campaign that year (18). Londinium was then the financial and commercial centre of the province; scholars think the governor’s seat may have been here, but Tacitus does not say so.

Before his arrival the Ordovices of north Wales had almost wiped out a cavalry squadron. Despite the late summer Agricola gathered the troops and almost exterminated the tribe. Then he wanted to take the island of Mona; there were no ships at hand, so he made auxiliaries who knew the ground and the fords swim the strait with their horses; the surprised islanders surrendered (18). Mona had already been attacked by Suetonius Paulinus in 60, but abandoned because of Boudicca’s revolt. The line starts from the legionary fortress of Deva (Chester); Tacitus does not name the starting point.

s.d: the first winter and second summer (78/79)
s.t:
Agricola put an end to his predecessors’ abuses in the collection of the grain tax (19). In summer he marched with the army, chose the camp sites himself and reconnoitred the estuaries and forests; many tribes gave hostages, and forts were built among them (20).

In winter he encouraged the Britons to build temples, forums and houses; he had the sons of chiefs educated in Latin culture, and the toga, baths and banquets came into fashion. Tacitus remarks bitterly: the ignorant called this civilisation, when it was part of their servitude (21). The fragmentary inscription of the forum of Verulamium dates the building in 79 with Agricola’s name – one of the rare archaeological confirmations of Tacitus’ account.

s.h: The third year: to the estuary of the Taus
s.t: The third year opened up new peoples; the ravaging reached as far as the estuary of the Taus (usually identified with the Tay). The enemy did not dare to attack the army, though it was battered by storms; forts were also built, and experts noted that no site chosen by Agricola was ever taken by the enemy (22). Trimontium was one of the main forts on Dere Street in Scotland; scholars date its foundation to Agricola’s time, but Tacitus does not mention it.

In the fourth summer he consolidated the conquered territory. The estuaries of the Clota (Clyde) and the Bodotria (Forth), carried far inland by the tides of two opposite seas, are separated only by a narrow strip of land; he secured it with garrisons, so that the enemy was pushed back as if into another island (23). Later the Antonine Wall was built here (around 142).

s.n: South-west Scotland facing Ireland (symbolic point; the crossing is disputed)
s.t: In the fifth year Agricola, crossing in the first ship, defeated peoples hitherto unknown, and posted troops in the part of Britain facing Ireland. The meaning of the Latin sentence is disputed: whether he crossed the Clota, or landed from the sea. According to Tacitus Agricola often said that Ireland could be conquered with one legion and a few auxiliaries; he kept an exiled Irish petty king with him under a show of friendship (24). The Romans never occupied Ireland.

s.n: Beyond the Bodotria (around Inchtuthil; symbolic point)
s.h: The sixth summer: the attack on the Ninth Legion
s.t:
In the sixth summer he marched against the tribes beyond the Bodotria; the fleet accompanied him along the coast and explored the harbours. The Caledonians attacked the Roman forts; Agricola divided the army into three columns. At night the enemy fell on the camp of the Ninth Legion, thought the weakest, and was already fighting inside when Agricola attacked them from the rear; only marshes and forests saved them from total defeat (25–26).

In the same summer a cohort of Usipi recruited in Germany mutinied, killed its centurion, seized three ships and sailed round Britain; in their hunger they ate one another, and were finally captured by the Suebi and Frisii (28). In the area of this point, at Inchtuthil, a legionary fortress was built in Agricola’s time or under his successors, and abandoned unfinished soon after.

s.n: Mons Graupius (site unknown; shown at the Durno camp and Bennachie)
s.t:
Agricola had lost his little son the year before. He sent the fleet ahead to raid the coasts and marched himself to Mount Graupius, which the enemy had already occupied: more than 30,000 armed men. Here Tacitus gives the famous speech of the Caledonian leader Calgacus against the Romans: “they make a desert and call it peace” (29–32).

Agricola placed 8,000 auxiliary infantry in the centre and 3,000 cavalry on the wings, keeping the legions in reserve before the camp. The Batavian and Tungrian cohorts opened the fight; those who fled into the woods were also surrounded. According to Tacitus 10,000 Britons fell, while the Romans lost 360 men, among them the cohort commander Aulus Atticus (35–37). The site of the battle is unknown; the large marching camp at Durno and the hill of Bennachie are among the most often suggested.

s.n: Winter quarters and the fleet’s voyage (symbolic point)
s.h: The Boresti, the fleet and the recall
s.t:
After the victory Agricola led the army into the territory of the Boresti, took hostages from them, then withdrew slowly into winter quarters, so that his very slowness should spread fear. The fleet sailed round Britain and returned to the Trucculensian harbour (38); according to Tacitus it was then proved that Britain was an island, and the fleet conquered the Orcades (Orkney) and saw Thule from afar (10).

Domitian received the news of the victory with jealousy. He recalled Agricola in 84 and gave him triumphal honours but no further command; he died in 93 (39–44). Elsewhere Tacitus writes bitterly that Britain was completely conquered and at once let go (Histories 1.2): the Scottish forts, Inchtuthil among them, were evacuated within a few years.

t: Trajan’s First Dacian War (AD 101–102)
intro:
In 89 Domitian had made peace with the Dacian king Decebalus, and Rome paid him money every year. Trajan considered this humiliating: according to Dio he judged the Dacians’ past deeds deserving of punishment, resented the annual payments, and saw that their power and pride were growing (Dio 68.6.1). In 101 he led the army across the Danube himself.

Few written sources survive on the war. Trajan wrote his own commentaries (Dacica), but only a single sentence of them survives, in a late antique grammar book. Cassius Dio’s history survives only in a Byzantine epitome. The reliefs of Trajan’s Column in Rome depict the war in detail, but linking the scenes to places is the interpretation of scholars. The places and the route can therefore often be given only as assumptions; the text says so.

s.t: According to the inscribed records of the priestly college of the Arval Brethren, on 25 March 101 extraordinary vows were made for the safety and fortunate return of the emperor; scholars think Trajan set out for the Dacian war on that day or the next. According to Dio, Trajan was in his forty-second year when he began to rule, at the height of his bodily and mental strength (Dio 68.6.3); at the start of the war he was thus about forty-seven.

s.n: Lederata (Ram) – the crossing place is an assumption
s.t: The first scenes of Trajan’s Column show the Danube frontier posts and an army marching over a bridge laid on boats. Most scholars place one of the crossings at Lederata near Viminacium; this is an assumption. Apollodorus, the emperor’s engineer, had earlier had a road cut into the cliffs of the Iron Gates; the Tabula Traiana inscription on the Serbian bank of the Danube preserves its memory.

img.c: A river crossing in a scene of Trajan’s Column (plaster cast, National History Museum of Romania, Bucharest).

s.t: Of Trajan’s own war commentaries a single sentence has come down to us, because the grammarian Priscian quoted it as an example of a grammatical rule: “inde Berzobim, deinde Aizi processimus” – “from there we advanced to Berzobis, then to Aizis”. Berzobis stood on the site of modern Berzovia in the Banat; later the camp of the Fourth Legion Flavia was here.

Aizis is the second station of the sentence; a Roman fort was later built on the site of the Dacian settlement. From the two names scholars think the main army marched through the Banat towards the Dacian mountains. The surviving sentence also shows that Trajan, like Caesar, wrote – but in the first person.

s.n: Tapae (near the “Iron Gate” pass; the site is disputed)
s.h: Tapae: a mushroom with a message
s.t: Near Tapae, where the Dacians were encamped, a large mushroom was brought to Trajan, on which the advice of the Buri and other allies was written in Latin, that he should turn back and keep the peace. Trajan nevertheless engaged them. Many of his soldiers were wounded, but he killed many of the enemy; when the bandages ran out he tore up his own clothing for the wounded. In honour of the fallen he had an altar raised and ordered yearly funeral rites (Dio 68.8). The exact site of the battle is disputed; the marker stands near the pass leading from the Bistra valley into Transylvania.

s.h: The Dacian winter counterattack in Moesia
s.t: According to the usual interpretation of the scenes of Trajan’s Column, during the winter the Dacians and their allies crossed the Danube and attacked Lower Moesia, and Trajan hurried by ship to the region under attack. Dio’s account of this stage has not survived. Some scholars think the decisive battle took place near modern Adamclisi: here Trajan raised in 109 the huge victory monument dedicated to Mars the Avenger, the Tropaeum Traiani, and here also stands an altar bearing the names of fallen soldiers. Which battle they commemorate is disputed.

img.c: The Tropaeum Traiani victory monument at Adamclisi, 1977 reconstruction.

s.t: In 102 Trajan seized fortified heights and found weapons, siege engines and the standard captured from Fuscus’ army in Domitian’s time. Maximus captured Decebalus’ sister. Decebalus then accepted the terms: he would surrender his arms, engines and engineers and the deserters, demolish his forts, withdraw from captured land, and treat Rome’s friends and enemies as his own – but according to Dio he had no intention of keeping them. Trajan left a garrison in the camp at Sarmizegetusa and returned to Italy (Dio 68.9).

img.c: Sarmizegetusa Regia, the sacred precinct of the Dacian capital: andesite sanctuaries and the so-called solar disc.

s.t: Decebalus’ envoys made their submission before the senate, and the senate ratified the peace. Trajan celebrated a triumph and took the title Dacicus; he staged gladiatorial games and brought back the pantomime dancers (Dio 68.10.1–2). The peace, however, lasted only three years (see the next walk). The line of the return journey shows only the direction.

t: Trajan’s Second Dacian War (AD 105–106)
intro:
Decebalus did not keep the peace: he gathered arms, received deserters, repaired his forts, and seized part of the land of the Iazyges, allies of Rome. The senate again declared him an enemy, and Trajan once more went to war in person (Dio 68.10.3–4). This war ended with the conquest of Dacia and its organisation as a province.

The main written source is again Cassius Dio’s epitome; alongside it, a few inscriptions and the second half of Trajan’s Column. The route from the Danube to Sarmizegetusa is not known; the line shows only the direction.

s.t: According to the town chronicle of Ostia, the Fasti Ostienses, Trajan set out for Dacia on the day before the Nones of June, 4 June. The Arval Brethren again made vows for his safety. By what route he reached the Danube we do not know; at the start of the second part of Trajan’s Column a voyage from a harbour is shown, which scholars identify with Ancona or Brundisium.

s.h: The stone bridge over the Danube
s.t:
Trajan had a stone bridge built over the Danube, which Dio regards as the emperor’s greatest work. It had twenty piers of squared stone, each 150 feet high above the foundations and 60 feet wide; the piers stood 170 feet apart and were joined by arches. The river is narrowest here, but deep, swift and eddying, which made the building especially difficult (Dio 68.13.1–4). The bridge was designed by Apollodorus of Damascus. In Dio’s time only the piers stood: Hadrian had the superstructure removed so that the barbarians could not cross by it (68.13.5–6). Remains of the piers can still be seen.

Meanwhile Decebalus sent deserters to kill the emperor in Moesia, where he received everyone; one was caught and confessed. The Dacian king captured the Roman commander Longinus by a trick and demanded territory and war compensation for him. Longinus obtained poison through a freedman and poisoned himself so that he could not be used for blackmail (Dio 68.11–12).

img.c: Scenes XCVIII–C of Trajan’s Column in C. Cichorius’ edition (1896–1900): in scene XCIX the emperor sacrifices by the Danube, with the stone bridge behind.
img.a: Attributed to Apollodorus of Damascus / Conrad Cichorius

s.h: The fall of Sarmizegetusa and the death of Decebalus
s.t:
Trajan crossed the Danube and conducted the war cautiously but in hard fighting; Dio mentions a mortally wounded horseman who returned to the line and died fighting (68.14.1–2). When the Dacian capital and the country had fallen and Decebalus was threatened with capture, he killed himself; his head was taken to Rome (68.14.3).

According to a tombstone found near Philippi, Tiberius Claudius Maximus, a scout of the Second Pannonian cavalry regiment, “captured Decebalus and brought his head to [the emperor] at Ranisstorum”; for this he was promoted decurion. The site of Ranisstorum is unknown. According to Dio, Decebalus’ treasure was hidden under the bed of the river Sargetia, which he had diverted with the help of captives; the captives were then killed, but a confidant, Bicilis, betrayed the hiding place (68.14.4–5) – several scholars doubt this story.

img.c: The suicide of Decebalus on Trajan’s Column (plaster cast, Bucharest).

s.t: According to Dio, Dacia thus became Roman, and Trajan founded cities in it (68.14.3). The capital of the province was a new Roman colony built on a plain about 40 km west of the old Dacian capital, named Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa. In these years Pannonia was divided in two; among the first governors of Lower Pannonia was the future emperor Hadrian, who resided at Aquincum (HA, Hadrian 3.9).

img.c: Silver denarius of Trajan inscribed DAC CAP (“Dacia capta”, Dacia conquered): Dacia in mourning sits on captured arms (AD 103–111; found in England).
img.a: Salisbury and South Wiltshire Museum, Richard Henry, 2014-06-23…

s.t: Trajan returned to Rome, to which many peoples, including Indians, sent embassies. He held games on 123 days, at which about 11,000 wild and tame animals were killed and 10,000 gladiators fought (Dio 68.15.1). From the Dacian booty he built his forum; beside it, the 30 m relief column depicting the war was dedicated in 113. The line of the return journey shows only the direction.

t: Trajan’s Parthian War, part 1: Armenia and Mesopotamia (AD 113–115)
intro:
The pretext of the war was that the Parthian king, Osroes, had placed a king on the throne of Armenia without Rome’s consent. According to Dio, Trajan’s real aim was glory (Dio 68.17.1). The campaign was at first successful: Armenia and northern Mesopotamia became Roman provinces.

The order and years of the war’s events are uncertain, because Dio’s work survives only in a fragmentary epitome, and the epitomator at times confused the order. The walk follows the summary of the Encyclopaedia Iranica; the exact dates come from the chronicle of Malalas, which several scholars consider unreliable.

s.t: Trajan set out from Rome in the autumn of 113. In the same year the column depicting the Dacian wars was dedicated in his forum.

img.c: Trajan’s Column in Rome, in Trajan’s Forum.

s.t: At Athens envoys of the Parthian king Osroes met him with gifts and an offer of peace. They asked that Parthamasiris be king of Armenia, and indicated that Osroes had already removed the previous king, Axidares. Trajan did not accept the gifts and answered only that friendship is proved by deeds, not words (Dio 68.17.2–3).

According to Dio, Trajan went by way of Asia, Lycia and the neighbouring provinces to Seleucia (Pieria), then to Antioch (68.18.1); according to Malalas he entered the city on 7 January. Abgarus, king of Osroene, sent gifts and a message of friendship but did not come in person, because he feared both Trajan and the Parthians (68.18.1). The sea line shows only the direction.
In spring Trajan set out north from Antioch and took Arsamosata, on the Armenian border, without a fight (Dio 68.19.2). The line shows the probable route via Melitene.

At Satala, the easternmost legionary camp of the Anatolian frontier, Trajan honoured Anchialus, king of the Heniochi and Machelones, with gifts (Dio 68.19.2). In this way he bound the kings of the peoples between the Black Sea and the Caucasus to Rome.

At Elegeia Trajan was sitting on a tribunal in the camp when Parthamasiris appeared, saluted him, took the diadem from his head and laid it at his feet, hoping to receive it back. The soldiers then hailed Trajan as imperator; the prince took this as an insult and a threat, and tried to flee. Later he declared publicly that he had come voluntarily, not as one defeated, and expected to receive his kingdom back as Tiridates had received it from Nero. Trajan, however, declared that Armenia belonged to Rome and would have a Roman governor; he sent Parthamasiris away under cavalry escort and kept the Armenians in the camp as subjects (Dio 68.19.3–20.3). According to other sources Parthamasiris died soon afterwards.

Abgarus, king of Osroene, finally received Trajan at Edessa; his son Arbandes won the emperor’s favour through his good looks, and his father was pardoned. Abgarus gave the emperor a banquet, at which his son also performed a barbarian dance. Mannus and Sporaces, the neighbouring rulers, also submitted (Dio 68.21). According to the Iranica, Trajan left Armenia at the end of July 114 and reached Nisibis by September; others put all this in 115.

The senate voted Trajan many honours, among them the title Optimus, “the best”. The emperor always marched on foot at the head of his troops and forded rivers with them. After taking Nisibis and Batnae he received, according to Dio, the title Parthicus as well (68.23); inscriptions and coins, however, use it only from early 116. Meanwhile Lusius Quietus took Singara and other places without a fight (68.22.2).

img.c: Sestertius of Trajan inscribed ARMENIA ET MESOPOTAMIA IN POTESTATEM P R REDACTAE: “Armenia and Mesopotamia brought under the power of the Roman people” (AD 116–117).

s.t: Trajan was spending the winter at Antioch when a terrible earthquake destroyed the city; because the emperor was there, many people from every part of the empire were in the city. Many died, among them Pedo, one of the consuls. A woman and her infant were pulled alive from the ruins days later: the mother had kept herself and her child alive with her own milk. Trajan escaped through a window with slight injuries; in the following days he lived in the open air in the hippodrome. Even Mount Casius shook (Dio 68.24–25). According to Malalas it happened on 13 December.

t: Trajan’s Parthian War, part 2: to the Persian Gulf and back (AD 116–117)
intro:
In the spring of 116 Trajan took the field again, this time aiming to conquer all Mesopotamia. He took Adiabene and the Parthian capital, Ctesiphon, and reached the Persian Gulf – Roman armies never got so far again. Meanwhile, however, the conquered lands revolted, and the Jewish revolt broke out in the eastern part of the empire. The siege of Hatra ended in failure, Trajan fell ill, and he died on the way to Italy.

The main source is Cassius Dio’s epitome (68.26–33). The order and places of the events are disputed at several points; the line shows the probable route along the Tigris and the Euphrates.

s.t: At the beginning of spring Trajan hurried into enemy territory. Since there was not enough timber along the Tigris for shipbuilding, he had boats built in the forests around Nisibis and carried to the river on wagons; they were made so that they could be taken apart for transport (Dio 68.26.1).

s.n: Crossing the Tigris (approximate site, around Cizre)
s.t: Opposite the Gordyaean mountains a bridge of boats was thrown across the Tigris. The barbarians on the far bank tried to prevent it, but the Romans deceived them with feigned crossings by many boats and with boats loaded with archers and heavy infantry, and got across (Dio 68.26.2). The exact place is unknown; the marker stands near modern Cizre, where the Tigris leaves the mountains.

The Romans took Adiabene, the district of Assyria around Ninus, to which Arbela and Gaugamela also belonged – where Alexander the Great defeated Darius (Dio 68.26.4). The fortress of Adenystrae was taken by the centurion Sentius: a prisoner, he freed himself and his comrades, killed the commander and opened the gate to the Romans (68.22.3). The site of Adenystrae is unknown; the marker stands at Arbela.

From here Trajan pressed on as far as Babylon without fighting, because internal strife had weakened the Parthians. He also saw the asphalt built into the walls of Babylon (Dio 68.26.4–27.1). Dio notes that the circuit of Babylon was 400 stades.

Trajan wanted to dig a canal between the Euphrates and the Tigris to bring his boats across, but since the Euphrates stood higher, it was feared the river would flood the land. So the boats were hauled overland at the narrowest point between the two rivers, he crossed the Tigris and entered Ctesiphon. His soldiers hailed him imperator, he confirmed the name Parthicus, and the senate voted that he might celebrate as many triumphs as he wished (Dio 68.28.1–2).

img.c: Gold coin of Trajan inscribed PARTHIA CAPTA (“Parthia conquered”), struck in summer AD 116.
