s.n: Mesene and the Persian Gulf (Spasinou Charax; approximate site)
s.h: On the shore of the Ocean
s.t:
Trajan wanted to sail down to the Erythraean Sea. He won over Mesene, an island in the Tigris, whose king Athambelus remained loyal to him, although he was ordered to pay tribute. The fleet was nearly lost because of the current of the Tigris, the tide and a storm. The people of the “Palisade of Spasinus” (Spasinou Charax) received him in friendship (Dio 68.28.3–4).

When he reached the Ocean and saw a ship setting sail for India, he said: “I should certainly have crossed over to the Indi too, if I were still young.” He was thinking of Alexander the Great and called him fortunate, but he also claimed that he had gone further than Alexander, and wrote so to the senate (Dio 68.29.1). The marker stands at the supposed site of Charax, near Basra.

s.h: Sacrifice in the room where Alexander died
s.t:
At Babylon, where he had gone because of its fame and because of Alexander, he sacrificed to Alexander’s spirit in the room where the Macedonian king had died. Here he learned that the conquered lands had revolted and that their garrisons had been driven out or killed. He sent Lusius Quietus and Maximus against them: Maximus was defeated and fell, but Lusius recovered Nisibis and took and burned Edessa; Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander burned Seleucia (Dio 68.29.4–30.2).

Meanwhile the Jewish revolt broke out in Cyrene, Egypt and Cyprus; according to Dio 220,000 people perished in Cyrene and 240,000 in Cyprus. The revolt was put down by Lusius (68.32).

So that the Parthians would not revolt, Trajan assembled the Romans and Parthians on a great plain near Ctesiphon, spoke from a tribunal, and made Parthamaspates their king, placing the diadem on his head (Dio 68.30.3). According to Dio the Parthians later refused to accept him and drove him out (68.33.2).

img.c: Sestertius of Trajan inscribed REX PARTHIS DATVS (“a king given to the Parthians”): the emperor, seated on a platform, places the diadem on Parthamaspates’ head (AD 116).

s.t: Hatra was a small and poor city in the desert, with little and bad water and no timber or fodder; these hardships, and its being consecrated to the Sun-god, protected it. Trajan’s cavalry attacked the walls but were repulsed. The emperor had taken off his imperial dress so as not to be recognised, but his grey hair and dignified face betrayed him: they shot at him and killed a horseman in his escort. Thunder, rain, hail and lightning struck the besiegers, and flies swarmed over their food and drink. Trajan withdrew, and from then on his health began to decline (Dio 68.31).

img.c: Temple ruins at Hatra (photo c. 1988).

s.t: Trajan was preparing another campaign into Mesopotamia, but his illness grew worse, and he took ship to return to Italy. He entrusted the army in Syria to Hadrian. At Selinus in Cilicia, which was afterwards called Traianopolis, he died suddenly, having reigned 19 years, 6 months and 15 days (Dio 68.33.1–3). His death was kept secret for some days, and Hadrian was proclaimed emperor at Antioch (Dio 69.1; see the Hadrian walks). Hadrian gave up the conquests beyond the Tigris and the Euphrates. The line from Hatra via Antioch and by sea shows only the direction.

t: The third journey of the Apostle Paul (c. AD 53–57)
intro:
The centre of the third journey is Ephesus, the great city of the province of Asia, where Paul spent more than two years. From here he set off back to Jerusalem through Macedonia and Greece; the text describes the sea stretch of the return day by day, port by port. This part shows well how coastal ships travelled: they sailed by day and put in at night.

Paul wanted to be in Jerusalem by Pentecost (the fiftieth day after Passover); the departure after Passover therefore places the journey in the spring sailing season. Here too the years are only approximate. The numbers in brackets give chapter and verse. On land the line is the probable route found on the map’s road network; at sea, where the text moves from port to port, the line consists of straight stretches through the named ports, islands and capes – it shows only the probable direction, not the ship’s exact course.

s.t: From Antioch Paul “went through the region of Galatia and Phrygia in order”, strengthening the disciples (18:23).

s.h: Ephesus: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
s.t:
Through the “upper country” he came to Ephesus (19:1). For three months he spoke in the synagogue; then, meeting opposition there, he taught daily for two years in the school of Tyrannus, “so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord” (19:8–10). Later, in his farewell speech, Paul himself speaks of three years (20:31). Many who practised magic burned their books; their value was reckoned at fifty thousand pieces of silver (19:19).

Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, called the craftsmen together: Paul’s teaching endangered their trade and the worship of the great goddess whom “all Asia and the world” worshipped. The crowd rushed into the theatre, dragging two of Paul’s companions with them; for about two hours they shouted, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” In the end the town clerk calmed them: if they had a complaint, there were the courts and the proconsuls (19:23–40). The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world; the ruins of the theatre still stand.

img.c: The Great Theatre of Ephesus, where according to Acts the riot broke out (Acts 19:29).

s.t:
After the uproar Paul took leave of the disciples and went to Macedonia; he went through those parts and then came to Greece, where he stayed three months (20:1–3). The text does not name the city; most scholars think of Corinth, because the Letter to the Romans is usually dated to this stay at Corinth. The marker is therefore uncertain.

When he was about to sail for Syria, the Jews plotted against him, so he decided to return through Macedonia instead (20:3). The text also lists his companions: Sopater of Beroea, Aristarchus and Secundus of Thessalonica, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia (20:4).

His companions went ahead and waited for him at Troas; “we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread” – here the first-person plural narrative begins again (20:5–6). The feast of Unleavened Bread lasts the seven days after Passover; the departure therefore fell in spring, at the end of March or in April.

From Philippi (more precisely from its port, Neapolis) they reached Troas in five days and spent seven days there (20:6). On the second journey the same stretch in the opposite direction had taken about two days (16:11).

On the first day of the week they gathered to break bread in an upper room where there were many lamps. Paul spoke until midnight, as he intended to leave the next day. A young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window, fell asleep and fell down from the third storey; he was taken up dead. Paul went down, embraced him and said, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.” Then he went back up, talked with them until daybreak, and departed (20:7–12).

f: Col. Augusta Iulia Philippensis|Assyla|Col. Victrix Philippensis|Philippes|Κρηνίδες Καβάλας
calc.src: According to the text they reached Troas from Philippi in five days (20:6); on the second journey the opposite direction took about two days (16:11). The date is an estimate: c. AD 57, mid-April – after the days of Unleavened Bread. The calculator counts a separate day for boarding and unloading; its estimate for the sea part (with favourable and unfavourable winds) is worth comparing with the five days.

s.t: His companions went ahead on the ship to Assos, where they were to take Paul on board, for he had arranged to go there on foot (20:13). Troas and Assos are some 33 km apart in a straight line across the Troad; the ship, however, had to round Cape Lectum.
At Assos they took Paul on board and went to Mitylene, the chief city of the island of Lesbos (20:14).

s.h: Miletus: farewell to the Ephesian elders
s.t:
They travelled day by day: the next day they were opposite the island of Chios, the following day they touched at Samos, and the day after they came to Miletus (20:15). Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so as not to spend time in Asia: he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost (20:16).

From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to him. In his farewell speech he said that he was now going to Jerusalem, bound by the Spirit, not knowing what would happen to him there, except that in every city bonds and afflictions awaited him; and that they would see his face no more. They knelt and prayed, wept much and embraced him, and accompanied him to the ship (20:17–38).

img.c: The theatre of Miletus.

s.t: “With a straight course” they came to the island of Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara, a port of Lycia (21:1). At Patara they changed ships: they found one crossing over to Phoenicia and went aboard (21:2). They moved from a coastal vessel to a ship crossing the open sea – the route from Lycia to Phoenicia was one of the main sailing routes of the Mediterranean.

They sighted Cyprus and left it on the left hand – that is, they sailed past the south side of the island –, sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo. Seeking out the disciples, they stayed seven days; the disciples, through the Spirit, warned Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. When they left, the disciples with their wives and children escorted them out of the city, and they knelt on the beach and prayed (21:3–6).
From Tyre they sailed to Ptolemais (Acre), thus finishing the voyage; they greeted the brothers and stayed with them one day (21:7).

The next day they came to Caesarea and stayed in the house of Philip the evangelist, who had four unmarried daughters who prophesied. They stayed many days. Then the prophet Agabus came down from Judaea: he took Paul’s belt, bound his own hands and feet with it, and said that thus the Jews at Jerusalem would bind the man who owned this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles. In vain they begged Paul not to go up; he answered that he was ready not only to be bound but also to die at Jerusalem (21:8–14).

At Jerusalem the brothers received them gladly (21:17). A few days later, however, Jews from Asia recognised Paul in the Temple and accused him of bringing Greeks into the holy place; the crowd dragged him out and tried to kill him. The commander of the Roman garrison (chiliarch) intervened with soldiers and had Paul bound in chains and taken into the fortress (21:27–36).

When it came out that more than forty men had sworn neither to eat nor to drink until they had killed Paul, the commander, Claudius Lysias, sent him by night with a strong escort – two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen – through Antipatris to Caesarea, to the governor Felix (23:12–33). Paul remained a prisoner at Caesarea for two years; before Felix’s successor, Porcius Festus, he appealed to Caesar (24:27; 25:11). With this the journey to Rome begins – that is the next walk.

t: The Apostle Paul’s voyage to Rome and the shipwreck (c. AD 59–60)
intro:
In prison at Caesarea, before the governor Porcius Festus, Paul appealed to Caesar (25:11), and so he was taken to Rome as a prisoner. Chapters 27–28 of Acts are one of the most detailed descriptions of a sea voyage from antiquity: they give the ships, the ports, the winds, the depth of water, the number of people on board and the length of the stays.

The account shows well the seasons of Roman sailing. According to Vegetius (4th century) sailing was safe between 27 May and 14 September, uncertain until 11 November, and between 11 November and 10 March the sea was “closed”. Paul’s ship left Crete at the end of the uncertain season and was driven by a storm to Malta, where it had to wait out the winter. The calculator uses the same seasonal model. The years are approximate (Festus’ arrival is usually placed around AD 59 or 60). The numbers in brackets give chapter and verse. On land the line is the probable route found on the map’s road network; at sea, where the text moves from port to port, the line consists of straight stretches through the named ports, islands and capes – it shows only the probable direction, not the ship’s exact course.

s.t: Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan cohort. They boarded a ship of Adramyttium bound for places on the coast of Asia; Aristarchus of Thessalonica was with them (27:1–2). From here the text again speaks in the first person plural.
The next day they touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends and be cared for (27:3).

Sailing from Sidon they went under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary; crossing the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia they came to Myra in Lycia (27:4–5). Because of the north-westerly summer winds, ships heading west went along the east and north side of Cyprus, near the coast of Asia Minor.

At Myra the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put them on board (27:6). Later it turns out that it was carrying wheat (27:38): it was one of the grain ships that supplied Rome from Egypt, which regularly went round by the coasts of Lycia.
“When we had sailed slowly many days”, with difficulty they came opposite Cnidus; the wind would not let them go further (27:7). Myra and Cnidus are some 240 km apart in a straight line.

s.h: Fair Havens: “the Fast had already gone by”
s.t:
From Cnidus they turned to the lee, the south side of Crete, by Cape Salmone, and coasting along with difficulty came to a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea (27:7–8).

“When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous, because the Fast had now already gone by”, Paul warned them that the voyage would bring injury and much loss (27:9–10). The Fast is the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), which falls at the end of September or the beginning of October; so they were already in Vegetius’ “uncertain” season. But the centurion put more trust in the helmsman and the owner of the ship. As the harbour was not suitable for wintering, the majority decided to try to reach Phoenix, a harbour of Crete facing south-west and north-west, and to winter there (27:11–12).

When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had attained their purpose: they weighed anchor and sailed close along the shore. But before long a stormy wind called Euraquilo (a north-easter) struck down from the island; the ship could not face the wind, so they let it drive (27:13–15).

Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, they managed with difficulty to hoist the boat aboard; they undergirded the hull with cables and, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis (the shallow gulfs of the Libyan coast), they lowered the gear (or a sea anchor) and were driven along. The next day they threw part of the cargo overboard, and on the third day the ship’s tackle with their own hands (27:16–19).

s.n: Malta (the traditional shipwreck site, St Paul’s Bay)
s.h: Fourteen days of storm, shipwreck and three months on Malta
s.t:
For many days neither sun nor stars appeared, and all hope was lost. According to the text Paul encouraged them: in the night an angel had appeared to him and said that he must stand before Caesar, and that no one would be lost, only the ship (27:20–26).

On the fourteenth night, as they were driven across the Adria, the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. They took soundings: twenty, then fifteen fathoms (about 37, then 27 m); fearing that they would run onto rocks, they let go four anchors from the stern. The sailors tried to escape in the boat, but the soldiers cut its ropes (27:27–32). Before dawn Paul urged them to eat; “in all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship” (27:37). Afterwards they threw the wheat into the sea to lighten the ship (27:38).

By day they noticed a bay with a beach and tried to run the ship ashore there, but it struck a shoal “where two seas met”: the bow stuck fast, and the stern was broken up by the waves. The soldiers wanted to kill the prisoners so that none would escape, but the centurion, wishing to save Paul, prevented them; those who could swim got ashore first, the rest on planks, and all escaped safely (27:39–44). The island was Malta (28:1).

Between Cauda and St Paul’s Bay the distance is about 880 km in a straight line; reckoning with about thirteen days of drifting, that is about 65–70 km a day.

The islanders showed “uncommon kindness”: they kindled a fire, because it was raining and cold. As Paul put sticks on the fire, a viper fastened on his hand; the natives thought he was a murderer whom Justice would not let live even though he had escaped from the sea, but when no harm came to him, they said he was a god (28:1–6).

On the estate of Publius, the “chief man” of the island, they were entertained for three days; Paul healed Publius’ father, who lay sick with fever and dysentery, and then the other sick people of the island (28:7–9). The title protos (“first”) also occurs in Maltese inscriptions. They stayed on the island three months (28:11) – roughly Vegetius’ closed winter season.

After three months they set out on a ship of Alexandria which had wintered at the island, and whose sign was the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux, protectors of sailors). They landed at Syracuse and stayed three days (28:11–12). If the shipwreck fell in early November, the departure can be put at the end of February or the beginning of March: still the end of Vegetius’ closed season, but grain ships set out at the very start of spring sailing.
From Syracuse they made a circuit – according to the text, “fetching a compass” – and came to Rhegium, on the Italian shore of the Strait of Messina (28:13).

s.h: With a south wind to Puteoli
s.t: After one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day they came to Puteoli (Pozzuoli) (28:13). Puteoli was the great commercial harbour on the Bay of Naples where the Egyptian grain ships arrived, before Claudius and Trajan built the harbours of Ostia. Here they found brothers, who asked them to stay with them seven days (28:14).

calc.src: According to the text, after one day at Rhegium a south wind sprang up, and on the second day they came to Puteoli (28:13). The date is an estimate: c. AD 60, late February (three months after the November shipwreck); the calculator therefore allows winter sailing too, and warns about the closed season. The calculator uses average ship speeds and a day for boarding and unloading; with the favourable south wind the voyage in the text was faster.

img.c: The market hall (macellum) of Puteoli, the so-called Serapeum.

s.t: From Puteoli they set off overland, on the Via Appia, towards Rome. The brothers at Rome, hearing of them, came out to meet them as far as Forum Appii and Three Taverns; when Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage (28:15). Forum Appii lay about 43 miles, Three Taverns about 33 miles from Rome along the Via Appia.

In Rome Paul was allowed to live by himself with the soldier who guarded him (28:16). After three days he called together the leaders of the Jews of Rome and explained his case to them (28:17–28). For “two whole years” he lived in his own rented house, received all who came to him, and proclaimed the Kingdom of God “with all boldness, without hindrance” (28:30–31).

The Acts of the Apostles ends here; it does not describe his later fate. According to later Christian tradition Paul died a martyr in Rome under Nero.

t: The Amber Road from Aquileia to the Baltic
intro:
The Amber Road was the trade route along which amber gathered on the shores of the Baltic reached the Roman Empire. Within the empire it followed the Roman road linking northern Italy with the Danube through Pannonia: from Aquileia through Emona, Celeia, Poetovio, Salla, Savaria and Scarbantia to Carnuntum. North of Carnuntum it continued outside the empire, through the regions of the Morava and the Vistula, to the Baltic; its exact course is not known.

The only detailed ancient account is in Pliny’s Natural History (37.45): in Nero’s time a Roman knight was sent to the northern coasts for amber. The walk connects Pliny’s account with the archaeological sites of the road, which also crosses today’s Hungary. Within the empire the line is the route found on the map’s road network; north of Carnuntum it is a straight line that only indicates the direction.

s.t:
The Italian end of the Amber Road was Aquileia, the great trading city on the northern Adriatic. Here raw amber was worked: the carved amber jewellery, small vessels and figurines of the 1st-century workshops of Aquileia, found in the city’s graves, can be seen today in the archaeological museum of Aquileia, and reached many parts of the empire.

According to Pliny, Roman women valued amber as highly as precious stones; a small amber figurine cost more than a healthy slave (37.49) – Pliny censures this as a sign of luxury.
From Aquileia the road led over the low passes of the Julian Alps to Emona (Ljubljana), a colony founded under Augustus or Tiberius.
Celeia (Celje) was a town of the province of Noricum; it received municipal status under Claudius.
Poetovio (Ptuj) was a legionary base, and under Trajan a colony, on the bank of the Drava; here the Amber Road crossed the river and entered Pannonia.

Salla was built at the crossing of the river Zala along the Amber Road; under Hadrian it became a municipium. At Zalalövő archaeologists have excavated the town’s streets and houses and a stretch of the Amber Road; the finds can be seen in the Göcsej Museum at Zalaegerszeg.

Savaria was founded by the emperor Claudius as a colony (Colonia Claudia Savaria) along the Amber Road; it is one of the earliest towns of Pannonia, and Pliny too mentions it (3.146). Paved stretches of the Amber Road have also come to light in Szombathely; the town’s best-known Roman monument is the sanctuary of Isis (Iseum), whose partly rebuilt building can be visited today, as can the Járdányi Paulovics István Ruin Garden.

Scarbantia was built near Lake Fertő (Neusiedl), along the Amber Road; Pliny mentions it as “Scarabantia Iulia” (3.146), and under the Flavians it became a municipium. Remains of the Roman forum have come to light under today’s Main Square; the town’s medieval walls were partly built on the Roman walls.

Carnuntum stood on the Danube, at the frontier of the empire. Pliny measures the distance from here: “From Carnuntum in Pannonia it is about six hundred miles to the coast of Germany from which amber is brought; this was established only recently” (37.45). Six hundred Roman miles is about 890 km.

According to Pliny the Roman knight is still alive whom Julianus, the organiser of Nero’s gladiatorial games, sent out to get amber. The knight travelled round the coasts and markets and brought back so much amber that the knots of the nets protecting the podium from the wild beasts were decorated with amber, and even the weapons, the biers and all the equipment of one day’s games were of amber; the largest piece weighed thirteen pounds (37.45), about 4.3 kg.

img.c: Carnuntum: the 4th-century so-called Heidentor.

s.n: The Baltic coast (the marker shows the Sambian peninsula)
s.t:
The largest source of amber is the south-eastern coast of the Baltic, especially the Sambian peninsula (today’s Kaliningrad region). According to Tacitus the Aestii gather amber, which they call “glaesum”, from the shallows of the sea and from the shore; they do not use it themselves, but bring it to market unworked, and receive the price with astonishment (Germania 45).

The exact course between Carnuntum and the Baltic is not known; archaeological finds – Roman coins, vessels and amber stores – point to a route through the regions of the Morava, the Oder and the Vistula. Here the line shows only the direction.

img.c: Raw Baltic amber.

t: Pliny the Younger’s journey to the province of Bithynia (AD 109/111)
intro:
The emperor Trajan sent Pliny the Younger, senator and writer, with an extraordinary commission to govern the province of Bithynia and Pontus and put the cities’ finances in order. The correspondence of Pliny and Trajan (book X of the Letters) survives in full; the first letters concern the journey out. It is a short journey, but it shows well how much the wind and the summer heat mattered: the sea stretches were slowed by the northerly summer winds of the Aegean, the Etesians.

Scholars put the year at 109, 110 or 111; the month and day, however, are certain. The letters do not say where he set out from or where he entered the province; at sea the line consists of straight stretches and shows only the probable direction.

s.t: In his first letter Pliny reports to the emperor that he has safely rounded Cape Malea – the south-eastern tip of the Peloponnese, known among sailors as a dangerous, stormy cape – and arrived at Ephesus with all his retinue, although contrary winds held him up for a time (Ep. 10.15).

From Ephesus Pliny writes that he intends to go on partly by coastal vessels and partly by carriage: the land journey is made difficult by the heat, the sea journey by the persistent Etesian winds (Ep. 10.15). In his reply Trajan thanks him for the news of his journey, about which he is most interested (Ep. 10.16).

“As I had a very favourable voyage to Ephesus, so in travelling by carriage from there I was greatly troubled by the heat and some slight attacks of fever, and halted at Pergamum” – he writes (Ep. 10.17A). The road between Ephesus and Pergamum was one of the province’s main roads.

img.c: The theatre on the acropolis of Pergamon.

s.t:
From Pergamum he took to coastal vessels, but contrary winds held him up, so he reached Bithynia considerably later than expected, on 17 September. Yet he does not complain, for this way he could celebrate the emperor’s birthday in the province itself, a good omen (Ep. 10.17A). He set to work at once: he is examining the public accounts of the city of Prusa, and already sees that there have been many abuses (Ep. 10.17A).

In his reply Trajan writes that he wishes Pliny and his companions had reached Bithynia without illness or inconvenience, and that his journey from Ephesus had been as pleasant as before (Ep. 10.18). The letters do not say where he entered the province; the marker shows Prusa, the first city whose affairs he dealt with.

t: Ignatius of Antioch’s journey to martyrdom (c. AD 110)
intro:
Ignatius was bishop of Antioch. He was condemned and taken under military escort to Rome, to be thrown to wild beasts there. On the way he wrote seven letters to churches in Asia Minor, to the Christians of Rome and to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna; they are among the earliest works of Christian literature and the first witnesses of church organisation under a bishop. Why he was taken to Rome is not known.

Eusebius places the martyrdom under Trajan (98–117); scholars mostly date it to about 110, though some put it later (even around 140). The route is only partly known: from the letters Philadelphia, Smyrna, Troas and Neapolis are certain, and from Polycarp’s letter Philippi. The stretch from Antioch to Asia Minor (by land or by sea) and the journey after Philippi (probably along the Via Egnatia to Dyrrachium, then by ship to Italy) are conjecture. The line is a route found on the Roman road network; the abbreviations in brackets refer to the letters.

s.t: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch; the letters do not describe his condemnation, only that he was being taken in chains to Rome, where he would be thrown to wild beasts. He describes his journey: “From Syria even unto Rome I fight with wild beasts, by land and sea, by night and day, being bound to ten leopards, that is, a band of soldiers, who only grow worse when they are kindly treated” (Rom 5). According to the later, legendary martyr acts Trajan himself condemned him at Antioch – scholars do not consider this reliable.

The escort took him by the inland road, bypassing Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles. At Philadelphia Ignatius spoke to the congregation in a loud voice about unity: they should hold to their bishop, presbyters and deacons (Phld 7). He found division in the city and later warned them by letter as well.

At Smyrna he spent a longer time; bishop Polycarp received him. The churches of the region sent envoys to him here: from Ephesus bishop Onesimus and his companions, from Magnesia bishop Damas, from Tralles bishop Polybius. From here he wrote to the churches of Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles, and to the Christians of Rome.

In his letter to the Romans he begged them not to try to save him: “I am God’s wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts that I may be found pure bread of Christ” (Rom 4). He dated the letter on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, that is 24 August (Rom 10).

img.c: Remains of the agora of Smyrna (from the rebuilding after the earthquake of 178).

s.h: Troas: three letters and good news
s.t: At Troas Ignatius received good news: the church at Antioch was at peace. From here he wrote to the Philadelphians, the Smyrnaeans and Polycarp; the letters were carried partly by the Ephesian deacon Burrhus. He asked the churches to send an envoy to Antioch to rejoice with them. He could not write to every church, because he had to sail suddenly for Neapolis; so he asked Polycarp to write in his name (Pol 8).
From Troas he was taken by ship to Neapolis, the port of Macedonia (Pol 8) – along the same route by which the apostle Paul had first entered Europe.

From Polycarp’s letter to the Philippians we know that the Philippians received the prisoners wearing “chains befitting saints” and escorted them on their way (Phil 1); they saw Ignatius, and Zosimus and Rufus, with their own eyes (Phil 9). At their request Polycarp sent them the letters of Ignatius he had, and asked them for news of Ignatius’ fate (Polycarp, Phil 13). It is to this collection that we owe the survival of the letters.

After Philippi we have no more sources. The most likely conjecture is that he was taken along the Via Egnatia through Thessalonica to Dyrrachium, where they took ship for Italy. A later, legendary martyr act describes a different sea route; scholars do not accept it.

There is no eyewitness account of the circumstances of Ignatius’ death. Polycarp’s letter speaks of the ‘blessed’ Ignatius as though he were dead (Phil 9); Irenaeus (around 180) quotes Ignatius’ saying about the wheat and the teeth of the beasts (Adv. haer. 5.28.4); Eusebius dates the martyrdom to Trajan’s reign (Church History 3.36). The tradition that he died in the Colosseum is much later. According to Jerome his remains were taken back to Antioch.

t: Hadrian’s journey from Antioch to Rome (AD 117–118)
intro:
Trajan died in Cilicia in August 117, and Hadrian, governor of Syria, was proclaimed emperor at Antioch. The new emperor did not hurry straight to Rome: he went through Asia Minor to the lower Danube, where the Sarmatians and Roxolani were attacking, and reached the capital only in the summer of 118 (HA 5.9–7.3).

One stretch of this journey is known day by day – if we accept a scholarly assumption. A fragmentary stone inscription found in Rome (CIL VI 5076) lists the stations of the main road from Tarsus to Cappadocia with dates from 12 to 19 October, giving the distances in days. The inscription names neither the emperor nor the year; W. Weber in 1907 and A. von Domaszewski suggested that it records Hadrian’s journey of 117, and Halfmann and Birley use it in this way. The days may differ by one according to different transcriptions (Birley: Tyana 17 October; an older reading: 18 October). A certain date is the letter from Juliopolis (11 November).

s.t: When he was proclaimed emperor, Hadrian was at Antioch, the capital of Syria, as governor of the province (Dio 69.2.1). According to the HA he received Trajan’s remains, escorted by Attianus, Plotina and Matidia, and sent them to Rome by ship; he put Catilius Severus in charge of Syria, then set out for Rome by way of Illyricum (HA 5.9–10). According to Birley he left Antioch at the beginning of October. The stretch between Antioch and Tarsus is not known; the line shows only the direction.

img.c: Gold coin (aureus) of Hadrian from AD 117: Trajan and Hadrian clasp hands, below ADOPTIO – the adoption on which Hadrian’s rule rested (Rome mint, RIC II 3).

s.t: According to scholars, Hadrian reached the capital of Cilicia on 12 October; this date is an inference counted back from the next, stone-recorded station. The city later took the name Hadriane.

s.h: Mopsucrene: the first station of the inscription
s.t: Mopsucrene was a road station at the southern foot of the Taurus, the last halt before the Cilician Gates, 12 miles from Tarsus according to the itineraries. According to the inscription from Rome he was here on 13 October (a. d. III Id. Oct.). From here on the stone lists the stations day by day. The emperor Constantius II later died at Mopsucrene, in 361.

According to the inscription the journey from Mopsucrene to Panhormos took one day. On the way the emperor passed through the Cilician Gates, the most famous pass of the Taurus, through which Alexander the Great’s army had once marched. The inscription gives the distance in days, not miles.

Aquae Calidae, the “Hot Waters”, stood on the site of the thermal springs of modern Çiftehan, on the road into Cappadocia. According to the inscription, the emperor reached Tyana from here in two days.

s.h: By way of Tynna to Tyana
s.t: He spent the night at Tynna (near modern Porsuk; the site is approximate), then reached Tyana, the main city of southern Cappadocia; according to Birley on 17 October, according to an older reading on the 18th. Tyana was the home town of Apollonius, the famous wonder-working philosopher.

s.h: Andabalis: the end of the inscription
s.t: The fragmentary inscription ends at Andabalis, a station on the road to Caesarea (Kayseri); the next station is unknown. From the days recorded on the stone and the miles of the itineraries, scholars have calculated a pace of about 25 Roman miles (about 37 km) a day.

In the capital of Galatia an inscription (IGR III 208) honours a local notable named Latinius Alexander, who helped with quartering the imperial army. When exactly Hadrian arrived, we do not know; “late October” is an estimate fitted between the two known dates.

At the road station of Juliopolis the emperor was overtaken by Claudius Cyrus, envoy of the association of young men (neoi) of Pergamum, who congratulated him on his accession. In a brief reply Hadrian thanked them for sharing his joy; the letter is dated “on the 3rd day before the Ides of November, from Juliopolis”, that is 11 November. A copy was carved in marble at Pergamum (IGR IV 349). Most of the ancient town now lies under the Sarıyar reservoir.
According to Birley he reached Nicaea at the end of November and spent the winter at Nicomedia and/or Byzantium. No ancient source states this; the “or” marks the uncertainty.

According to the HA, when news came of an incursion by the Sarmatians and Roxolani, Hadrian sent troops ahead and went to Moesia himself. The king of the Roxolani complained that his subsidy had been reduced; the emperor looked into the matter and made peace with him. He placed Marcius Turbo temporarily in charge of Pannonia and Dacia with the insignia of a prefect (HA 6.6–8). Where the talks took place, we do not know; the marker stands at Durostorum on the lower Danube for orientation only.

Meanwhile a conspiracy against the emperor was discovered: according to the HA, Nigrinus intended to kill him during a sacrifice, with the knowledge of Lusius Quietus and others. By order of the senate four former consuls were executed – Palma at Tarracina, Celsus at Baiae, Nigrinus at Faventia, Quietus on his journey – Hadrian later claimed against his will. He entrusted Dacia to Turbo and hurried to Rome to dispel the ill feeling caused by the four executions (HA 7.1–3).

According to Birley he arrived on 9 July; coins also celebrated his arrival. His route led through Illyricum (HA 5.10); the line through Viminacium, Sirmium and Aquileia shows only the probable direction. Three years later, in 121, he set out on his first great journey (see the Hadrian 1/1 walk).

t: Hadrian’s first great journey, part 1: from Gaul to Spain (AD 121–123)
intro:
Hadrian (reigned 117–138) spent the greater part of his reign on the road: according to Cassius Dio he went from province to province, inspected every garrison and fort, and travelled on foot or on horseback, never by carriage; he went bareheaded in the German snows and in the Egyptian heat alike (Dio 69.9). The only continuous account of the journey is the late antique Historia Augusta life of Hadrian, but it names only the provinces and a few events. Scholars have pieced together a more exact chronology from inscriptions, coins and papyri (Halfmann 1986, Birley 2003); these dates are marked in the text as “according to Birley”.

The first great journey lasted from 121 to 125; this walk shows its western part. Where it is only a scholarly assumption that Hadrian was in a given city, the text says so. The line follows known Roman roads, but nowhere do we know the actual route.

s.t: According to the Historia Augusta, after his measures in the capital Hadrian set out for Gaul (HA 10.1). According to Birley this was after the spring of 121. He did not return to Rome for four years.

In Gaul, according to the HA, Hadrian helped every community with various benefactions (HA 10.1). The biography names no cities; that he also visited Lugdunum, the centre of the Gallic provinces, is Birley’s assumption.

s.h: Germany: camp life and the palisade
s.t:
In Germany the emperor, although he preferred peace, trained the soldiers as if war were imminent. He himself lived among the soldiers, ate camp food – bacon, cheese and vinegar-water – and would walk as much as twenty miles in full armour. He tightened discipline, which had slackened since Augustus (HA 10.2–4). According to Dio he went bareheaded in the German snows (Dio 69.9.4).

According to the HA, where no river separated the Romans from the barbarians, he had a palisade built of great stakes driven deep into the ground (HA 12.6). The line of posts of the Upper German–Raetian limes may be its remains. According to Birley he spent the winter at Mogontiacum and also reached Raetia and Noricum.

img.c: A 1912 reconstruction of a watchtower and palisade of the Upper Germanic limes at Bendorf.

s.t: According to Birley he went in spring to Lower Germany, whose governor was Aulus Platorius Nepos, a friend of the emperor (HA 4.2 and 23.4 also name him among his friends). Nepos then became governor of Britain, and the Wall was built under his direction; the assumption is that he crossed to the island together with the emperor. That Hadrian was at Cologne is not certain; the marker shows the seat of the governor of Lower Germany.

According to the HA, Hadrian, having reformed the army “in the manner of a monarch”, set out for Britain (HA 11.2). At the start of his reign, according to the HA, the Britons could not be kept under control (HA 5.2). According to Birley he arrived in June 122; the marker shows Londinium, the main city of the province. The line down the Rhine and across the North Sea shows only the direction.

img.c: Head of a bronze statue of Hadrian, found in the River Thames in London (British Museum).

s.t:
In Britain Hadrian “corrected many abuses” and was the first to build a wall eighty miles long to separate the barbarians from the Romans (HA 11.2). The Wall ran from the mouth of the Tyne to the Solway Firth, about 117 km long; it was built by the legions stationed here. The bridge and fort on the Tyne took the name Pons Aelius from the emperor’s family name – Newcastle stands on the site today.

The HA also links to this British journey the emperor’s dismissal of his praetorian prefect Septicius Clarus and his secretary Suetonius Tranquillus, author of the Lives of the Caesars, because they had behaved more familiarly than was proper in the company of the empress Sabina (HA 11.3).

img.c: Hadrian’s Wall west of the Roman fort at Housesteads (Northumberland).

s.t:
According to the HA he returned from Britain to Gaul because of the news of a riot in Alexandria: a dispute had broken out there over a new Apis bull (HA 12.1). According to Dio, Hadrian loved his horses and dogs so much that he had tombs made for them; for his favourite hunting horse, Borysthenes, he set up a tomb, a slab and an inscription (Dio 69.10.2).

At Apt a Latin verse epitaph has been found for an Alan horse named Borysthenes, “Caesar’s horse”, which used to “fly” over plain, marshes and Etruscan hills after Pannonian boars. Scholars identify it with Hadrian’s horse, and so assume that the emperor visited Apt at this time. Whether before or after Nemausus, we do not know.

s.h: Nemausus: a basilica in honour of Plotina
s.t: At Nemausus Hadrian built a basilica of wonderful workmanship in honour of Plotina, Trajan’s widow (HA 12.2). Plotina had died between 121 and 123; she had helped Hadrian to the throne, and according to Dio the emperor mourned her for nine days and built her a temple (Dio 69.10.3). Plotina’s family probably came from Nemausus; the remains of the basilica have not been identified.

s.h: Tarraco: winter, assembly and an attack
s.t:
Arriving in Spain, Hadrian spent the winter at Tarraco and restored the temple of Augustus at his own expense. He summoned delegates from all Spain to an assembly at Tarraco; the matter of the levy, against which – in Marius Maximus’ jesting phrase, as quoted – the descendants of the Italian settlers protested most vehemently, he handled wisely and cautiously with the others (HA 12.3–4).

It was then that a household slave attacked him with a sword in the garden. Hadrian seized him, handed him over to the attendants, and when the man proved to be insane, did not punish him but entrusted him to physicians – according to the HA he was not alarmed for a moment (HA 12.5). Spain was the homeland of Hadrian’s family (Italica), but as emperor he never visited his native city (Dio 69.10.1).

img.c: Silver denarius of Hadrian with the reverse HISPANIA (AD 134–138, RIC II 305). Scholars link the series personifying the provinces with the emperor’s journeys.

s.n: Legio (León), camp of the Seventh Legion
s.t:
According to Birley, Hadrian also visited the camp of the Seventh Legion Gemina, which stood on the site of modern León; it was the only legion in Spain. No ancient text mentions the visit; it is inferred from Hadrian’s habit of inspecting every garrison.

According to the HA, at this time the emperor gave the Germans a king, suppressed unrest among the Moors of Mauretania, and averted a threatening Parthian war by personal negotiation (HA 12.7–8) – the latter took him to the East (see the next walk).

y: Hadrian 1/2: the East and Asia Minor (123–124)
t: Hadrian’s first great journey, part 2: from the Euphrates to Ephesus (AD 123–124)
intro:
In 123, on news of a threatening Parthian war, Hadrian hurried from Spain to the East. The Historia Augusta sums up this stage in a single sentence: he averted the war by personal negotiation, then sailed by way of Asia and the islands to Greece (HA 12.8–13.1). Where exactly he went is shown mainly by the cities’ inscriptions and coins and by later accounts; the chronology follows Birley’s (2003) summary.

By what route he reached Syria from Spain, we do not know; the walk therefore begins at Antioch. The lines of the sea stretches are straight and show only the direction.

s.t: Antioch was familiar ground for Hadrian: on Trajan’s death he was proclaimed emperor here as governor of Syria in 117 (Dio 69.2.1). According to Birley he reached it from Spain by the summer of 123 – perhaps by way of Mauretania, Africa, Crete and Cyprus, but that is only an assumption.

s.n: The Euphrates (marker at Zeugma; the place is unknown)
s.t: According to the HA, Hadrian checked the Parthian war, which was then in preparation, by personal negotiation (HA 12.8). Scholars think the meeting took place on the Euphrates, at the empire’s frontier, but no source gives the exact place. The marker stands at Zeugma, the most important crossing of the Euphrates, for orientation only.

According to Birley, Hadrian went from here along the Cappadocian frontier and in the autumn reached Trapezus on the Black Sea coast. Eight years later Arrian, governor of Cappadocia, wrote to Hadrian from Trapezus that the emperor’s statue standing in the city was well conceived – it points towards the sea – but did not resemble him, so he asked for a new one (Arrian, Periplus 1; see Arrian’s walk).

According to Birley he sailed west along the Pontic coast by way of Amisus, Sinope and Amastris, and spent the winter in Bithynia, at Nicomedia; he also visited Claudiopolis and Nicaea. Claudiopolis (Bithynium) was the home town of Antinous (Dio 69.11.2); that Hadrian met the youth here is only an assumption, though a likely one.

According to Birley he went to Thrace in the spring, where an older settlement took the emperor’s name: Hadrianopolis, modern Edirne. The city later became famous for many battles, among them that of 378, in which the Goths killed the emperor Valens.

In the summer he came by way of Cyzicus to Ilium, the city on the site of Homer’s Troy. According to Philostratus, Hadrian restored the tomb of Ajax at nearby Rhoeteum after the sea had damaged it (Philostratus, Heroicus). Honouring the tombs of heroes is a recurring feature of Hadrian’s Greek journeys.

img.c: The walls of Troy at Hisarlık.

s.t: Hadrian was a passionate hunter; according to Dio he once broke his collarbone while hunting and nearly injured his leg (Dio 69.10.2). In Mysia, where he had killed a bear on a successful hunt, he founded a city and named it Hadrianutherae, “Hadrian’s Hunting Grounds” (HA 20.13; Dio 69.10.2).

According to Birley he went by way of Pergamum and Sardis to Smyrna. Travelling in his retinue was one of the most famous orators of the age, Polemo. According to Philostratus, Polemo won the emperor over to Smyrna’s cause against Ephesus so completely that in a single day Hadrian gave the city ten million drachmas; from this a grain market, the most magnificent gymnasium in Asia and a temple visible from afar were built (Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 1.25). An inscription from Smyrna confirms the gifts.

According to Birley he was at Ephesus on 29 August. From here he went on by ship to Rhodes. This is proved by a letter written years later and preserved carved in stone in the council house of Ephesus: Hadrian recommends to the Ephesians that they admit to their council Lucius Erastus, the shipmaster who had carried him twice – first from Ephesus to Rhodes, the second time from Eleusis to Ephesus – and offers to pay the admission fee himself (I.Ephesos 1487). The continuation in Greece is shown in the next walk.

img.c: The so-called Temple of Hadrian at Ephesus, on Curetes Street.

t: Hadrian’s first great journey, part 3: Greece and Sicily (AD 124–125)
intro:
In his youth Hadrian was mocked as “Graeculus”, the little Greek, for his enthusiasm for Greek culture. As emperor he came to Greece again in 124 and, following the example of Heracles and Philip of Macedon, had himself initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries (HA 13.1). He spent the winter in the Peloponnese; his journey is shown by Pausanias’ Description of Greece and by the cities’ inscriptions and coins. Pausanias visited these places about a generation later and saw many of Hadrian’s foundations.

The chronology follows Birley’s (2003) summary. The land lines follow known roads; the sea stretches are straight.

s.t: Lucius Erastus’ ship carried Hadrian from Ephesus to Rhodes (I.Ephesos 1487). According to Birley he sailed from here in mid-September through the Cyclades to Greece, so as to arrive in time for the initiation at Eleusis.

Hadrian sailed by way of Asia and the islands to Greece and, following the example of Heracles and Philip, had himself initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries (HA 13.1). The Greater Mysteries were held every autumn, in the month of Boedromion; the secret of the initiation was strictly kept. Four years later, at the start of his second journey, Hadrian also attained the highest grade of initiation (Dio 69.11.1).

img.c: Remains of the Telesterion, the hall of initiation at Eleusis.

s.t: He granted the Athenians many favours and presided over the games. The HA notes that while he was in Greece no one came armed to the sacrifices, although many usually carried knives (HA 13.1–2). Scholars think it was now that he decided to complete the vast temple of Olympian Zeus, begun by the Peisistratids six and a half centuries earlier; it was dedicated at the end of his second journey (see the Hadrian 2/2 walk).

img.c: The Arch of Hadrian in Athens.

s.t: According to Birley the Peloponnesian tour began at Megara. According to Pausanias, Hadrian widened the rocky, dangerous Scironian road from Megara to Corinth, so that even two carriages could pass each other (Pausanias 1.44.6); one of the road’s milestones is dated to 125. Megara named a new phyle (citizen division) after the emperor.

s.h: Argos: a golden peacock for Hera
s.t: According to Birley he reached Argos by way of Epidaurus, Troezen and Hermione, and was there on 30 December. Among the votive offerings of the Argive Heraion, Pausanias saw a peacock of gold and gleaming stones given by Hadrian; the emperor dedicated it because the peacock is held sacred to Hera (Pausanias 2.17.6).

s.h: Mantinea and the tomb of Epaminondas
s.t:
Mantinea enjoyed Hadrian’s special favour. The emperor gave back to the city its old name in place of the Macedonian-era Antigonea (Pausanias 8.8.12). Around the ancient sanctuary of Poseidon Hippios he had a new temple built, and set overseers over the workmen so that nobody could look into the old sanctuary and nothing would be removed from the ruins (8.10.2). At the tomb of Epaminondas on the battlefield there were two slabs: an old one with a Boeotian inscription, and one set up by Hadrian, who wrote its inscription himself (8.11.8).

After the death of Antinous, Mantinea built a temple for the youth and worshipped him as a god; according to Pausanias because the people of Bithynium in Bithynia regarded themselves as of Mantinean origin (8.9.7).

According to Birley he went from Mantinea by way of Tegea to Sparta, then to Corinth. According to Pausanias, Hadrian built an aqueduct to Corinth from the springs of Stymphalus; its remains can still be seen in the northern Peloponnese. The line shows the tour along known roads.

According to Birley he presided over the Great Dionysia at Athens in March, then went through Boeotia and Phocis to Delphi. At Thespiae, according to a verse inscription, he dedicated to Eros the spoils of a bear he had killed on horseback.

According to the late Greek text “The Contest of Homer and Hesiod”, Hadrian asked the Pythia at Delphi where Homer was born and who his father was. The oracle said that Homer was an Ithacan, his father Telemachus and his mother Epicaste, daughter of Nestor. The text adds that this must be believed because of who asked and who answered – some scholars read this as subtle mockery.

img.c: Delphi: the theatre and the Temple of Apollo.

s.d: May AD 125 (according to Birley, with a question mark)
s.t: Birley places Hadrian at Dyrrachium, with a question mark, on 20 May; from here, the most important crossing port of the Adriatic, he may have set out for Italy. The evidence for this is only indirect, so the stop is uncertain. The line shows only the direction along known roads.

s.n: Mount Etna (marker on the mountain’s slope)
s.t: From Dyrrachium Hadrian sailed to Sicily. There he climbed Etna to see the sunrise, which is said to be many-coloured like a rainbow (HA 13.3). This climb is one of the famous examples of Hadrian’s curiosity; on his second journey he repeated it on Mount Casius in Syria (see walk 2/1).

img.c: The summit craters of Mount Etna.

s.t: From Sicily Hadrian returned to Rome (HA 13.3), four years after setting out. According to Birley, in 125–126 he spent much time at his villa at Tibur; in 127 he travelled in northern Italy, in the Po valley. The next great journey led in 128 to Africa, then to the East. The line via Puteoli shows only the direction at sea.

t: Hadrian in Africa: the manoeuvres at Lambaesis (AD 128)
intro:
In the summer of 128 Hadrian sailed to Africa and reviewed the Third Legion Augusta and its auxiliaries in Numidia. A unique source survives for this short journey: the emperor’s speeches to the troops were carved on the base of a memorial column on the parade ground at Lambaesis. It is the only longer surviving text in which a Roman emperor speaks to his soldiers; it is fragmentary, but it even gives the days.

The HA adds only that the emperor bestowed many benefits on the provinces of Africa, and that few rulers travelled so quickly over so much land (HA 13.4). The passages from the speeches are our own summaries.

s.t: According to Birley, Hadrian came to Africa by way of Sicily. According to the HA, when he arrived it rained for the first time in five years, and for this the Africans came to love him (HA 22.14). According to the HA he crossed from Rome to Africa and bestowed many benefits on the provinces (HA 13.4).

img.c: Silver denarius of Hadrian with the reverse AFRICA: Africa in an elephant headdress (AD 134–138; from the province series, found in England).
img.a: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Matthew Fittock, 2019-10-17 09:50:51

s.t: According to the Lambaesis inscription, a few days before 1 July Hadrian also addressed the Second Cohort of Hamians (Syrian archers). Speidel suggests that this cohort was stationed at Theveste and that the emperor stopped here on the road from Carthage to Lambaesis; this, however, is uncertain.

s.n: Lambaesis (Tazoult), camp of the Third Legion Augusta
s.t:
On 1 July Hadrian watched the legion’s exercises on the Lambaesis parade ground and addressed the soldiers group by group: the officers of the first centuries, the legionary cavalry and the infantry units. His words are detailed professional critiques: he praises the quick building of ramparts and the accurate javelin throwing, the horsemen’s skill in vaulting onto their horses, and elsewhere urges caution. He also mentions that several units of the legion had been detached elsewhere, yet it had performed excellently.

The speeches were carved on the base of a column raised in the middle of the parade ground, and the soldiers could see them for centuries. The camp of Lambaesis lies today in Algeria, near Batna; remains of the parade ground are also known.

img.c: The central building of the legionary fortress at Lambaesis, the so-called praetorium; its present form results from a rebuilding after Hadrian.

s.h: Zarai and the other auxiliary units
s.t:
One fragment of the inscription, dated to the Nones of July (7th), preserves a speech to a cohort stationed at Zarai; Zarai is about 70 km west of Lambaesis. On 12 or 13 July, at an unknown place, he addressed the First Pannonian ala and the horsemen of the Sixth Commagenian cohort; he praised the Pannonian cavalry for throwing javelins in legionary armour.

According to Birley he went on from here to Mauretania Caesariensis, then sailed home; according to the HA, on returning to Rome he set out at once for the East by way of Athens (HA 13.6) – this is shown in the next walk.

t: Hadrian’s second great journey, part 1: from Athens to Pelusium (AD 128–130)
intro:
Returning from Africa, Hadrian set out again in the summer of 128, this time with his wife Sabina and a large retinue; Antinous went with them too. The HA gives the order: Athens, Asia, Cappadocia, Antioch, Mount Casius, Arabia, Pelusium and Egypt (HA 13.6–14.4). The more exact chronology and the cities visited are shown by inscriptions: for the emperor’s arrival cities raised triumphal arches, took new names and set up commemorative inscriptions.

The chronology follows Birley’s (2003) summary; where it is only an assumption, the text says so. The lines of the sea stretches are straight.

s.t: Arriving in Greece, Hadrian also had himself initiated into the highest grade of the Mysteries at Eleusis (Dio 69.11.1). According to the HA, on this journey he dedicated at Athens the works he had begun there, among them the temple of Olympian Zeus (HA 13.6); scholars think the dedication actually took place in 131/132 (see walk 2/2). According to inscriptions, the emperor received the epithet “Olympios” at this time. According to Birley he spent the winter at Athens, visiting Sparta in the meantime.

In spring Lucius Erastus, the Ephesian shipmaster, carried him from Eleusis across the Aegean to Ephesus – their second voyage together. Hadrian then recommended Erastus to the Ephesian council by letter (I.Ephesos 1487). The Ephesians called the emperor their “founder and saviour”, and named one of their citizen divisions after him.

From Ephesus he went to Miletus and the oracle of Apollo at Didyma; an inscription from Didyma confirms this. From here he went up the Maeander valley, by way of Tralles, towards the interior. According to Birley he was at Laodicea on 29 June and at Celaenae in Phrygia on 23 July; after that he went through Galatia to Cappadocia.

s.n: Cappadocia (marker at Caesarea; it may have been Melitene)
s.t: In Cappadocia, according to the HA, he accepted slaves for military service. He invited the lesser kings to his friendship, and even the Parthian Osroes: he sent back his daughter, taken captive by Trajan, and promised to return the captured throne too. Some kings came to him, and he treated them so that those who had not come regretted it; Pharasmanes, king of the Iberians, haughtily stayed away (HA 13.7–9). Where the meeting was held, we do not know; Birley thinks Caesarea or Melitene likely.

According to Birley he spent the winter at Antioch. According to the HA, Hadrian came to hate the people of Antioch so much that he wanted to separate Syria from Phoenicia, so that Antioch would not be the “metropolis of so many cities” (HA 14.1). The source does not say why; the Antiochenes were famous for their sharp tongues.

s.h: A night sacrifice on Mount Casius
s.t: Hadrian climbed by night Mount Casius, which rises steeply from the coast south of Antioch, to watch the sunrise from there, as he had earlier on Etna. During the sacrifice a storm broke, and lightning struck both the victim and the attendant offering it (HA 14.3). The mountain was the sacred place of Zeus Casius; today it stands on the Turkish–Syrian border, 1,700 m high.

According to Birley he went in spring to the desert caravan city of Palmyra. A Palmyrene inscription honours a leading citizen named Male Agrippa, who “at the visit of the divine Hadrian” entertained the emperor and his soldiers and saw to their provisions. The city then used the name Hadriane Palmyra.

img.c: The colonnaded main street of Palmyra.

s.t: According to the HA, after Syria he went through Arabia to Pelusium (HA 14.4). The seat of the province of Arabia was Bostra; Petra, the Nabataean rock city, took the name Hadriane Petra in the emperor’s honour. In exactly what order he visited the province’s cities, we do not know; the line through Damascus, Bostra and Philadelphia (Amman) shows the probable route.

img.c: Al-Khazneh, the best-known rock-cut façade of Petra.

s.t: Gerasa raised a triple-gated triumphal arch south of the city for the emperor’s visit; its inscription dates it to 129/130 and mentions the bequest of a citizen named Flavius Agrippa. The huge arch, 21 m high, still stands at the entrance to Jerash.

img.c: The Arch of Hadrian at Gerasa (Jerash).

s.t:
According to Dio, Hadrian founded a new city on the site of Jerusalem, destroyed in 70, under the name Aelia Capitolina – after the emperor’s family name and Capitoline Jupiter – and had a temple of Jupiter built on the site of the old Temple (Dio 69.12.1). A recently found inscription from Jerusalem preserves a dedication of the Tenth Legion Fretensis to Hadrian, which scholars link to this visit.

According to Dio, while the emperor was nearby, in Egypt and Syria, the Jews kept quiet, but when he went further away they revolted (Dio 69.12.2). The resulting Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135) became one of the bloodiest wars of the empire.

img.c: Bronze coin of Aelia Capitolina with Hadrian’s name, AD 136; the reverse legend reads COL(ONIA) AEL(IA) CAPIT(OLINA) COND(ITA): “the colony of Aelia Capitolina founded”.

s.t: According to Birley he was at Gaza in July, then reached Pelusium, the gateway of Egypt. According to the HA, he rebuilt Pompey’s tomb here on a grander scale (HA 14.4). Pompey had been murdered on this shore in 48 BC, fleeing to Egypt after Pharsalus. According to Dio, Hadrian sacrificed to him and quoted a verse about how the hero with so many temples barely had a tomb (Dio 69.11.1). According to Appian, Hadrian had the small tomb and statues, buried in sand, searched out and restored (Civil Wars 2.86).

t: Hadrian’s second great journey, part 2: Egypt, the Nile and the return (AD 130–134)
intro:
In the summer of 130 Hadrian reached Egypt and, sailing up the Nile, viewed the country’s ancient monuments. This journey became bound up with perhaps the best-known event of the emperor’s life, the death of his favourite, Antinous. The Egyptian journey is better known than usual: papyri, the verses carved on the Colossus of Memnon and the foundation of Antinoopolis give the dates.

The chronology follows Birley’s (2003) summary. In Egypt the line runs along the Nile; the lines of the sea stretches are straight.

s.t: According to Birley, Hadrian arrived at Alexandria before 29 August. According to the HA, he debated with the scholars of the Alexandrian Museum, put questions to them and answered them himself (HA 20.2). The Alexandrian mint celebrated the emperor’s arrival on coins.

img.c: Gold coin of Hadrian with the reverse AEGYPTOS: Egypt reclining with a sistrum, an ibis at her feet (AD 134–138, RIC II 296; from the province series).

s.n: The Libyan desert (the place is unknown)
s.t:
According to Athenaeus, Pancrates, an Alexandrian poet, showed the emperor a rose-coloured lotus and said it should be named after Antinous, because it had sprung from the earth that drank the blood of the Mauretanian lion Hadrian had killed while hunting in the part of Libya near Alexandria – a huge beast that had long ravaged the region. For the novel idea the emperor granted him maintenance in the Museum (Athenaeus 15.677d–f). According to the papyrus fragment of Pancrates’ poem, Antinous took part in the hunt too.

The exact place of the hunt is not known; the marker only shows the direction of “Libya near Alexandria”.

s.h: The death of Antinous in the Nile
s.t:
The imperial flotilla went up the Nile by way of Memphis; papyri from Oxyrhynchus show how great the provisions were that the towns had to prepare. Near Hermopolis Antinous drowned in the Nile. According to the HA, Hadrian wept for him “like a woman” (HA 14.5). Dio knew two versions: that the youth fell into the river, or that he willingly sacrificed himself for the emperor (Dio 69.11.2–3). The exact circumstances remain unknown to this day.

Near the spot Hadrian founded a city and named it Antinoopolis; according to tradition on 30 October. Antinous was deified, and the emperor believed he had seen a new star, which he held to be the youth’s soul (Dio 69.11.4). The cult spread quickly; Pausanias saw a temple of Antinous at Mantinea too (8.9.7). The line runs along the Nile.

img.c: Marble bust of Antinous from Patras (AD 130–138; Athens, National Archaeological Museum).

s.t:
At Thebes, on the west bank of the Nile, stand two huge seated statues: statues of the pharaoh Amenhotep III, which the Greeks took to be Memnon, son of the Dawn. One colossus, cracked in an earthquake, gave out a faint sound at dawn – probably as the stone warmed – so Roman tourists came in crowds, and many carved on its legs that they had “heard Memnon”.

Travelling in the imperial couple’s retinue was the poet Julia Balbilla, who had four of her poems carved on the colossus’ leg. According to them, on the first day Memnon was silent when the empress Sabina was there – according to Balbilla so that the lovely Sabina would come back again – but the next day he spoke; Hadrian the statue greeted even before sunrise. One of the poems dates the visit exactly.

img.c: The Colossi of Memnon on the west bank at Thebes.

s.t: According to Birley he was at Oxyrhynchus at the end of November and in the Fayum oasis at the beginning of December, and spent the winter at Alexandria; in spring he visited the rising city of Antinoopolis once more. The city was organised on a Greek model, its citizens received privileges, and the games commemorating its foundation were still held in the 3rd century.

According to Birley, in the summer of 131 he sailed along the coasts of Cilicia, Pamphylia (Attaleia, Phaselis) and Lycia (Patara) to Ephesus, then to Athens. Here he completed the temple of Olympian Zeus, in which his own statue also stood, and dedicated in it a serpent brought from India. As archon, in Athenian dress, he presided over the Dionysia; he allowed the Panhellenion, the league of Greek cities, to be built, and founded Panhellenic games (Dio 69.16.1–2). According to Philostratus, Polemo gave the dedication speech. Hadrian’s Gate still stands beside the Olympieion.

img.c: The Olympieion in Athens, the temple of Olympian Zeus completed by Hadrian.

s.t:
In 132 the Jewish revolt broke out. According to Dio, the rebels fortified hiding places connected by underground passages; Hadrian summoned his best general, Julius Severus, from Britain, who wore them down in small engagements. According to Dio fifty fortresses and 985 villages were destroyed, and 580,000 men fell in the fighting; Roman losses too were so heavy that in his letter to the senate the emperor omitted the usual phrase “I and the army are well” (Dio 69.12–14).

Whether Hadrian himself went to Judaea is disputed; Birley places it, with a question mark, in the summer of 132. The line from Athens shows only the direction.

img.c: Silver coin (zuz) of the Bar Kokhba revolt, c. AD 134/135: grape bunch and “Shim‘on” in Hebrew; on the reverse a palm frond and “for the freedom of Jerusalem”.

s.t:
According to Birley, Hadrian returned from Athens to Italy by way of Macedonia, Thrace, Moesia, Dalmatia and Pannonia, and was in Rome by April 133 at the latest; others put the return in 134. He never made another great journey.

According to the HA, he built his villa at Tibur wonderfully and named its parts after the most famous names of provinces and places: it had a Lyceum, an Academy, a Prytaneum, a Canopus, a Poecile and a Tempe, and he even built an underworld (HA 26.5). The villa still stands near Tivoli and is a World Heritage Site. Hadrian died at Baiae on 10 July 138 (HA 25). The line from Athens to Tibur shows only the direction.

img.c: The Canopus pool at Hadrian’s Villa, Tivoli.

t: Arrian’s tour of the eastern Black Sea coast (AD 131/132)
intro:
Arrian, the Roman senator of Greek origin, historian and philosopher, became governor of Cappadocia around 131. In his first year he toured by ship the forts on the eastern Black Sea coast belonging to the province, and wrote a letter in Greek about his journey to the emperor Hadrian (Periplus Ponti Euxini); the official report in Latin has not survived. The first part of the letter describes a real tour of inspection from Trapezus to Sebastopolis (Dioscurias); it gives the distances between rivers and harbours in stades.

Arrian took Xenophon as his model, and his journey begins at Trapezus, where Xenophon’s ten thousand Greek mercenaries had once sighted the sea. We have reckoned the km values with a stade of about 185 m. Some of the forts stood outside the empire’s border, in the land of allied peoples; at sea the line consists of straight stretches.

s.h: Trapezus: altars and a bad statue
s.t: At Trapezus Arrian visited the place from which Xenophon and the Ten Thousand had sighted the sea. He found two altars of rough stone and writes that he will have new ones set up in marble, as the inscriptions are poorly legible. He criticises Hadrian’s statue: it does not resemble the emperor, so he asks for a new one. He also asks for statues for the temple of Hermes; he sacrificed an ox supplied by the people of Trapezus, praying first for the emperor (§1–3).
The first stop was the harbour of Hyssus, 180 stades (about 33 km) from Trapezus, where a garrison of infantry and twenty horsemen was stationed; Arrian drilled the foot soldiers here (§4).

From Hyssus they sailed on along the coast past a series of river mouths (Ophis, Psychrus, Calus, Rhizius, Ascurus, Adienus – Arrian gives the distances river by river). Not far out a storm from the east struck them: waves broke over the rowers’ benches, the water had to be bailed constantly, and they reached Athenae only with great hardship. At Athenae there was a Greek sanctuary of Athena, an abandoned fort and an anchorage; because of a night storm most ships were hauled ashore; one ship was wrecked, but the crew and gear were saved. The storm lasted two days (§4–6).

Five cohorts were stationed at Apsarus. Arrian paid them, inspected their arms, the walls, the ditch, the sick and the stores of provisions. He notes that according to tradition Medea killed her brother Apsyrtus here, and his tomb is shown (§7). Here Arrian speaks of sailing “more than five hundred stades” from Athenae, while his own list of distances (§8) gives only about 280 stades for this stretch.

img.c: The Gonio–Apsaros fortress, site of ancient Apsaros; much of the visible wall is from later periods.

s.h: Phasis: the anchor of the Argo
s.t: The fort at the mouth of the river Phasis was garrisoned by four hundred picked soldiers (§12). Arrian describes the river’s water: light and fresh on the surface, brackish when drawn from deeper down; according to the locals it does not spoil for more than ten years, and even grows sweeter with time (§10). He was shown the iron anchor of the Argo – which in Arrian’s view looked too recent to be genuine – and fragments of an older stone anchor (§11).

The end of the journey was Sebastopolis, the former Milesian colony of Dioscurias. Here too Arrian paid the soldiers, reviewed the horses and arms, and watched the cavalry mount (§14). By his reckoning Sebastopolis was 2,260 stades (about 420 km) from the naval base at Trapezus; the listed details add up to this (about 1,450 stades to the Phasis, about 810 from there).

The further parts of the letter – from the Thracian Bosporus to Trapezus and from Sebastopolis to Byzantium – probably do not describe Arrian’s own journey, but a coastal description compiled from other accounts. In the letter he also reports that he has received news of the death of Cotys, king of the Cimmerian Bosporus (§26); the letter is dated to 131/132 on this basis.

t: The Marcomannic wars of Marcus Aurelius (AD 166–180)
intro:
In the mid-160s the Germanic and Sarmatian peoples living across the Danube – Marcomanni, Quadi, Iazyges and others – repeatedly invaded the empire; around 170 a Germanic army got as far as Aquileia. The emperor Marcus Aurelius spent much of his reign along the Danube, in Pannonia; according to Cassius Dio he fought the barbarians in the region of the Ister “almost his entire life”, using Pannonia as his base (Dio 72.3). Meanwhile he wrote the notes in Greek that we know today as the Meditations.

There is no continuous account of the wars: Dio’s book survives only in a Byzantine abridgement, the Historia Augusta is unreliable, and the reliefs of the Column of Marcus in Rome give no place names. The emperor’s route is therefore unknown in most places, and the years are often disputed too. The walk stops at places certainly or probably connected with him – several of them in today’s Hungary and Slovakia – and says in each case what the connection rests on. The line is for orientation and does not show the emperor’s known route; beyond the Danube it consists of straight stretches.

s.h: Aquileia: the beginning of the war
s.t:
In one of the first invasions six thousand Langobardi and Obii crossed the Danube; the cavalry under Vindex and the infantry under Candidus routed them (Dio 72.3). In 168 Marcus and his co-emperor Lucius Verus went to Aquileia to direct the defence from there; meanwhile the empire was being ravaged by the epidemic brought from the East, the so-called Antonine plague. Verus died early in 169 near Altinum, on his way to Rome (Historia Augusta, Verus 9).

Around 170 the Marcomanni and Quadi invaded Italy: according to Ammianus they besieged Aquileia and destroyed Opitergium (29.6.1). It was the first time in centuries that an enemy army had set foot on Italian soil.

Carnuntum, the seat of Pannonia Superior and a legionary base, was Marcus’ main headquarters in the first phase of the war, roughly between 171 and 173. In the manuscript of the Meditations, between the second and third books, stand the words “At Carnuntum” – so part of the work was written here. Marcus’ stay here is also supported by inscriptions.

From here the campaigns against the Marcomanni and Quadi set out across the Danube. The archaeological park of Carnuntum today presents one of the best-excavated frontier cities of the empire.

s.n: The Hron (Granua) – the marker shows its mouth, opposite Esztergom; the exact place is unknown
s.h: “Among the Quadi, at the Granua”; the rain miracle
s.t:
In the manuscript, between the first and second books of the Meditations, stands the note: “Among the Quadi, at the Granua”. The Granua is the Hron (Hungarian Garam), which flows into the Danube opposite Esztergom; the Quadi lived north of the Danube, in what is now Slovakia and Moravia. So the note shows that Marcus was writing beyond the Danube, in enemy territory, during a campaign. On which stretch of the Hron, we do not know.

During one of the campaigns against the Quadi the so-called rain miracle took place. According to Dio’s abridgement the Quadi surrounded a Roman army and cut it off from water; the soldiers were already collapsing from heat and thirst when a sudden downpour broke out, the Romans caught the water in their helmets and shields, and hail and lightning fell upon the enemy. Dio ascribes the miracle to an Egyptian magician called Arnuphis, who invoked Mercury; the Byzantine author of the abridgement, however, ascribes it to the prayers of Christian soldiers (72.8–10). The scene can also be seen on the Column of Marcus in Rome.

img.c: The rain miracle on the Column of Marcus Aurelius, Rome: the winged rain god pours down water in the land of the Quadi.

s.t:
Aquincum, the seat of Pannonia Inferior and the base of the II Adiutrix legion, stood below the Danube bend; across the river, on the plain between the Danube and the Tisza, lived the Iazyges, a Sarmatian people of horsemen. Dio describes one scene of the fighting against them: the Romans pursued them across the frozen Danube and, standing on their shields on the ice, defeated the horsemen in close combat (72.7).

In 175 Marcus made peace with them: according to Dio the Iazyges returned a hundred thousand captives – after many had already been sold, had died or had escaped –, provided eight thousand horsemen for the Roman army, of whom five thousand five hundred were sent to Britain, and had to live twice as far from the Danube as the Quadi and Marcomanni (72.16).

The sources do not say whether Marcus was ever at Aquincum; the often-repeated claim that part of the Meditations was written here cannot be supported from the sources. But Aquincum’s legion played an important part at the end of the war (see Laugaricio).

Sirmium on the Sava was the main base of the eastern phase of the war, against the Iazyges. According to Philostratus, it was here, at the headquarters in Pannonia, that Marcus judged the case of Herodes Atticus of Athens, against whom the Athenians had brought complaints (Lives of the Sophists 2.1). In 175, at the time of the peace negotiations, the revolt of Avidius Cassius broke out in the East, which made Marcus break off the Danube war.

According to the Christian writer Tertullian, Marcus died at Sirmium (Apologeticum 25); other sources name Vindobona (see the last stop).

In 178 Marcus set out for the Danube again, with his son Commodus. According to Dio, before leaving he hurled a bloody spear from the temple of Bellona towards “enemy territory”, after the ancient Roman custom (72.33). The aim of the second expedition was apparently a lasting occupation of the lands beyond the Danube: according to Dio twenty thousand soldiers were stationed in forts in the land of the Marcomanni and Quadi, which hindered their grazing, farming and movement (72.20).

One archaeological trace of this is the Burgstall hill near Mušov in southern Moravia, where archaeologists have excavated Roman military camps and buildings from the time of the Marcomannic wars, about 80 km north of the Danube.

s.h: Laugaricio: the rock inscription at Trenčín
s.t:
The Latin inscription carved into the castle rock of Trenčín is one of the northernmost memorials of the Roman army in Central Europe: “To the victory of the emperors, the army stationed at Laugaricio, 855 soldiers of the II legion. Marcus Valerius Maximianus, legate of the II Adiutrix legion, saw to its making.” So the soldiers came from the legion of Aquincum, and wintered in the Váh valley, in the land of the Quadi, some 120 km from the Danube.

Maximianus’ career is also described by an inscription from Algeria (Zana, ancient Diana Veteranorum), which likewise mentions the wintering at Laugaricio. Most scholars date the winter quarters to 179/180; some to 178/179.

Marcus Aurelius died on 17 March 180 (Dio 72.33). Dio does not name the place; according to Aurelius Victor he died at Vindobona (De Caesaribus 16.14), according to Tertullian at Sirmium. According to Dio his last words to a tribune were: “Go to the rising sun; I am already setting” (72.34).

His son Commodus soon made peace with the Marcomanni and Quadi and returned to Rome; with this the plan to occupy the lands beyond the Danube was dropped.

img.c: The bronze equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius, the original (Rome, Capitoline Museums).

t: The campaigns of Septimius Severus (AD 193–211)
intro:
In AD 193, after the murders of Commodus and Pertinax, the praetorian guard sold the imperial office to Didius Julianus for money. Thereupon three provincial governors were proclaimed emperor by their armies: Pescennius Niger in Syria, Clodius Albinus in Britain and Lucius Septimius Severus, governor of Pannonia Superior, at Carnuntum. In the next four years Severus defeated all three rivals, then fought the Parthians and in Britain; he died at Eboracum (York).

Two contemporaries described the events: the senator Cassius Dio, whose work for this period survives only in a Byzantine abridgement, and the Greek Herodian, who gives the most coherent sequence of events. The Historia Augusta’s life of Severus serves as a supplement, but is unreliable.
