The walk follows the main stages of Severus’ campaigns; the sources give the sites of the battles, but in most places not the routes of the armies, so the line shows only the probable direction. The numbers in brackets give the book and chapter of Dio or Herodian.

s.t: Severus, a senator born at Lepcis Magna, had been governor of Pannonia Superior since 191, with his seat at Carnuntum. According to Herodian, after the murder of Pertinax and the “auction” of the throne he won over the soldiers of Illyricum and their officers by letters, gathered the troops, and took the name Pertinax as well, to gain popularity from the memory of the murdered emperor. In his speech he urged his soldiers to forestall his rivals and seize Rome, the seat of the empire; the soldiers proclaimed him Augustus (Herodian 2.9–10). The day of the proclamation is usually put at 9 April, on the basis of later anniversaries.

img.c: Denarius of Septimius Severus inscribed LEG XIIII GEM M V (AD 193–194): honouring the XIV Gemina legion of Carnuntum, which first proclaimed him.
img.a: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Vincent Drost, 2016-04-08 10:22:40

s.t: According to Herodian, Severus ordered everyone to take only as much gear as he could conveniently carry; he distributed money and supplies and hurried on with prodigious effort: he stopped nowhere and allowed only as much rest as the soldiers absolutely needed after the march. Crossing Pannonia he came to the mountains of Italy, outstripping the news of his own approach; the Italian towns received him with laurel branches and open gates (Herodian 2.11). The source does not give the route; the line shows the road of the Amber Road through Poetovio and Emona to Aquileia, the shortest link between Pannonia and Italy.

In Rome Didius Julianus drilled the praetorians, had trenches dug, and even tried to train the elephants used in processions for battle (Herodian 2.11). Part of Severus’ army slipped into the city in small groups, in civilian clothes, with concealed weapons (2.12). The Senate then deprived Julianus of power and proclaimed Severus emperor; Julianus was killed in the palace – according to Dio he had reigned 66 days (Dio 74.17).

Before the city Severus summoned the praetorian guard unarmed, in ceremonial dress, surrounded them with his own soldiers, stripped them of their uniforms and weapons, and forbade them to come within a hundred miles of Rome (Herodian 2.13). He formed the new guard from soldiers of the Danube legions.

calc.src: Severus was proclaimed at Carnuntum in early April and entered Rome in early June: about two months passed between the two dates, including the gathering of the troops and the negotiations in Italy. Herodian stresses the speed of the march (2.11). The day of departure is an estimate.

s.h: Against Niger: the siege of Byzantium
s.t: From Rome Severus soon set off east against Pescennius Niger, who had been proclaimed in Syria. Niger’s supporters occupied Byzantium; according to Dio the city withstood the siege for three years. Dio describes in detail the walls and the war engines of an engineer called Priscus, with which the defenders long kept the Romans at bay; in the end they surrendered because of famine. Severus had the city’s walls demolished and deprived it of its status (Dio 75.10–14).

Severus’ generals defeated Niger’s armies at Cyzicus and Nicaea, then pushed through the passes of the Taurus into Cilicia. The decisive battle was fought at the Gulf of Issus, where Alexander the Great had defeated Darius. According to Dio a sudden storm that beat in the faces of Niger’s soldiers helped the Severans (Dio 75.6–7; Herodian 3.2–4). Niger fled towards Antioch, but was caught and killed; his head was taken to the walls of Byzantium to induce the besieged to surrender. Severus himself took no part in the battle.

Severus at first accepted Clodius Albinus, governor of Britain, as Caesar and his successor, then broke with him; Albinus crossed into Gaul, and Severus marched west with the Danube legions. The decisive battle was fought near Lugdunum on 19 February 197. According to Dio a hundred and fifty thousand soldiers fought on each side – some scholars take this as the combined strength of the two armies – and here Severus took part in a battle in person for the first time (Dio 76.6).

According to Dio’s account Severus’ troops defeated Albinus’ left wing, but the right wing lured them by a feigned retreat into hidden trenches. Severus’ horse went down; he threw off his cloak and, drawing his sword, tried to stop the fleeing men; in the end Laetus’ cavalry decided the battle. Albinus fled into Lugdunum and died there; Severus rode over the corpse and sent the head to Rome. The city was plundered and set on fire (Dio 76.6–7; Herodian 3.7–8).

After defeating Albinus Severus set out east against the Parthians, who had besieged Nisibis during the civil war. He had ships built on the Euphrates and, sailing downstream and then crossing to the Tigris, captured and plundered the Parthian capital, Ctesiphon; according to Dio about a hundred thousand captives were taken (Dio 76.9). On 28 January 198, the hundredth anniversary of Trajan’s accession, he took the title Parthicus Maximus (“greatest conqueror of the Parthians”).

Here the line shows the direction from Nisibis to Ctesiphon; the army’s actual route (down the Euphrates) cannot be followed exactly.

img.c: The Arch of Septimius Severus in the Forum Romanum (AD 203); its reliefs show the Parthian wars.

s.t: On the way back Severus twice besieged the desert trading city of Hatra, but could not take it either time. According to Dio the defenders poured burning naphtha on the besiegers, and according to Herodian earthenware pots full of poisonous flying insects too (3.9); at the second siege the soldiers had almost broken through the wall, but Severus called them back – according to Dio because he hoped the city would surrender of its own accord and its treasures remain intact; by the next day the soldiers refused to attack (Dio 76.10–12).

After the Parthian war Severus returned to Rome, where in 203 his arch, with its reliefs of the Parthian war, was set up in the Forum Romanum, where it still stands. His home town of Lepcis Magna in Africa was enriched under his reign with large building projects – a new forum, basilica, harbour and a four-sided monumental arch with reliefs of Severus and his family. According to the sources Severus visited Africa around 202–203; the exact route is not known.

img.c: The Arch of Septimius Severus in his home town, Lepcis Magna.

s.t:
According to Herodian, in 208 the governor of Britain reported that the barbarians had risen, and asked for reinforcements or the presence of the emperor himself. Severus, though already old and crippled by gout, set out gladly – partly to take his sons Caracalla and Geta away from the luxury of Rome into the discipline of military life (Herodian 3.14). He led campaigns in Caledonia (today’s Scotland); according to Dio the Romans lost a full fifty thousand men in the marshes, the forests and the guerrilla fighting, but Severus did not desist until he approached the end of the island (Dio 77.13).

Severus died at Eboracum (York) on 4 February 211. According to Dio his last words to his sons were: “Be harmonious, enrich the soldiers, and scorn all other men” (Dio 77.15). His ashes were taken to Rome by his sons (Herodian 3.15).

t: Aurelian’s first campaigns: Pannonia, Italy and the Danube (AD 270–271)
intro:
Aurelian (reigned 270–275) became emperor in the middle of the third-century crisis: the eastern part of the empire was ruled by Zenobia of Palmyra, the western part by the Gallic emperors, and Germanic and Gothic peoples were breaking in across the frontiers. He was a hard soldier of humble origin; according to Eutropius able in war, but of ungovernable temper and inclined to cruelty (Eutr. 9.13).

Few reliable sources survive for his reign. The most important is Zosimus (early 6th century), who wrote following an earlier historian, Dexippus; Eutropius and Aurelius Victor say little. The Historia Augusta life of Aurelian is the most detailed, but much of it is invented: the walk uses it only where scholars think it reliable, and says so every time. Some of the places of the first year and their order are disputed.

s.t: Claudius II died of plague at Sirmium in 270; Aurelian, commander of the cavalry, was proclaimed emperor by the Danube army (Zosimus 1.47). According to the HA he was born at Sirmium; other writers put his birthplace in Dacia Ripensis or Moesia. Claudius’ brother Quintillus reigned in Italy for a few weeks, then died.

According to Zosimus the new emperor first settled the affairs of the empire in Rome, and set out from there by way of Aquileia to Pannonia (1.48.1). Some scholars think the order was different, and that Aurelian went to Rome only after defeating the Juthungi; the line follows Zosimus’ order.

Hearing that the “Scythians” – according to scholars, Vandals – were preparing to invade Pannonia, he went by way of Aquileia to Pannonia. He ordered the inhabitants to bring their grain, livestock and everything that could be of use to the enemy into the towns, so that the invaders would be struck by hunger, from which the region was already suffering (Zosimus 1.48.1).

s.n: Pannonia (battle site unknown; marker at Poetovio)
s.t: The barbarians crossed the river into Pannonia and fought a roughly even engagement with the Romans. That same night they recrossed the river, and at dawn they sent envoys asking for peace (Zosimus 1.48.2). According to the fragments of Dexippus, the Vandals gave hostages and horsemen for the Roman army. No source names the battle site; the marker stands at Poetovio for orientation only.

According to Zosimus, Aurelian learned that the Alemanni and their neighbours were preparing to attack Italy, and since he was more anxious about Rome than about distant provinces, he left a strong garrison in Pannonia and set out for Italy (1.49.1). According to scholars, the invaders were Juthungi.

According to the HA, near Placentia the Germans attacked the Roman army from ambush and defeated it, and panic broke out in Rome (HA, Aurelian 21.1–4). Scholars think this is the only surviving source that records this defeat correctly; a short late antique epitome (Epitome de Caesaribus 35.2) lists Placentia among the victories.

The Juthungi pressed south along the Via Aemilia and the Via Flaminia towards Rome. Aurelian’s army had not been destroyed by the defeat at Placentia: near the river Metaurus, close to Fanum Fortunae, he defeated them (Epitome de Caesaribus 35.2). The Romans had defeated Hasdrubal at the same place in 207 BC. The walls of Fanum Fortunae were strengthened in Aurelian’s time.

Aurelian finally destroyed the retreating Juthungi on the fields of Ticinum (Epitome de Caesaribus 35.2). According to Zosimus he killed many thousands of barbarians in a single battle near the Ister, at the frontier of Italy (1.49.1) – according to scholars this is the end of the same war, but the place in Zosimus is inaccurate.

In Rome Aurelian had several senators executed who were accused of conspiracy. He surrounded the city, which had previously had no wall, with a wall; he began the building and Probus completed it (Zosimus 1.49.2). According to Eutropius, in his reign the workers of the Roman mint also rebelled; Aurelian put them down with the utmost cruelty and condemned many nobles to death (Eutr. 9.14). The Aurelian Wall, about 19 km long, still encircles the historic centre of Rome.

img.c: The Aurelian Walls at the Porta Asinaria, Rome (the wall was heightened in the early 5th century).

s.n: The Danube (HA only; place unknown; marker at Durostorum)
s.h: Gothic war and the abandonment of Dacia
s.t:
According to the HA, Aurelian fought in Illyricum and Thrace, then beyond the Danube defeated the Goths and their leader Cannabas or Cannabaudes, killing 5,000 of the enemy (HA, Aurelian 22.2). Only the HA preserves this; some scholars think the Gothic leader’s name may be genuine. The marker is for orientation only.

According to Eutropius, Aurelian gave up the province of Dacia that Trajan had founded beyond the Danube, despairing of being able to keep it; he settled its inhabitants in the interior of Moesia and called the new territory Dacia (Eutr. 9.15). When exactly this happened is disputed. After this he set out for the East, against Zenobia (see the next walk).

t: Aurelian and Zenobia: the Palmyrene war (AD 272–273)
intro:
Palmyra, the rich caravan city of the Syrian desert, had been Rome’s ally against the Persians under Odaenathus. After his death his widow Zenobia ruled in the name of their son Vaballathus and built an empire: the Palmyrenes took Egypt and the eastern provinces as far as Ancyra in Galatia, and threatened Bithynia too (Zosimus 1.50.1). In 272 Aurelian marched against them.

The campaign is described in most detail by Zosimus. The Historia Augusta adds many colourful stories – the siege of Tyana, the ghost of Apollonius, letters – most of which scholars consider invented, so the walk mentions them only with a label. The Historia Augusta and Eutropius conflate the battle of Immae and the fight at Daphne; the walk follows G. Downey’s generally accepted arrangement.

s.t: The Palmyrenes would have reached Chalcedon, opposite Byzantium, had the Bithynians not heard of Aurelian’s accession and thrown off Palmyrene rule (Zosimus 1.50.1). Aurelian crossed the Bosporus into Asia.
When the emperor set out eastward, Ancyra was the first to submit to Rome (Zosimus 1.50.2).

According to Zosimus, after Ancyra, Tyana and the other towns between Tyana and Antioch also submitted (1.50.2). The HA tells a more colourful story: Tyana closed its gates, and Aurelian swore in his anger that he would “not leave a dog alive” in the city. A citizen named Heraclammon betrayed the city; Aurelian left the traitor to his fate, and told the soldiers, who demanded the plunder, to kill the city’s dogs. According to the HA the ghost of Apollonius, the sage of Tyana, warned him to spare the city (HA, Aurelian 22.5–24.9). These details appear only in the HA, and scholars consider most of them invented.

Near Antioch Zenobia awaited him with a large army. Aurelian saw that the Palmyrene cavalry surpassed his own in its heavy, strong armour and in horsemanship. So he placed his infantry separately on the far side of the Orontes, and ordered the cavalry not to attack at once, but to await the charge and then, with feigned flight, to keep withdrawing until the enemy’s horses and riders were exhausted by the heat and the weight of their armour. The plan worked: the Roman horsemen turned, and many Palmyrenes were cut down or trampled together with their horses (Zosimus 1.50.3–4). Following Downey, the battle is identified with Immae, east of Antioch.

The defeated army withdrew into Antioch. Zabdas, Zenobia’s general, feared that if news of the defeat spread the city would revolt, so he had a man resembling Aurelian, dressed in the emperor’s clothing, led through the city as though the emperor had been captured. Then at night he fled with Zenobia and the rest of the army towards Emesa. Aurelian entered Antioch next day, and by proclamations called back the inhabitants who had fled for fear of punishment (Zosimus 1.51).

img.c: Antoninianus of the Antioch mint, 270–272: Aurelian on one side, Vaballathus, Zenobia’s son, on the other – the brief period of joint rule.

s.t: On the way to Emesa, Aurelian learned that a Palmyrene detachment had seized a steep hill above the suburb of Daphne to block the road. He ordered his soldiers to climb with their shields locked tightly together, so that javelins and stones would glance off. At the top they fought on equal terms, and many Palmyrenes were driven over the precipice (Zosimus 1.52.1–2).

Apamea, Larissa and Arethusa gave the emperor a warm reception. At Emesa the Palmyrene army – according to Zosimus 70,000 Palmyrenes and allies – awaited him in battle order. Aurelian’s army included Dalmatian horsemen, troops from Moesia and Pannonia, the “Celtic” legions of Noricum and Raetia, picked Moorish cavalry, and troops from Tyana, Mesopotamia, Syria, Phoenicia and Palestine; the Palestinians fought with clubs and staves as well (1.52.2–4).

Here too the Roman cavalry began a feigned flight, but the Palmyrenes were many and cut down many Romans. The infantry saved the day: they noticed that the pursuing horsemen had broken formation and attacked them; the Palmyrenes fled, trampling one another (1.53). Zenobia’s advisers proposed that, since Emesa favoured Rome, they should withdraw to Palmyra (1.54.1).

Aurelian entered Emesa and seized the part of Zenobia’s treasure she had been unable to take with her; then he surrounded Palmyra, while the surrounding country supplied his army with everything. The defenders mocked the besiegers from the walls, one of them even the emperor himself; a Persian archer shot him down with the emperor’s permission (Zosimus 1.54.2–3). According to the HA, Aurelian too was wounded by an arrow during the siege – only the HA says so.

When the besieged ran out of food, they decided to flee to the Euphrates and ask the Persians for help. They put Zenobia on a swift female camel, faster even than horses, and got her out of the city. Aurelian sent horsemen after her, who caught her as she was about to cross the Euphrates by boat and brought her back to the emperor. According to Zosimus, Aurelian was pleased, but also feared that posterity would not think it a great glory to have defeated a woman (1.55). The place is unknown; the line shows only the direction.

img.c: Antoninianus struck in Zenobia’s own name (S ZENOBIA AVG), Antioch, spring AD 272.

s.t: Some of the Palmyrenes left in the city wanted to fight, others begged forgiveness from the walls; Aurelian pardoned them, accepted their gifts and respected the sacred objects. He then returned to Emesa and put Zenobia and her associates on trial. Zenobia blamed others who, she said, had led her astray; among them was Longinus, the philosopher and orator, who was condemned to death and died calmly, comforting his friends (Zosimus 1.56).

According to Zosimus, Aurelian was on his way to Europe when he learned that the troops left at Palmyra had won over Apsaeus, leader of the earlier revolt, and had proclaimed Antiochus emperor (1.59–60); according to scholars the news reached him on the Danube, after fighting the Carpi. He hurried back, arrived unexpectedly at Antioch while the people were watching a horse race, then took and demolished Palmyra without a fight; he spared Antiochus as too insignificant. After this he also subdued the restless Alexandrians (1.61.1). Palmyra never again became an important city. The line shows the second campaign from Antioch.

The sources contradict each other on Zenobia’s fate: according to Zosimus she died of illness or hunger on the way to Europe (1.59), but according to Eutropius she was led in Aurelian’s triumph, and her descendants still lived in Rome in his day (9.13).

t: Aurelian’s last years: Gaul, triumph, death (AD 274–275)
intro:
After recovering the East, Aurelian turned against the western Gallic empire, which since 260 had ruled Gaul, Britain and for a time Spain too. After his victory he held a huge triumph in Rome and used the title “restorer of the world” (restitutor orbis). A year later, setting out on a Persian campaign, he was killed by his own officers.

The sources say little about the Gallic war; the chronology is disputed (the battle of Catalaunum is put in 273 or 274). The walk follows Eutropius, Zosimus and Aurelius Victor, and gives the Historia Augusta’s information with a label.

s.t: The Gallic empire was then headed by Tetricus, a senator who had been proclaimed emperor in his absence at Burdigala while governor of Aquitania (Eutr. 9.10). According to Eutropius, Tetricus could not bear his soldiers’ constant mutinies, and in secret letters begged Aurelian to march against him; in his letter he quoted Virgil’s line: “Rescue me from these ills, unconquered one!” (Eutr. 9.13; Aeneid 6.365).

Aurelian defeated Tetricus at Catalaunum, Tetricus himself betraying his army (Eutr. 9.13). According to the HA, Tetricus deserted to Aurelian during the battle, and the leaderless Gallic army suffered heavy losses (HA, Aurelian 32.3). Gaul and Britain thus returned to the empire. The line via Lugdunum shows only the probable direction.

img.c: Antoninianus of Tetricus I, the last emperor of the Gallic Empire, with Pax (Peace) on the reverse.

s.n: Rome: the triumph and the temple of the Sun
s.t: Aurelian held a splendid triumph in Rome as recoverer of the East and the West; Tetricus and Zenobia walked before his chariot. Tetricus later became governor of Lucania and lived long as a private man; Zenobia’s descendants still lived in Rome in Eutropius’ day (Eutr. 9.13). He built a magnificent temple in honour of the Sun-god (Sol), adorned with statues of Helios and Bel brought from Palmyra; he withdrew the debased coins and struck new money, and had bread distributed to the people (Zosimus 1.61; Eutr. 9.15).

In 275 Aurelian set out for the East; according to later sources he was preparing for war against the Persians. At Perinthus in Thrace, then already called Heraclea, a conspiracy was hatched against him. Eros, the secretary who conveyed the emperor’s replies, whom Aurelian had threatened over some offence, feared punishment. He turned to the members of the guard he thought most daring, and with a long-practised forgery imitating Aurelian’s handwriting persuaded them that the emperor had condemned them all to death (Zosimus 1.62.1).

When Aurelian left the city with a small escort, the guards rushed upon him and killed him; the army buried him on the spot with great honour (Zosimus 1.62.2). According to Eutropius the murder took place on the old paved road between Constantinople and Heraclea, at Caenophrurium, and it did not go unavenged (9.15). According to later sources (Aurelius Victor, HA), a strange situation arose after his death: for months the army and the senate left the choice of a new emperor to each other. The exact site is unknown.

t: Constantine’s Italian campaign and the battle of the Milvian Bridge (AD 312)
intro:
After the break-up of the Tetrarchy the western half of the empire was shared by two rulers: Constantine in Gaul, Britain and Spain, and in Italy and Africa Maxentius, son of the emperor Maximian, who had seized power in Rome on 28 October 306. Relations between the two brothers-in-law became hostile. In the summer of 312 Constantine crossed the Alps, took northern Italy in a few months, and on 28 October before Rome, at the Milvian Bridge, defeated Maxentius, who drowned in the Tiber.

There is no eyewitness account of the campaign. The earliest source is a panegyric delivered at Trier in 313 (Panegyric XII); the Christians Lactantius and Eusebius attribute the victory to the sign of Christ, and Eusebius later, citing Constantine’s own account, describes the famous vision in the sky. The pagan Zosimus wrote a century later. Of the dates only the day of the battle and the entry are certain. The numbers in brackets are chapters of the sources; the Alpine pass (probably the Mont Cenis or the Mont Genèvre) is not named.

s.t: Constantine’s main residence was Trier; the sources do not name the starting point of the campaign. According to the panegyric of 313 he took scarcely a quarter of his army, because he also had to guard the Rhine frontier, and his advisers, even the soothsayers, tried to talk him out of the campaign (Pan. XII 2–3). According to Zosimus Constantine had 90,000 infantry and 8,000 cavalry, Maxentius 170,000 infantry and 18,000 cavalry (2.15) – these figures are surely exaggerated.

After crossing the Alps the first fortified town, Segusio, shut its gates. Constantine took it not with siege engines but by assault: the gates were set on fire and ladders were set against the walls. According to the panegyric he even had the fire put out, and spared the town and its people (Pan. XII 5–6).

Before Augusta Taurinorum Maxentius’ heavy armoured cavalry (clibanarii, cataphracti) barred the way; horse and rider were both clad in iron. Constantine opened his line so that the armoured wedge charged into empty space, then surrounded them from the flanks and had them clubbed down with maces. The city shut its gates on the fugitives, who were slaughtered beneath the walls; the city then opened its gates to Constantine (Pan. XII 6–7; Pan. IV 22–24).

Mediolanum, one of the imperial residences of the Tetrarchy, received Constantine solemnly; according to the panegyric the women watched from the rooftops and the city celebrated with joy (Pan. XII 7). Constantine stayed here for some time. A year later, in 313, here he agreed with the emperor Licinius on religious freedom for Christians (the so-called Edict of Milan).
Near Brixia a large enemy cavalry force was encamped; it fled at Constantine’s first charge and escaped to Verona (Pan. XII 8).

s.h: The siege of Verona and the death of Pompeianus
s.t: At Verona Maxentius’ best general, the praetorian prefect Ruricius Pompeianus, had gathered a large army. Constantine invested the city; Pompeianus broke out to bring a relief army. In the battle, which lasted into the night, Constantine himself threw himself among the fighters; Pompeianus fell, Verona surrendered, and the prisoners were put in fetters forged from their own swords (Pan. XII 8–11). Then Aquileia and Mutina also submitted (Pan. XII 11).

s.n: Saxa Rubra on the Via Flaminia (symbolic point)
s.t: Constantine approached Rome along the Via Flaminia without opposition. According to Lactantius, on the night before the battle he was told in a dream to mark the heavenly sign of God on his soldiers’ shields; he had an X with its top bent over – that is, the monogram of Christ – put on them (DMP 44.5). Eusebius, much later, citing Constantine’s own account, writes that during the campaign the emperor saw at midday a shining cross in the sky with the words “By this conquer”, and that Christ then appeared to him at night; from this the labarum standard was made (Life of Constantine 1.28–31). The two accounts contradict each other, and scholars dispute where and when it happened.

s.h: The battle of the Milvian Bridge
s.t:
Maxentius had at first intended to hold out behind the walls of Rome, and made the Milvian Bridge unusable. According to Lactantius, on the anniversary of his accession, 28 October, the people mocked him in the circus; in the Sibylline books it was found that on that day “the enemy of Rome would perish” – not taking it to apply to himself, he marched out (DMP 44.7–9). He crossed the Tiber with his army on a bridge of boats and drew up with his back to the river.

Constantine’s cavalry broke through the lines; the praetorians fell fighting where they stood. The bridge of boats collapsed under the fugitives, and Maxentius drowned in the Tiber in his armour (Lact. DMP 44.9; Zosimus 2.16). According to the panegyrics his severed head was carried into Rome on a spear. The battle is also shown on one of the reliefs of the Arch of Constantine.

The next day, 29 October, Constantine entered Rome; the senate and people celebrated him. He disbanded the praetorian guard, which had supported Maxentius, and demolished its camp (Aurelius Victor 40.25). In 315 the senate dedicated an arch to him beside the Colosseum; its inscription says he conquered “at the prompting of the divinity” (instinctu divinitatis) – a wording acceptable to pagans and Christians alike. After the victory Constantine openly supported the Christian Church; the battle thus became the symbol of the beginning of the Christian Roman Empire.

t: The journey of the Bordeaux pilgrim (AD 333)
intro:
The Itinerarium Burdigalense is the oldest surviving Christian pilgrimage account. It was written by an unnamed traveller from Bordeaux who in AD 333 went overland from Burdigala (Bordeaux) through Italy, Pannonia and the Balkans to Constantinople, from there through Asia Minor and Syria to Jerusalem, and returned through Macedonia and Italy as far as Mediolanum (Milan).

Most of the text is a dry list of the route: it names in turn the relay stations (mutatio) and the overnight stations (mansio), gives the distances between them in miles – at first, in Gaul, in Gallic leagues (leuga) – and adds them up section by section. Only here and there does it comment on a place; in Palestine, however, it describes the holy sites in detail. This exact list of stations is what makes it special: it shows how the road network of the imperial courier service (cursus publicus) worked in the age of Constantine.

The walk stops at the larger towns and the comments of the text. Distances are given from the text’s section totals (after A. Jacobs’ translation) and compared with the route found on the map’s road network. Note that the numbers differ in places between manuscripts and transcriptions, and the listed distances between stations do not always add up to the text’s totals.

s.t: The journey begins at Burdigala, “where the river Garonne is”; the text notes that the tide of the Ocean can be felt on the river for some hundred leagues. From here the route runs through Vasates, Elusa and Tolosa (Toulouse), then through Carcaso and Narbo into the valley of the Rhodanus. For the first stations the text still gives distances in leagues, Gallic miles, about one and a half Roman miles.

img.c: Remains of the amphitheatre of Burdigala (Bordeaux), the so-called Palais Gallien.

s.t: The first section ends at Arelate (Arles): according to the text 372 miles from Burdigala, with 30 relay stations and 11 overnight stations. From here the route runs north along the Rhodanus through Avenio, Arausio (Orange) and Valentia, then through the town of the Vocontii, Dea Vocontiorum, towards the Alps.

img.c: The amphitheatre of Arelate (Arles).

s.t: On the stretch over the Alps the text makes unusually many comments: it marks where the Cottian Alps begin, where one has to climb Mount Matrona (the Mont Genèvre pass), and that at Segusio (Susa) “Italy begins”. This road over the Mont Genèvre, which Caesar too had crossed in 58 BC, was the main courier route between Gaul and Italy in Constantine’s time.

Through Ticinum (Pavia) the road leads to Mediolanum, an imperial residence in the 4th century. According to the text it is 475 miles from Arelate, with 73 relay stations and 22 overnight stations. From here the road runs through Bergomum, Brixia, Verona, Vicetia, Patavium and Altinum towards Aquileia.

Aquileia, one of the largest trading cities of northern Italy, was the starting point of the roads to Pannonia. From Mediolanum it is, according to the text, 251 miles, with 24 relay stations and 9 overnight stations. From here the road goes east, over the pass called Ad Pirum (where the text marks “the summit of the Julian Alps”), to Emona (Ljubljana).

s.h: On the border of Pannonia: Poetovio
s.t: Between Emona and Celeia (Celje) the text marks the border of Italy and Noricum. After Poetovio (Ptuj) the traveller crossed the Dravus (Drava) by a bridge and entered “Lower Pannonia”. From here the road runs along the Drava through Iovia, Mursa (Osijek) and Cibalae (Vinkovci) towards Sirmium; on the way the text also marks the border of Upper Pannonia. The route does not touch the territory of modern Hungary, but it runs through the Pannonian provinces.

Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica) was an imperial residence in the early 4th century; Constantine too often stayed here. According to the text it is 412 miles from Aquileia, with 38 relay stations and 17 overnight stations; the listed distances between stations add up to slightly less, about 400 miles.

After Singidunum (Belgrade) the text marks the border of Pannonia and Moesia. At Viminacium it notes that Diocletian killed Carinus here – a reference to the civil war of AD 285. Through Naissus (Niš) the road leads to Serdica (Sofia); according to the text it is 314 miles from Sirmium, with 24 relay stations and 13 overnight stations.

Through Philippopolis (Plovdiv) and Heraclea the road reaches Constantinople, which Constantine had dedicated as his new capital only three years earlier, in 330. According to the text it is 414 miles from Serdica (the listed stations add up to less), and from Burdigala to Constantinople 2,221 miles in all, with 230 relay stations and 112 overnight stations.

Here stands the first exact date in the account: in the consulship of Dalmatius and Zenophilus (AD 333), on the third day before the Kalends of June (30 May), “we travelled” – from here the text leads on across the Bosporus to Chalcedon in Bithynia.

In Bithynia, before Nicomedia (İzmit), the text notes at the station of Libyssa: “there lies King Hannibal, who was of the Africans” (Annibalianus in the Latin). This is Hannibal of Carthage, who fled from Roman pursuit to Bithynia and died there around 183 BC; his tomb was still pointed out more than five hundred years later. From Constantinople to Nicomedia it is 58 miles according to the text.

Through Nicaea (İznik) and Iuliopolis the road leads into Galatia, to Ancyra (Ankara); on the way the text also marks the border of Bithynia and Galatia. From Nicomedia to Ancyra it is 258 miles according to the text, with 26 relay stations and 12 overnight stations.

In Cappadocia the text makes two comments: at one station it mentions the villa of Pammatus, from which the curule horses come – the horses used in the processions of magistrates – and at Tyana that Apollonius the magician came from here. Apollonius of Tyana was a 1st-century Neopythagorean sage whose miracles Philostratus described in a biography.

Over the Taurus mountains the road reaches Cilicia and Tarsus; here the text mentions Christian tradition explicitly for the first time: the Apostle Paul came from Tarsus. From Ancyra to Tarsus it is 344 miles according to the text, with 35 relay stations and 18 overnight stations.

Through Adana and Mopsuestia the road leads to Antioch, the capital of Syria; from Tarsus it is 141 miles according to the text. From here it runs south along the coast through Laodicea, Tripolis, Berytus (Beirut), Sidon and Tyre. In Phoenicia the text already marks biblical places: at Sarepta, where the prophet Elijah asked the widow for food, and by Mount Carmel, where he offered sacrifice.

From Caesarea Maritima it is 116 miles to Jerusalem according to the text, and from Constantinople 1,164 miles in all, with 69 relay stations and 58 overnight stations. The 116 miles are much more than the direct road, because the text’s route turns north-east from Caesarea: it runs through Maximianopolis, Scythopolis (Beth Shean), Neapolis (Nablus) and past Jacob’s well to Jerusalem; the line follows it too. In Palestine the genre of the account changes: instead of a list of stations it describes the holy places in detail.

Beside the Temple it mentions two large pools which, according to the text, Solomon had built, and the pool of Siloam, whose spring flows for six days and rests on the seventh. It describes the ruins of Pilate’s praetorium in the valley outside the wall of Sion, where, according to the text, the Lord was heard, and Golgotha, the little hill where he was crucified; beside it a basilica had been built over the tomb by order of Constantine. This was the predecessor of today’s Church of the Holy Sepulchre, dedicated in 335 – so the pilgrim may have seen it still under construction.

According to the text the pilgrim returned to Constantinople on the seventh day before the Kalends of January (26 December; some translations give 25 December). The text does not detail the way back through Asia Minor; the line therefore shows the outward route. From here he continued towards Heraclea (Perinthus) and then through Macedonia.

On the stretch through Macedonia along the Via Egnatia the text again makes several comments: at Philippi it notes that Paul and Silas were imprisoned here; at one station that the poet Euripides lies buried there (the manuscript names the station Peripidis, which some editors read as Euripidis); and at Pella that Alexander the Great, the Macedonian, came from here.

The Balkan section ends on the Adriatic coast at Aulon (Vlorë): according to the text it is 688 miles from Heraclea through Macedonia to Aulon, with 58 relay stations and 25 overnight stations. From here he crossed by ship to Italy; the text puts it thus: “crossing of the sea, 1,000 stades, which makes 100 miles”.
After the sea crossing the traveller landed at Hydruntum (Otranto) and from there set off north through the peninsula by way of Brundisium.
The text counts 289 miles from Aulon to Capua – including the 100-mile sea crossing – with 25 relay stations and 13 overnight stations.

From Capua to Rome it is 136 miles according to the text, with 13 relay stations and 9 overnight stations; from Heraclea through Aulon to Rome 1,113 miles in all. The text says nothing about Rome; the route continues through Ariminum (Rimini) towards Mediolanum.

The Itinerarium ends at Mediolanum: from Rome it is 416 miles according to the text, with 44 relay stations and 24 overnight stations. The text does not repeat the road from Mediolanum to Burdigala, since it had already described it on the way out.

t: The journeys of St Martin of Tours from Savaria to Candes (c. 336–397)
intro:
Martin was born at Savaria in Pannonia (Szombathely), served as a soldier in Gaul, then became a monk and finally bishop of Tours; after his death he became one of the most popular saints of the western Church. His life was written by his disciple and admirer, the Aquitanian Sulpicius Severus, while Martin was still alive (Vita Martini, c. 396), and continued in his letters and Dialogues. The Vita is hagiography: its aim is to show Martin’s miracles and virtues, not to give an exact biography; it gives no dates and tells the events of his years as bishop out of chronological order.

The year of his birth is disputed: Sulpicius’ narrative implies about 336, but Gregory of Tours writes that Martin died in the 81st year of his life (397), which would give 316. The numbers in brackets refer to chapters of the Vita; the identification of some places (Ligugé, Marmoutier, Candes) rests on later tradition, mainly Gregory of Tours. The line is a route found on the Roman road network, not Martin’s known route.

s.t: Martin was born at Sabaria (Savaria) in Pannonia, of a not undistinguished family; his parents were pagans. His father was a soldier, first a private, later a military tribune (2).

img.c: Savaria (Szombathely): the restored façade of the sanctuary of Isis (Iseum).

s.t: He was brought up at Ticinum in Italy. At ten, against his parents’ will, he fled to the church and asked to become a catechumen; at twelve the life of a desert hermit attracted him. An imperial edict required the sons of veterans to be enrolled: at fifteen he was betrayed by his own father, put in chains and bound by the military oath to the imperial cavalry guard, first under Constantius, then under the Caesar Julian (2).

In an unusually harsh winter, at the gate of Amiens, he met an almost naked beggar whom no one pitied. Having nothing but his arms and his military cloak, he cut the cloak in two with his sword and gave half to the beggar; some laughed at him. That night he saw Christ in a dream wearing the half-cloak and saying to the angels: “Martin, still a catechumen, has clothed me with this garment” (3). He was then baptised at 18, but at the request of his tribune remained a soldier for two more years.

This became the best-known scene of Martin in later art.

When the barbarians invaded Gaul, the Caesar Julian assembled the army at the city of the Vangiones (Worms) and distributed a bounty (donativum). Martin did not accept it but asked for his discharge: “I am Christ’s soldier; I may not fight.” Julian accused him of cowardice; Martin offered to stand before the battle line the next day unarmed, with only the sign of the cross. But next day the enemy sent envoys and surrendered, so peace came without a battle (4). The year is a modern inference from Julian’s campaigns in Gaul.

img.c: Solidus of Julian as Caesar (Sirmium, 355–360).

s.t: On leaving the army Martin went to Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, whose faith was already well known. Hilary wanted to ordain him deacon, but Martin refused out of humility; in the end he was ordained an exorcist (5).

s.n: Pannonia, Martin’s homeland (the Vita does not name the place)
s.h: Robbers in the Alps; his mother’s conversion
s.t:
In a dream he was warned to visit his homeland and his pagan parents; with Hilary’s consent he set out. In the Alps he was seized by robbers; one already had an axe raised over him, but Martin’s calm and his words converted him, and he later became a monk. Beyond Milan the devil confronted him in human form (5–6).

In Pannonia he converted his mother, but his father remained a pagan. When the Arian teaching spread in Illyricum, Martin stood almost alone against the bishops; he was publicly scourged and driven out of the city (6). The Vita does not name the city; the point stands only symbolically at Savaria.

Since Hilary had been exiled from Gaul by the Arians, Martin founded a monastery for himself at Milan. Here the Arian bishop Auxentius persecuted him, inflicted many injuries on him and drove him out of the city (6).

s.n: The island of Gallinaria (Isola Gallinara, off Albenga)
s.h: Hermit on the island of Gallinaria
s.t: Martin withdrew with a presbyter to the island of Gallinaria and lived on roots. Once he ate poisonous hellebore; when he felt death approaching he drove the danger away by prayer (6). When he learned that the emperor had allowed Hilary to return, he set out for Rome to meet him.

Hilary had already passed by the time Martin arrived, so he followed in his tracks and was warmly received. Not far from the town (Poitiers) he founded a monastery (7); tradition identifies it with today’s Ligugé, where excavations have uncovered remains of late antique buildings. It is often named as one of the first monasteries of the West.

Here a catechumen died unbaptised while Martin was away; Martin prayed stretched over the body, and according to the Vita the young man came back to life (7). With this his fame as a miracle-worker began.

The see of Tours fell vacant, but it was hard to lure Martin from his monastery. A citizen named Ruricius threw himself at his feet claiming that his wife was ill; so he was brought into the city, where the people in great crowds wanted to make him bishop. Some bishops – most loudly one named Defensor – despised him for his appearance: they thought him contemptible, poorly dressed, with unkempt hair. A psalm verse read at the ceremony (“out of the mouth of babes and sucklings… to destroy the enemy and the defender”, in Latin defensor) was taken by the people as aimed at Defensor (9). The year is a calculation based on Gregory of Tours.

Even as bishop he lived as a monk. First he lived in a cell next to the church, then about two miles from the city he built a monastery: a steep cliff on one side and the Loire on the others enclosed the plain, which could only be reached by a narrow path. Martin lived in a wooden hut, some of the monks in caves cut into the rock. His eighty disciples held everything in common; they bought and sold nothing, the young ones were occupied with copying, they drank wine only when ill, and many wore garments of camel hair (10). Later many of them became bishops.

img.c: Marmoutier: the bell tower of the later, medieval abbey.

s.h: The destruction of a pagan temple
s.t:
As bishop Martin made missionary journeys in the countryside and had pagan shrines destroyed. In the village of Leprosum he wanted to pull down a very rich temple held in superstitious reverence, but the pagans drove him off. For three days he fasted and prayed in sackcloth and ashes; then, according to the Vita, two angels with spears and shields appeared and destroyed the shrine before the terrified villagers. Most of the inhabitants were converted (14).

Similar stories are told of a village in the territory of the Aedui (15); these conversions also show the violent side of temple destruction.

s.h: The leper’s kiss at the gate of Paris
s.t: As he entered the gate of Paris with a large company, he met a leper of pitiful appearance whom everyone shrank from. Martin kissed and blessed him, and according to the Vita the man was healed at once and came to the church next day with clean skin to give thanks. Even threads from his clothing worked cures (18).

s.h: Trier: at the court of the emperor Maximus
s.t:
At Trier he healed a paralysed girl with prayer and consecrated oil (16). At the court of the usurper emperor Magnus Maximus (383–388), which resided at Trier, Martin long refused to sit at the emperor’s table. When at last he went and the emperor handed him the cup, he passed it not back to the emperor but to his own presbyter, as he thought him more worthy. He foretold that Maximus’ Italian campaign would at first succeed but that he would die soon after – Maximus was killed at Aquileia in 388 (20).

According to Sulpicius’ Chronicle (II.50), Martin also asked Maximus here not to execute Priscillian and his companions, accused of heresy; yet he could not prevent their deaths (c. 385).

img.c: Gold coin (solidus) of Magnus Maximus (383–388), struck at Trier.

s.t:
According to Sulpicius’ Letter 3 to Bassula, the clergy of the church at Condate had quarrelled; Martin, though he felt his death approaching, went there to make peace. On the river bank he saw water-birds catching fish, compared them to demons lying in wait, and ordered them away; the birds flew off towards the mountains and woods. After peace was restored he fell ill with fever; his disciples wept, and he prayed that if he was still needed he would not refuse the labour. He lay on sackcloth and ashes, for he held that a Christian should die in ashes; he asked the priests to let him look at heaven rather than at the earth. So he died.

The text only mentions the church of ‘Condate’; according to Gregory of Tours this is Candes, a village of Martin’s diocese at the confluence of the Vienne and the Loire. Gregory says that Martin died in the 81st year of his life and the 26th of his episcopate.

According to Gregory of Tours, the people of Poitiers and Tours quarrelled over the body; at night the men of Tours lifted it out through a window, put it in a boat and carried it down the Vienne and then the Loire to Tours. According to Sulpicius the whole city went out to meet it, many came from the villages around and from neighbouring cities, and almost two thousand monks escorted it to the grave singing hymns.

Over Martin’s grave his successor Brictius built a small chapel, and bishop Perpetuus a great basilica in the 5th century; Tours became one of the greatest pilgrimage centres of the Middle Ages. His feast, Martinmas, 11 November, is traditionally the day of the burial.

t: Egeria’s pilgrimage from Mount Sinai to Constantinople (AD 383–384)
intro:
Egeria was a Christian woman from the west, probably from Gallaecia or southern Gaul, who in the early 380s spent three years in the Holy Land and reported on her journeys in a Latin letter to her “sisters” at home. It is the earliest account of its kind, and one of the earliest surviving longer Latin texts written by a woman. A single eleventh-century manuscript preserved it; its beginning and end are missing, and the text opens with the approach to Mount Sinai.

Egeria travelled in an already Christian empire: she used the roads and stations (mansiones) of the cursus publicus, soldiers escorted her on dangerous stretches, and bishops and monks guided her everywhere. The years follow P. Devos’s reckoning (the feast at Carrhae falls in 384); some of the months are uncertain. The lines of the excursions made from Jerusalem start from Jerusalem.

s.t:
The surviving text begins here. Egeria reached the mountain late on the Sabbath and on Sunday early in the morning climbed to the summit on foot with the monks, since the steep side could not be climbed riding. At the top stood a small church; after the service the monks gave her fruit as a gift. From the summit they showed her Egypt, Palestine, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean (the “Parthenian Sea”) and the boundless land of the Saracens – she writes that she could hardly believe how far below them everything lay (1–3).

On the way down she also saw the site of the Burning Bush, where there was a church and a garden; at every place the monks read the biblical passage belonging to it and prayed – this is the constant routine of Egeria’s journeys (4).

img.c: Sunrise from the summit of Jebel Musa, traditionally identified with Mount Sinai.

s.h: Clysma: on the Red Sea shore
s.t: From Mount Sinai Egeria returned to Clysma on the Red Sea shore; her route followed the stations of the Israelites’ exodus. After the tiring journey along the sandy desert road they rested at Clysma. In the dangerous region between Sinai and Egypt Roman soldiers escorted them (6–7).

s.h: Through the land of Goshen to Pelusium
s.t: From Clysma the road led through the land of Goshen, ruined Rameses and the city called “Arabia”. At Arabia they sent back the military escort, since from here they were travelling on the public road through Egypt, where it was not needed. Tanis came next. Egeria visited every biblical site that the local monks and priests knew of. From Pelusium she returned by the coastal road, station by station, to Palestine and Jerusalem (7–9). The marker stands on the site of ancient Pelusium.

Jerusalem was Egeria’s base during her years in the Holy Land. The second half of the letter describes the liturgy of the Jerusalem church in detail: the daily hours of prayer, Holy Week, Easter and the feast of the dedication of the church – it is the most important early source for this. Egeria also writes that the bishop preached in Greek; a priest interpreted into Syriac, and for those who knew only Latin, bilingual members of the congregation explained it (47).

From Jerusalem she made several excursions: to Mount Nebo and to the tomb of Job (see the next stops). After three years had passed she set out for home; by Devos’s reckoning after Easter 384 (17).

s.h: Mount Nebo: the view from Moses’ place
s.t: From Jerusalem they went by way of Jericho to the Jordan, then to Livias, and climbed Mount Nebo, from where according to tradition Moses saw the Promised Land. A small church stood on the summit. They were shown the Jordan, the Dead Sea, Jericho and Segor; also the place where Lot’s wife was turned into a pillar of salt – but the pillar itself they did not see, because according to the bishop of Segor the sea had covered it years before (10–12).

img.c: View from Mount Nebo over the Dead Sea and the Jordan valley.

s.t: On another journey Egeria visited the tomb of Job at Carneas, in the land of Ausitis, in today’s southern Syria. On the way she stopped at Salem, the city of Melchizedek, and at Tishbe, the town of the prophet Elijah. At Carneas the tomb held to be Job’s had, according to tradition, been revealed to a monk, and a church was built over it (13–16). The line shows the excursion from Jerusalem; the real route led through the Jordan valley.

From Jerusalem Egeria went to Antioch. From here, however, she did not head straight for Constantinople, but made a detour eastwards into Mesopotamia, because she wanted to see the holy monks and the tomb of the apostle Thomas at Edessa (17).

After Hierapolis, the capital of the province of Augusta Euphratensis, Egeria crossed the Euphrates. She writes that the river is great and fearsome, flowing as swiftly as the Rhône, only greater; it could be crossed only in large ships (18). This is the only European geographical reference in the text, which is why some scholars think Egeria came from southern Gaul.

After Batnae she reached Edessa, and since there was much she wanted to see, she stayed three days. She prayed at the tomb of the apostle Thomas. The bishop accompanied her to King Abgar’s palace, showed her the statues of the king and his son, and read out the correspondence of Abgar and Jesus, which the city held in great honour; Egeria received the letters from him. The bishop remarked too that Egeria had come here “from the far ends of the earth” (19).

She also saw the city’s springs and the pools full of fish; the bishop told her how Abgar’s letter had saved the city from a Persian siege (19).

At Carrhae, the biblical Haran, Egeria was present for the feast of St Helpidius; from this date (23 April) Devos established that the journey took place in 384. She saw the church on the site of Abraham’s house, and the well six miles from the city where Jacob watered Rachel’s flock. Hardly anyone in the city was Christian, apart from a few clergy and monks (20–21).

She would gladly have gone on to Nisibis and to Ur of the Chaldees as well, but the bishop told her these were in Persian hands, so Romans could not go there (20).

s.n: Seleucia and the shrine of St Thecla (Silifke)
s.t:
Returning to Antioch, Egeria spent a week there preparing for the journey, then continued by way of Tarsus. From there she made one more detour: through Pompeiopolis and Corycus – on the third day from Corycus – to Seleucia in Isauria, about 1,500 paces from which stood the shrine of St Thecla, a place especially venerated by women (22–23).

Here she met a dear friend, the deaconess Marthana, whom she knew from Jerusalem; she governed the cells of male and female ascetics around the shrine. Egeria spent two days here, the Acts of Thecla were read at the shrine, and then returned to Tarsus (23). The line shows the detour from Tarsus.

From Tarsus she crossed the mountains by way of Mopsucrene at the foot of the Taurus, then reached Chalcedon through Cappadocia, Galatia and Bithynia, and prayed there at the famous tomb of the martyr St Euphemia (23). Egeria describes this long stretch in only a few words; she does not name the stations along the way. The line follows the probable main road through Ancyra and Nicaea.

Crossing the Bosporus, Egeria reached Constantinople, where she gave thanks in the churches and at the tomb of the apostles. From here she wrote her letter to the “sisters”. She writes too that she intends to go on to Asia, to Ephesus, to the tomb of the apostle John; if she remains alive, she will report from there as well – and if not, she asks them to remember her (23). Whether she reached home, we do not know.

t: Paula’s pilgrimage from Rome to the Holy Land and Egypt (AD 385–386)
intro:
Paula (347–404) was a wealthy Roman aristocratic widow who, under Jerome’s influence, chose an ascetic life. In 385, shortly after Jerome had left Rome, she sailed east with her daughter Eustochium; they toured the biblical sites of the Holy Land and the monastic settlements of Egypt, then settled at Bethlehem, where Paula’s wealth built monasteries and a pilgrims’ hostel. Here Jerome translated most of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).

The account of the journey was written by Jerome after Paula’s death, in 404, in a letter of consolation to Eustochium (Letter 108); it is both a biography and an ascetic exemplum. From Joppa onwards Jerome also writes in the first person plural, so it is likely that they travelled together for part of the way. At each place the letter mainly recalls the biblical stories; the walk summarises these briefly. The numbers in brackets are chapters of the letter; the lines of the sea passages are only approximate.

s.t: Paula went down to Portus with her brother, kinsfolk and children. The ship was already under way, but her little son Toxotius stretched out his hands to her from the shore in entreaty, and Rufina, of marriageable age, silently begged her through her tears to wait for her wedding. Paula kept her eyes dry, and in Jerome’s view her love of God overcame her love as a mother. Only Eustochium went with her (6).

The ship put in at the island of Pontia, made famous, Jerome says, by the exile of Flavia Domitilla, the noblewoman banished under the emperor Domitian for her Christian faith; Paula saw the cells where she had suffered her long martyrdom (7).

Methone stood at the south-western tip of the Peloponnese; here Paula went ashore briefly to rest her weary body, while the sailors took on water (7). Jerome decorates the Greek sea passage with quotations from Virgil. The route through the Strait of Messina is only an assumption.
Sailing among the Greek islands they passed Rhodes and Lycia (7).

In Cyprus Paula fell at the feet of bishop Epiphanius, who kept her for ten days – not for rest but for work, for Paula visited the monasteries of the island and gave the monks what help she could (7). Epiphanius was bishop of Salamis (by then called Constantia); he had earlier stayed in Paula’s house at Rome.
After a short crossing they landed at Seleucia, the port of Antioch (7).

At Antioch the holy confessor, bishop Paulinus, detained her for a while. Then in the middle of winter, warmed by her burning faith, she set out again riding on a donkey – she who had formerly been carried in a litter on the shoulders of eunuchs (7).

s.h: Along the Phoenician coast: Berytus, Sidon, Zarephath
s.t: Through Coele-Syria and Phoenicia she travelled by the coast road: through the Roman colony of Berytus and ancient Sidon to Zarephath, where she entered Elijah’s little tower and prayed, as Elijah had once in the widow’s house. On the sands of Tyre she knelt where Paul had knelt; she went on through Acco (Ptolemais) and the plain of Megiddo (8).

s.h: Caesarea: the houses of Cornelius and Philip
s.t: At Caesarea, the capital of Palestine, she saw the house of the centurion Cornelius, by then a church, and the house of Philip the evangelist and the rooms of his four prophesying daughters (8).

Through Antipatris and Lydda (Diospolis), where Dorcas and Aeneas were healed, she reached Joppa, the port of Jonah’s flight; according to the poets Andromeda was chained to the rock here (8). From here on Jerome also writes in the first person plural.

s.h: Jerusalem: the Cross and the Tomb
s.t: Through Emmaus (Nicopolis), the two Beth-horons and Gibeon she came to Jerusalem. The proconsul of Palestine, who knew her family, had a palace prepared for her, but she chose a humble cell. Prostrate before the Cross she prayed as if she saw Christ hanging on it; in the tomb of the Resurrection she kissed the stone that the angel had rolled away. She also climbed Mount Zion (9).

Passing Rachel’s tomb she came to Bethlehem, where she entered the Saviour’s cave and saw the manger; according to Jerome she swore that with the eyes of faith she saw the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes. Then she went down to the shepherds’ tower of Eder (10).

s.h: Hebron and the Dead Sea country
s.t: She travelled along the road to Gaza, then through Eshcol, Sarah’s dwelling and Abraham’s oak to Hebron, the tomb of the patriarchs. From the height of Capharbarucha she looked down on the waste of Sodom and Gomorrah and on Zoar (11).

She returned to Jerusalem, climbed the Mount of Olives, saw the tomb of Lazarus at Bethany, then went down through Adummim to Jericho. She saw the sycamore of Zacchaeus and Gilgal, and went to the Jordan, where at sunrise she remembered Christ’s baptism (12).

Through Bethel and Shiloh she went to Shechem (Neapolis), where she saw Jacob’s well. At Sebaste, the former Samaria, at the tomb of John the Baptist, according to Jerome she saw harrowing scenes: the possessed howling before the tombs of the saints (13).

With great haste she toured Galilee: Nazareth, where Christ was brought up, Cana and Capernaum, the scenes of the miracles, Mount Tabor and the Sea of Galilee, then Nain, where the widow’s son was raised (13).

Through Socoh, Samson’s spring, Moresheth and Lachish she crossed the desert to the river Sihor (the Nile), then through the land of Goshen and the plain of Zoan came to the city of No, which Jerome says is now Alexandria (14). The exact route cannot be reconstructed from the letter.

At Nitria she was met by bishop Isidore the confessor and a countless multitude of monks, many of them priests and Levites. Paula visited the cells of the Macarii, Arsenius, Serapion and other famous hermits, and honoured Christ in each of them. She would gladly have stayed in the desert, but a greater love drew her back to the Holy Land (14).

s.h: By sea from Pelusium to Maiuma
s.t: To escape the heat she took ship at Pelusium and crossed to Maiuma, the port of Gaza; from there she quickly returned to Bethlehem (14).

At Bethlehem she lived for three years in a poor lodging until the cells and monasteries were built, and beside the road the pilgrims’ hostel, “because Mary and Joseph had found no room at the inn” (14). In Paula’s convent the women lived in three groups; Jerome lived in the nearby men’s monastery.

Paula spent twenty years at Bethlehem. She died in January 404 (the year of Honorius’ sixth consulship), aged 56 years, 8 months and 21 days. Bishops carried her bier on their shoulders, psalms were sung in Greek, Latin and Syriac, and she was buried beneath the church beside the cave of the Nativity. Jerome wrote her epitaph: she was the first Roman woman to choose hardship and Bethlehem for Christ (end of the letter).

t: St Augustine’s journey from Thagaste via Carthage and Rome to Milan and back (AD 354–391)
intro:
Aurelius Augustinus (354–430) was born in a small town of Numidia in the province of Africa, became a teacher of rhetoric, and after long inner struggles was converted at Milan. In his Confessions (c. 397–400), written as a prayer addressed to God, he tells his life up to his conversion and the death of his mother Monica. The work is the first great autobiography in European literature; his journey from North Africa to Italy also shows the path of education in the late Roman world.

The Confessions are not a travel account: Augustine mentions places and years only in passing, so the dates are scholars’ calculations. His return home and later years were described by his disciple Possidius. The numbers in brackets are book and chapter of the Confessions; the lines of the sea voyages are only symbolic.

s.t: Augustine was born at Thagaste, a municipium of Numidia; his father Patricius was a town councillor of modest property and a pagan, his mother Monica a devout Christian. In the Confessions he tells how he hated Greek and the beatings at school (1.9–14), and how at sixteen he and his friends stole pears from a neighbour’s tree, not from hunger but for the sake of wrongdoing (2.4).
In nearby Madauros, the birthplace of Apuleius, he studied literature and rhetoric. At sixteen he spent a year at home, because his father had to gather the money for his studies at Carthage (2.3).

“I came to Carthage, where a cauldron of unholy loves seethed and bubbled all around me” – so he begins Book 3. Here he lived with a woman, who bore him a son, Adeodatus; Cicero’s Hortensius turned him towards philosophy, and for nine years he was a follower of the Manichees (3.1–6). Later he taught rhetoric at Carthage; because of the unruliness of the students he decided to go to Rome (5.8).

His mother did not want to let him go. Augustine deceived her: he said he was seeing a friend off at the ship, and leaving Monica at the memorial of St Cyprian he sailed away by night (5.8).

In Rome he fell seriously ill in the house of a Manichee. After recovering he taught rhetoric; the Roman students were not as unruly as the Carthaginians, but they conspired to leave their teacher before paying him (5.9–12). He was also disappointed in the Manichaean teaching and turned towards the sceptical ‘Academics’ (5.10).

Milan, the seat of the western imperial court, was looking for a teacher of rhetoric; the city prefect Symmachus, after a trial speech, sent Augustine there by the imperial post (5.13). Here he listened to the sermons of bishop Ambrose, who showed him the figurative interpretation of the Old Testament; Monica followed him to Italy (5.13–6.1).

In the summer of 386, weeping under a fig tree in the garden of a house in Milan, he heard a child’s voice from next door: “Take up and read!” (Tolle, lege). He opened the letters of the apostle Paul, and at the words of Romans (13:13–14) he was converted (8.12).

He gave up his teaching post and spent the autumn and winter at Cassiciacum, the country estate of his friend Verecundus, with his mother, son and friends; here his first philosophical dialogues were written (9.3–4). At Easter 387 Ambrose baptised him, his son Adeodatus and his friend Alypius at Milan (9.6). Cassiciacum is usually identified with Cassago Brianza, north of Milan.

s.h: Ostia: the vision and Monica’s death
s.t: On their way home they waited for a ship at Ostia. At a window, looking out on a garden, he and his mother talked of eternal life, and for a moment together they ‘touched’ it – one of the most famous scenes of the Confessions (9.10). A few days later Monica fell ill with fever and died nine days later, in her 56th year, when Augustine was 33; she asked to be buried anywhere, only to be remembered at the altar (9.11). She was buried at Ostia; a fragment of her epitaph was found in 1945.

After Monica’s death Augustine stayed for a while in Rome, then in 388 returned home via Carthage to Thagaste, where he lived with his friends in a monastic community; here Adeodatus too died young (Possidius 3). In 391 at Hippo Regius the people almost forced him into ordination as a priest, and a few years later he became bishop. He died at Hippo in 430 during the Vandal siege (Possidius 4–5, 28–31). The walk does not show the road to Hippo Regius.

t: Julian’s journey down the Danube (AD 361)
intro:
In AD 360 the army of Gaul proclaimed Julian, cousin and Caesar of the emperor Constantius, as Augustus. As Constantius would not recognise him, Julian set out east in the summer of 361. His journey is described by the contemporary historian Ammianus Marcellinus (Res gestae, book 21), who himself served under Julian.

Julian divided his army so that it would seem larger, while he himself travelled with a small escort along the Danube; where the river became navigable he took to boats and, avoiding the towns, sailed downstream all the way to the neighbourhood of Sirmium. His route also passed along the Danube in what is now Hungary.

Ammianus gives no exact dates; the dates therefore indicate only the season, except for the entry into Constantinople. Ammianus does not name the place where Julian embarked; the marker there shows only the upper Danube. On the navigable stretch the line follows the map’s river routes.

s.t:
At Augusta Raurica (Augst) Julian settled his affairs, sent Sallustius as prefect to Gaul and made Nevitta commander of the cavalry, because he did not trust Gomoarius, who had once betrayed Vetranio (21.8.1). He divided his army: one part, under Iovinus and Iovius, he sent ahead along the familiar roads of Italy, another with Nevitta through the middle of Raetia, so that appearing in various regions they would give the impression of a huge army – as, says Ammianus, Alexander the Great and many other generals had done (21.8.3).

He himself meant to travel through the Marcian woods (the Black Forest) and along the roads near the bank of the Danube, but was uncertain, fearing that his small retinue would be despised (21.8.2).

img.c: The theatre of Augusta Raurica (Augst).

s.n: The upper Danube – Ammianus does not name the place of embarkation (the marker shows Castra Regina)
s.h: Taking to boats on the Danube
s.t: Where he learned that the river was navigable, he embarked on boats, of which by chance there was a good supply, and was carried downstream as secretly as possible. According to Ammianus he escaped notice because he was hardy and strong, needed no choice food, was content with a scanty and simple diet, and passed the towns and forts without stopping. He followed the saying of Cyrus of old, who, asked at an inn what should be prepared for him, answered: nothing but bread, for he hoped to dine by a stream (21.9.2).

s.n: The Pannonian Danube (the marker shows Aquincum)
s.t:
The Danube carried the boats down along the border of Noricum and Pannonia and then along the Pannonian limes – past Carnuntum, Brigetio, Aquincum and the other forts. According to Ammianus, meanwhile Rumour, which exaggerates “with a thousand tongues”, spread through all Illyricum: Julian had overthrown many kings and nations in Gaul and was approaching with a great army. Upon this the praetorian prefect Taurus, as if fleeing a foreign enemy, crossed the Julian Alps using the relays of the courier service, taking the prefect Florentius with him (21.9.4).

Count Lucillianus, who commanded the troops of the region from Sirmium, had only slight intelligence of Julian’s approach; he gathered as many soldiers as haste allowed and prepared to resist (21.9.5).

Julian, in Ammianus’ words “like a meteor or a blazing dart”, hastened to his goal. At Bononia, nineteen miles from Sirmium, as the moon was waning and most of the night was dark, he landed unexpectedly and sent Dagalaifus with a light-armed force to fetch Lucillianus (21.9.6). The count was still asleep; awakened by the noise and seeing himself ringed by strangers, he understood the situation and, on hearing the emperor’s name, obeyed. He was set on the first horse that could be found and brought before Julian as a captive.

When he saw Julian and realised that he would live, he said: “Incautiously and rashly, my Emperor, you have trusted yourself with a few followers to another’s territory.” Julian answered with a bitter smile: “Keep these wise words for Constantius; I offered you the emblem of imperial majesty not as to a counsellor, but so that you might cease to fear” (21.9.7–8).

After getting rid of Lucillianus, Julian marched with rapid steps on the city, which he regarded as surrendered. When he reached the large suburbs, which extended a great distance, a crowd of soldiers and people of every kind escorted him to the palace with lights, flowers and good wishes, hailing him as Augustus and Lord. Encouraged by the good omen, he gave chariot races next day to the joy of the people, and at dawn on the third day, impatient of delay, hurried on along the highways (21.10.1–2).

At Sirmium he found two legions and a cohort of archers belonging to Constantius; he sent them to Gaul, but on the way they mutinied at Aquileia and shut the city’s gates against him (21.11).

As no one ventured to oppose him, he placed a garrison in the pass of Succi and entrusted it to the loyal Nevitta. Here Ammianus describes the pass: between the converging summits of the Haemus and Rhodope ranges it separates Illyricum and Thrace; on one side it faces Dacia and Serdica, on the other Thrace and Philippopolis. The side towards Illyricum rises gently, the Thracian side falls away steeply (21.10.2–4).

Julian then returned to Naissus, from where he could attend to everything without hindrance. Here he made Sextus Aurelius Victor, the historian, whom he had seen at Sirmium, governor of Pannonia Secunda, and honoured him with a bronze statue. He wrote a sharp letter to the Senate against Constantius; when it was read, the senators shouted with one voice: “We demand reverence for your own creator!” (21.10.5–7).

Julian was still within the borders of Dacia when the envoys Theolaifus and Aligildus brought news that Constantius had died in Cilicia and with his last words had made him his successor (22.2.1); so the civil war did not take place. He then set out over the slope of Succi into Thrace towards Philippopolis, and through Heraclea (Perinthus) reached Constantinople. According to Ammianus people of every age and sex poured out as if to see someone sent down from heaven, and on 11 December the Senate and the people received him with ceremony (22.2.4). Julian’s sole rule lasted less than two years: he fell in 363 on his campaign against the Persians.

t: Julian’s Persian campaign (AD 363)
intro:
In the spring of 363 the emperor Julian set out with a great army against Sasanian Persia, ruled by king Shapur II. The aims of the campaign were disputed even in antiquity; according to Ammianus Julian wanted to avenge earlier Persian attacks and longed for glory as a general. The main army marched down the Euphrates, accompanied by a fleet of about 1,100 ships; a second army of 30,000 men under Procopius and Sebastianus went towards the Tigris to join Arsaces, king of Armenia.

The historian Ammianus Marcellinus took part in the campaign; after the arrival of the fleet he describes events in the first person (“we arrived”). His account is our main source; he admired Julian and stresses the successes. Several places inside Persia cannot be identified today; the text says so, and there the line is straight. The numbers in brackets give Ammianus’ book, chapter and section.

s.t: Julian had spent the winter of 362–363 at Antioch, where the people mocked him. Before leaving he appointed as governor of Syria Alexander of Heliopolis, a hot-tempered and cruel man, saying that he did not deserve the post but the Antiochenes needed such a judge. When the crowd wished him a milder return, he answered that they would never see him again. He set out on 5 March (23.2.3–6).

He reached Hierapolis by the usual route. As he entered the gate of the great city, a colonnade on his left suddenly collapsed and buried fifty soldiers (23.2.6). Units of the army had already crossed the Euphrates from their winter quarters and were waiting for the emperor at their appointed posts (23.2.2).
He crossed the Euphrates on a bridge of boats and with the army and Scythian auxiliaries reached Batnae, a town of Osrhoene. Here a huge stack of chaff collapsed and crushed fifty grooms (23.2.7–8).

By a forced march he reached Carrhae, notorious for the disaster of the Crassi (53 BC). Here he sacrificed to the Moon in the local fashion; it was said that he secretly gave his purple cloak to his kinsman Procopius, so that he should become emperor if Julian died (23.3.1–2). According to Ammianus two royal roads led from here into Persia: on the left through Adiabene and across the Tigris, on the right through Assyria and across the Euphrates.

Julian entrusted 30,000 picked men to Procopius and Sebastianus, to keep watch on this side of the Tigris and, joined with Arsaces king of Armenia, to rejoin him. He himself feigned a march towards the Tigris but turned right, to the south (23.3.5–6).

Via the camp of Davana at the source of the Belias he reached Callinicum, a strong fortress known for its trade. Here on 27 March, when the procession of the Mother of the Gods was held at Rome, he performed the rites in the ancient fashion. The next day Saracen princes presented him with a golden crown and joined him (23.3.7–8).

Now the fleet arrived: about a thousand cargo ships, fifty warships and as many bridge-building vessels, about 1,100 in all (23.3.9). From here on Ammianus writes in the first person.

Circesium was a well-fortified frontier fortress at the confluence of the Khabur (Abora) and the Euphrates. Here he received a letter from Sallustius, prefect of Gaul, begging him to postpone the campaign – in vain. The army crossed the Abora on a bridge of boats, and Julian then had the bridge broken up so that no soldier might hope to return (23.5.1–5).

At Zaitha they passed the tomb of the emperor Gordian (†244), where Julian made offerings (23.5.7). The killing of a lion and a thunderbolt (7 April) caused new disputes over omens; from a mound Julian addressed the army, recalling the victorious Persian campaigns of Trajan, Verus and Severus (23.5.8–25).

At dawn he entered Persian territory in battle order, with 1,500 scouts ahead of the army (24.1.1–2). Two days later they reached the deserted town of Dura, where the soldiers killed a great many deer (24.1.5). Dura-Europos had been taken by the Persians in the 250s and had been empty since; its excavations revealed a synagogue and a Christian house.

img.c: The painted west wall of the Dura-Europos synagogue (mid-3rd century) in a photograph taken at the excavation (Yale; now in the Damascus museum).

s.n: Anatha (Anah, an island in the Euphrates; approximate point)
s.t:
After an easy march of four days count Lucillianus with a thousand light-armed troops blockaded the island fortress of Anatha by boat. On the word of Hormisdas (Shapur’s brother, who had fled to Rome) the defenders surrendered; the fortress was burned, its commander Pusaeus was made a tribune, and the inhabitants were settled at Chalcis in Syria (24.1.6–9).

The river fortresses of Thilutha and Achaiachala did not surrender, but did not attack the ships passing beneath them either: they said that if the Romans took the interior of the country, they too would come over (24.2.1–2).

In two days they covered 200 stades to Baraxmalcha, then seven miles further reached deserted Diacira, full of grain and excellent salt; it was burned. Passing a bitumen spring they came to deserted Ozogardana, where a tribunal of the emperor Trajan was shown; after two days’ rest this too was burned (24.2.3–4). The bitumen springs of the area around Hit are still known today.

Large, populous Pirisabora, surrounded by water, was invested with a triple cordon and a siege engine; in the end the defenders surrendered. The fortress was burned, 2,500 prisoners were taken, and many fled by boat (24.2.9–22). Pirisabora was one of the chief storehouses of the Persian kingdom, full of arms and supplies. After the victory Julian promised the soldiers a hundred denarii each; when they grumbled, he made them an angry speech.

From here they had to cross fields flooded by the Persians, who had cut the dykes; Julian had bridges made of skins and boats of palm trunks (24.3.10–11).

s.n: Maiozamalcha (site unknown; symbolic point before Ctesiphon)
s.h: Maiozamalcha: a tunnel under the walls
s.t: A town abandoned by its Jewish inhabitants because of its low walls was burned by the angry soldiers (24.4.1). At the strong city of Maiozamalcha Julian narrowly escaped an ambush while reconnoitring. The city was taken with siege engines and tunnels dug under the walls; its commander Nabdates was captured (24.4.3–26). Ammianus also describes the massacre of the inhabitants after the capture.

s.h: Battle under the walls of Ctesiphon
s.t:
After a royal palace built in Roman style and a game park, they camped for two days near Coche (Seleucia). In a city once destroyed by the emperor Carus, Julian saw the impaled kinsmen of the noble who had surrendered Pirisabora; Nabdates was burned alive (24.5.1–4). The dry Naarmalcha canal was cleared, and the fleet passed through 30 stades into the Tigris (24.6.1–3).

At night the fleet crossed the Tigris under fire; the Persians were driven back within the walls of Ctesiphon. According to Ammianus about 2,500 Persians fell, while the Romans lost 70 men (24.6.4–16). But the council of war did not dare to besiege the well-defended capital, towards which Shapur’s main army was approaching (24.7.1–2).

Julian decided to march into the interior and had almost every ship of the fleet burned, keeping only twelve smaller ones for bridging – so that the ships should not fall into enemy hands, and because towing them tied up twenty thousand men.
