Ammianus and other sources regard this as a fatal mistake (24.7.4–6). They could not bridge the flooded rivers; the omens were unfavourable, so they set out towards Corduene. They broke camp on 16 June (24.8.1–5).

s.n: Maranga and the fatal battle (sites uncertain; on the left bank of the Tigris, towards Samarra)
s.t:
The retreating army was constantly harassed by the Persians. At the estate of Hucumbra they rested for two days and burned what they could not carry; at Maranga a large Persian army with armoured cavalry and elephants attacked them, but the Romans won (25.1.4–19).

A few days later, during a surprise attack, Julian threw himself into the fighting without his breastplate; a cavalry spear pierced his side. In his tent, near a place called Phrygia, he died at midnight in his 32nd year, after talking with his officers about the immortality of the soul (25.3.1–23). By tradition he was wounded on 26 June. The next day the army proclaimed Jovian, commander of the household troops, emperor (25.5.1–4).

s.n: Dura on the Tigris (ad-Dawr?; identification uncertain)
s.t: Passing the fort of Charcha, on 1 July they reached Dura by the Tigris, where Saracens harassed the rearguard. The Gallic and German soldiers were the first to swim the flooded river (25.6.8–15). To save his starving army Jovian made a thirty-year peace with Shapur: he gave up the five regions beyond the Tigris (Arzanene, Moxoene, Zabdicene, Rehimene and Corduene, with fifteen fortresses), as well as Nisibis, Singara and Castra Maurorum (25.7.9–14). Ammianus thought it a shameful peace.

After crossing the Tigris the army marched across the waterless plain near long-deserted Hatra; they drank salt water and slaughtered the pack animals. At the Persian fort of Ur they received supplies, and at Thilsaphata the army of Procopius and Sebastianus joined them (25.8.4–16).

Nisibis, which had three times repulsed Shapur’s sieges, now passed into Persian hands under the peace. The inhabitants’ pleas were in vain: Jovian ordered them to leave the city, and Persian officials took it over (25.8.13–25.9.6). Many of the refugees moved to Amida; the famous Christian poet Ephrem the Syrian moved at this time to Edessa.

At the beginning of the campaign Julian had said that on his return he would winter at Tarsus. His body was taken to Tarsus by Procopius and buried in a suburb of the city with simple rites, as he had wished (23.2.5; 25.9.12–13). Ammianus thought it would have been more fitting for him to rest by the Tiber at Rome. Jovian died suddenly at Dadastana in February 364, after barely eight months’ reign (25.10.12–13).

t: Valentinian I’s last campaign in Pannonia (AD 374–375)
intro:
Valentinian I (364–375) was a native of Cibalae (Vinkovci) in Pannonia; he ruled the western half of the empire, mostly from Trier, and strengthened the Rhine and Danube frontiers with tireless work. In 374 the Quadi and Sarmatians invaded Pannonia and Valeria (the eastern part of today’s Transdanubia); the cause was the treachery of a Roman officer. The next year the emperor himself led a campaign against them, and at Brigetio (Komárom-Szőny), while receiving a Quadic embassy, he fell into a fit of rage and died.

The main source is Ammianus Marcellinus, who wrote as a contemporary but not an eyewitness; he portrays Valentinian as a harsh, wrathful ruler, but tireless in frontier defence. The walk follows one of the best-documented ancient episodes of the limes in today’s Hungary. The numbers in brackets give Ammianus’ book, chapter and section.

s.t:
Valentinian had a fort built across the Danube, on Quadic land. Gabinius, king of the Quadi, mildly protested; Marcellianus, commander in Valeria, feigned friendship, invited him to a banquet and had him murdered as he left. The enraged Quadi and Sarmatians crossed the Danube at harvest time and carried off captives and cattle (29.6.2–6).

Constantia, daughter of the emperor Constantius II, on her way to marry Gratian, was almost captured at the villa called Pristensis; the governor Messalla took her to safety at Sirmium. At Sirmium the praetorian prefect Probus at first wanted to flee, then had the moats cleared and strengthened the walls with stones collected for a theatre. The legions Pannonica and Moesiaca, rivalling each other, attacked separately, and the Sarmatians almost annihilated them (29.6.7–14).

At the news Valentinian set out from Trier in spring and marched quickly along familiar roads towards Illyricum (30.5.1). On the way Sarmatian envoys came to him and insisted that their people had taken no part in the invasion; the emperor replied that he would investigate this on the spot.

He entered Carnuntum, in Ammianus’ words a deserted and squalid town of Illyricum but well suited as a base of operations, and spent the three summer months gathering arms and supplies (30.5.2, 30.5.11). According to Ammianus he was harsh with minor officials but mild with men of rank, and tolerated the merciless taxation of the prefect Probus, which ruined Illyricum (30.5.3–10).

s.h: A bridge of boats at Aquincum
s.t: He sent Merobaudes and Sebastianus ahead with infantry to ravage the barbarian territory. He himself moved his camp to Acincum (Aquincum), had a bridge built of boats, and crossed into the land of the Quadi from another direction. Those he found unprepared he had killed, the villages burned, and he returned without loss (30.5.13–14).

As autumn approached he looked for winter quarters; he would have found Savaria suitable, but the town was then weak and had suffered greatly from the invasions (30.5.14). Here Ammianus lists the signs that foretold his death: comets appeared, a thunderbolt struck Sirmium, an owl perched on the roof of the imperial bath at Savaria; Valentinian saw his wife in mourning in a dream, and when his horse reared and would not let him mount, in his anger he ordered the groom’s hand to be cut off (30.5.15–19).

He moved to Brigetio. Here Quadic envoys came to him and begged for peace: in their view the invasion had been made not by the people but by foreign brigands, and they had been provoked by the fort built on the frontier. While replying, Valentinian flew into a rage and abused the whole people; suddenly he flushed, his voice failed, and he collapsed. The physicians tried to bleed him but could find no vein; shortly after he died, in the 55th year of his life and the 12th of his reign (30.6.1–6). By tradition he died on 17 November; Rolfe’s note gives the 18th.

A few days later the army proclaimed his four-year-old son, Valentinian II, emperor (30.10). Three years after Valentinian’s death the Goths destroyed the eastern army at Adrianople.

t: The Gothic war and Valens’ defeat at Adrianople (AD 376–378)
intro:
The appearance of the Huns north of the Black Sea drove the Gothic peoples from their homes. In 376 the Tervingi Goths, led by Alavivus and Fritigern, asked for and received permission from the eastern emperor Valens to cross the Danube and settle in the empire. The abuses of Roman officials led to an armed rising that ravaged Thrace for two years. On 9 August 378, near Adrianople, Valens’ army suffered a crushing defeat, and the emperor himself fell.

Book 31 of Ammianus Marcellinus, the final part of his Res gestae, is the main source; Ammianus was a contemporary but not an eyewitness. In his view there had been no such slaughter since Cannae. The exact site of the battle is not known; the numbers in brackets are Ammianus’ chapters and sections.

s.n: The Danube crossing (site uncertain; shown at Durostorum)
s.t: Ammianus describes at length the Huns, who defeated the Alans and the Greuthungi Goths and drove out the Tervingi (2–3). With Valens’ permission the Tervingi, led by Alavivus and Fritigern, were ferried day and night across the flooded river on boats, rafts and hollowed tree trunks; many drowned (4). According to Ammianus the Roman officials could not even count the multitude. He does not name the exact crossing point; the point is symbolic.

s.h: Marcianopolis: the banquet and the rising
s.t: The Roman commanders Lupicinus and Maximus exploited the starving refugees: according to Ammianus they asked a slave for a dog, and the Gothic nobles sold even their children. At Marcianopolis Lupicinus invited Alavivus and Fritigern to a banquet and meanwhile had their escort killed; Fritigern broke out sword in hand, and the Goths rose in revolt. Outside the city Lupicinus’ army was defeated (5).

The Goths ravaged Thrace; at Adrianople two Gothic leaders formerly in Roman service, Sueridus and Colias, also joined Fritigern (6). In 377 the Romans fought the Goths before their wagon fort at a place called Ad Salices (‘at the Willows’) in the province of Scythia; the battle was bloody and indecisive for both sides (7). According to Rolfe’s note the place lay between Tomis and Salmuris; it is not known more precisely.

Valens arrived at Constantinople from the Persian frontier, from Antioch, after a long journey; because of a minor popular disturbance he stayed only a few days, then moved to the imperial villa called Melanthias (according to Rolfe about 140 stades from the city), where he tried to win over the soldiers with pay, supplies and speeches (11.1). Meanwhile his nephew, the western emperor Gratian, was fighting the Alamanni and promised to hurry to his aid (10).

Sebastianus, in a night attack along the Hebrus (Maritsa), almost annihilated the Gothic raiders laden with plunder (11.2–4); Fritigern then drew his scattered bands together. Valens pitched a camp in the suburbs of Adrianople fortified with a palisade and ditch. Richomeres, Gratian’s general, brought a letter in which Gratian asked him to wait. Sebastianus urged an immediate attack, Victor, the Sarmatian-born commander of the cavalry, advised waiting; but Valens wanted the victory for himself alone (12.4–7). Fritigern sent a Christian priest as envoy, but Valens rejected him (12.8–9).

s.n: Site of the battle of Adrianople (not known exactly; symbolic point north of the city)
s.t:
On 9 August at dawn the army set out, leaving the baggage and the treasury at Adrianople, and at about two in the afternoon, exhausted by the heat, reached the Goths’ circular wagon fort. The Goths lit fires on the plain to torment the thirsty Romans further, and spun out negotiations until the cavalry of Alatheus and Saphrax returned. The returning Gothic and Alan cavalry struck the Roman army in the flank, and crowded together it was cut to pieces (12.10–13.11).

There were two versions of Valens’ death: an arrow struck him among the common soldiers, and his body was never found; or, wounded, he was carried into a farmhouse, which the Goths set on fire (13.12–16). The generals Trajanus and Sebastianus fell, with 35 tribunes, and barely a third of the army escaped. According to Ammianus there had been no such defeat since Cannae (13.18–19).

s.h: The attacks on Adrianople and Constantinople
s.t:
The victorious Goths besieged Adrianople, where Valens’ treasury and insignia had been left, but could not take it (15). With Hun and Alan allies they marched against Constantinople; Saracen troops sallying from the city, among them a warrior who drank the blood of a slain Goth, terrified them, and seeing the size of the city they withdrew, raiding as far as the Julian Alps (16.3–7). In the East the general Julius had the Gothic recruits scattered in the cities massacred on a single day (16.8). Ammianus’ work ends here.

The war was ended in 382 by a treaty of the emperor Theodosius, which settled the Goths in the empire as allies under their own leaders.

t: Rutilius Namatianus’ voyage home to Gaul (AD 416/417)
intro:
Claudius Rutilius Namatianus was a pagan Roman noble born in Gaul, prefect of the city of Rome in AD 414. A few years after the sack of Rome by the Goths in 410 he set out home to Gaul and described his journey in an elegiac poem (De reditu suo, “On his return”). The first book and the beginning of the second survive; the text breaks off at the harbour of Luna.

Rutilius chose the sea route because the roads of war-ravaged Italy were dangerous and the bridges were broken. They sailed along the coast by day and put in at night; because of the weather they had to wait several times for days. The voyage took place in autumn, already in Vegetius’ uncertain sailing season. The Loeb edition (Duff) dated it to 416; since Carcopino it is usually placed in the autumn of 417. The numbers in brackets give book and lines of the poem; at sea the line consists of straight stretches through the named places and shows only the probable direction.

s.t: The poem begins with a long farewell, one of the most famous praises of Rome in late antique literature: “Listen, O fairest queen of thy world, Rome” (1.47). According to Rutilius, Rome “made one fatherland of different peoples” and “made a city of what was once a world” (1.63–66). After the farewell he set out towards the mouth of the Tiber (1.165).

s.n: Portus (the harbour of Claudius and Trajan)
s.h: Fifteen days of waiting at Portus
s.t: At the mouth of the Tiber, in the harbour of Claudius and Trajan, they were held up by the weather for fifteen days, waiting for a favourable wind (1.165–216). During this time Rutilius could still hear the noise of the circus at Rome, and looked back at the city.

img.c: Portus: Claudius’ harbour and Trajan’s hexagonal basin.

s.t: When the sailors at last found a fair wind, the coasting, mainly daylight voyage began. On the first day they reached the harbour of Centumcellae, where they spent the night (1.217–276). Rutilius describes the artificial harbour that Trajan had built here.

They set out at dawn; they passed the mouth of the Munio and the pinewoods of Graviscae, sighted the deserted ruins of Cosa, and at nightfall put into Portus Herculis (1.277–312). Here Rutilius reflects on the family of the Lepidi, which in his view gave Rome a rebel in every generation.

They set out before sunrise and passed Mons Argentarius and the island of Igilium (Giglio); Rutilius notes that the island had recently given refuge to those fleeing from the Goths. At the mouth of the Umbro they paused but did not put in; night overtook them on the shore, where they made an improvised camp (1.313–348).

In the morning they had to row because of a calm. The island of Ilva (Elba) came into view, whose iron mines move Rutilius to praise iron: it is worth more than gold (1.349–428). Before midday they landed at Faleria, where the villagers were just celebrating the festival of Osiris. Here a Jewish tenant charged them heavily for resting by his fishpond; Rutilius turns this into a crude tirade against Judaism – the passage is a well-known text of late antique anti-Judaism.
Rowing on, they reached Populonia. Rutilius describes the ruins of the town – “cities too can die” – and here he receives news from Rome of the appointment of his friend Rufius (1.349–428).

Corsica came into view, then the island of Capraria, whose inhabitants, the hermit monks, Rutilius mocks as “men who shun the light”. At Vada Volaterrana they stayed at the villa of his friend Albinus; Rutilius describes the nearby salt-pans. A gale kept them there, but they unexpectedly met their friend Victorinus of Tolosa (1.429–510).

s.n: Triturrita and Portus Pisanus (site uncertain; near Livorno)
s.t:
They passed the rocks of the island of Gorgon (Gorgona), where a noble young Roman lived as a hermit – in Rutilius’ view gone astray. They reached the villa of Triturrita, which stood on a causeway beside the harbour of Pisa, where seaweed protected the ships from the waves (1.511–540).

A longer wait followed: first voluntarily, as Rutilius visited his friend Protadius at Pisa, then compulsorily, because a storm raged for days; they passed the time hunting boar. The first book ends with a description of the storm (1.541–644).
At Pisa Rutilius visited his friend Protadius and saw the statue of his own father, Lachanius, set up to him as a former governor of the region (1.541–614). This excursion was made by land.

s.h: Luna: the end of the poem
s.t: In the second book, when the storm had died down, they sailed on from Portus Pisanus to Luna (2.1–68). On the way Rutilius describes the shape of Italy and attacks the dead Stilicho, who in his view had the Sibylline books burned and let in the barbarians. At Luna he mentions the famous white marble quarries (today’s Carrara marble). Here the text breaks off at line 68; we do not know whether the end of the poem was lost or never written. A manuscript fragment found at Turin in 1973 preserves the ends of some further lines.

img.c: The amphitheatre of Luna (Luni).

t: Priscus’ embassy to the court of Attila (AD 449)
intro:
After the devastating Hunnic war of 447 the eastern Roman court and Attila were in dispute over the surrender of fugitives and a strip of land along the Danube. In AD 449 (some scholars say 448) the emperor Theodosius II sent the nobleman Maximinus as envoy to Attila; Maximinus invited his friend, the rhetor Priscus of Panium in Thrace, to accompany him. With them went the interpreter Bigilas and Rusticius, who spoke the Hun language, together with Attila’s returning envoys, Edeco and Orestes.

The embassy’s secret purpose – of which Maximinus and Priscus knew nothing – was the murder of Attila: in Constantinople the eunuch Chrysaphius, the emperor’s powerful chamberlain, had persuaded Edeco to kill his master for money (Edeco asked for 50 pounds of gold), and Bigilas was in the plot. But once home Edeco revealed everything to Attila.

Priscus later wrote a history; only fragments survive, but his account of the embassy (fragment 8) is the most detailed eyewitness description of Attila and the world of the Huns. North of the Danube the text names no place that can be identified today: the sites of Attila’s tents, of the rivers and of his residence are disputed, so these points on the map are only symbolic, and the line there is straight.

s.t: Attila’s envoy Edeco brought to Constantinople a letter in which Attila demanded the surrender of fugitives and forbade the Romans to farm the strip along the Danube that he had won. The eunuch Chrysaphius secretly won Edeco over to kill Attila; the emperor and Martialius, master of the offices, approved the plan. The official embassy was led by Maximinus, who knew nothing of the plot.

img.c: Gold coin (solidus) of Theodosius II, struck at Constantinople between 439 and 450.

s.t: According to Priscus, Serdica is 13 days’ journey from Constantinople for a fast (lightly equipped) traveller. Here the Romans invited Edeco and his companions to dinner; they bought sheep and oxen from the locals. At the toasts the Huns hailed Attila and the Romans the emperor, whereupon Bigilas remarked that it was not right to compare a man with a god – Attila being the man and Theodosius the god. The Huns grew angry; the Romans turned the conversation elsewhere, and Maximinus gave Edeco and Orestes silk garments and Indian gems.

s.d: on the way to the Danube
s.t:
Naissus had earlier been destroyed by the Huns: the city was almost empty, with only a few sick people lying in the churches. The embassy camped outside the city on the river bank, which was full of the bones of men killed in the war.

Next day, nearby, they visited Agintheus, commander of the troops in Illyricum (magister militum per Illyricum), who on the emperor’s orders handed over to them five of the seventeen fugitives demanded by Attila.

s.n: The Danube crossing (site uncertain; shown at Margum)
s.t:
From Naissus the road wound with many bends through a wooded valley; when at one bend the sun rose from the ‘wrong’ direction, those who did not know the country took it for a bad omen. Reaching the plain, Hun ferrymen took them across the Danube in boats hollowed from single tree trunks (monoxyla). According to Priscus, the many boats had really been prepared for Attila’s army: Attila said he wanted to hunt on Roman soil, but in fact he was preparing for war because not all the fugitives had been surrendered.

The text does not name the crossing point. Since the road north from Naissus runs down the valley of the Margus (Morava) to the Danube, the point is shown symbolically at Margum.

Beyond the Danube they travelled about 70 stades (about 13 km) with the Huns, then waited on a plain while Edeco rode ahead. Next afternoon they reached Attila’s many tents; they were not allowed to camp on the hill because Attila’s tent stood lower down. Attila first sent word that he would not receive them unless they had something new to say; only through Priscus’ intercession, with the help of Scottas (Onegesius’ brother), were they admitted. Attila sat on a wooden chair surrounded by many warriors; Maximinus handed over the emperor’s letter. Attila called Bigilas a ‘shameless beast’ and sent him home for the fugitives – Bigilas really went back for the money for the murder.

s.n: The journey north across the plain (symbolic point)
s.h: Rivers, millet and a storm by the lake
s.t:
Attila set off north to a village where he took another wife (the daughter of Escam); the embassy followed by another road. They travelled across level country and crossed navigable rivers; after the Danube the largest were the Drecon, the Tigas and the Tiphesas. These they crossed in the dugout boats of the riverside people, the smaller rivers on rafts carried on wagons. Instead of grain they were given millet, instead of wine mead (medos), and the servants a barley drink (kamos). The identification of the rivers is disputed: the Tiphesas is usually identified with the Timiș (Tibiscus), the Tigas often with the Tisza, the Drecon sometimes with the Körös, sometimes with the Bega.

One evening they camped by a lake; at night a storm tore down the tents and they scattered in the dark. They ended up in a village ruled by one of the widows of Bleda (Attila’s brother, who died c. 445 and according to the sources was killed on Attila’s orders); she sent them food and – by Hun custom – women. Next day they repaid her hospitality with silver bowls, skins, Indian pepper and dates. After seven more days they waited in a village for Attila to go ahead; here they met the western Roman embassy (count Romulus, Promotus the governor of Noricum, and Romanus), who had come about Silvanus, a Roman silversmith: because of church plate from Sirmium Attila demanded his surrender.

s.n: Attila’s residence (unknown site in the Tisza region; symbolic point)
s.t:
After crossing several rivers they reached a large village where Attila’s house was the most splendid: it was built of planed boards and surrounded by a decorative – not defensive – wooden fence. The second most famous house belonged to Onegesius, Attila’s chief man; beside it stood a bath whose stones he had brought from Pannonia, for this region has neither stone nor timber. Its builder was a captive from Sirmium who hoped for freedom, but Onegesius made him his bath attendant. When Attila arrived, girls under linen canopies sang Scythian songs, and Onegesius’ wife offered him food and wine, which Attila took sitting on horseback.

The site of the residence is unknown; since the 19th century many places on the Great Hungarian Plain have been proposed (for example the Tiszazug, the area around Csongrád). The point is therefore only symbolic.

s.n: Attila’s residence: the house of Onegesius
s.t:
While waiting at Onegesius’ door, Priscus was greeted in Greek by a man in Hun dress. He was a Greek merchant from Viminacium on the Danube; captured when the city was taken, he was given to Onegesius, then won his freedom fighting on the Huns’ side, married a Hun wife and thought his new life better. He criticised at length Roman taxes, corruption and justice; Priscus defended the Roman laws. In the end the man admitted in tears that the laws were good but the rulers were ruining the state. This dialogue is one of the most famous parts of Priscus’ work; it may be partly a literary creation.

Maximinus invited Onegesius to Constantinople to settle the disputes, but he refused to betray Attila.

Priscus took gifts to Attila’s wife Kreka, who had three sons; the eldest ruled over the Akatziri and other peoples by the Black Sea. Her house was built of carved boards and round logs; she reclined on a couch among her servants. Later he saw Attila in front of his house deciding lawsuits and receiving foreign envoys.

At three in the afternoon they were invited to a banquet. The guests sat along the walls and toasted each other with the cup in order of rank; the others ate from silver and gold dishes, but Attila ate only meat from a wooden plate and drank from a wooden cup. Two singers sang of Attila’s victories; Zercon, the Moorish dwarf, made the guests laugh with a jumble of Latin, Hun and Gothic words. Attila showed affection only for his youngest son, Ernac; a Latin-speaking Hun explained that the seers had foretold that Attila’s line would fall but that this boy would restore it. The Romans left late at night, before the drinking went on.

s.h: The return and the exposure of the plot
s.t:
After a few days and another banquet Attila dismissed the embassy; Maximinus returned by the same road he had come, with the Hun envoy Berichus, with whom he quarrelled on the way. On the road they met Bigilas returning to the Huns. In Attila’s camp he was arrested at once; in his bag was the gold for the murder. When Attila threatened to kill his son, Bigilas confessed everything; Attila spared his life for a ransom.

Attila then sent Orestes and Eslas to Constantinople: according to Gibbon, Orestes appeared before the emperor with the bag of gold hanging round his neck and asked Chrysaphius whether he recognised it. Attila demanded Chrysaphius’ head. In the end a splendid embassy led by Anatolius and Nomus made peace with him (according to Gibbon at the river Drenco). After the death of Theodosius II (450) Chrysaphius was executed. The length of the route on the map is only an estimate.

t: Sidonius Apollinaris’ journey from Lyon to Rome (AD 467)
intro:
Gaius Sollius Sidonius Apollinaris, born at Lyon, was a Gallo-Roman aristocrat, poet and letter-writer; his father-in-law Avitus was briefly western emperor (455–456), and he himself later became bishop of Clermont. In 467 the emperor Anthemius summoned him to Rome by letter. He describes the journey in a letter to his friend Heronius (1.5): the letter is both a travel report and a literary game, in which the memorials of Virgil, Caesar and Roman history pass by.

Sidonius travelled by the imperial post (cursus publicus), from Ticinum by boat on the Po, then along the Via Flaminia. In Rome on 1 January 468 he delivered a panegyric on Anthemius, and that same year became prefect of the city (1.9). It is one of the most vivid travel accounts of the last decades of the western empire. The numbers in brackets are sections of the letter; Sidonius does not name the Alpine pass, so the line there is a route found on the Roman road network, and the stretch along the Po is only approximate.

s.t: Summoned by an imperial letter, Sidonius set out by the imperial post from his native Lyon (Rhodanusia). On the way he stayed at the houses of friends and relatives; what delayed him was not a shortage of post-horses but the long farewells (2).

He climbed into the Alps, where the paths beaten through the snow made the ascent easy; on the unnavigable rivers he found fords and old arched bridges. At Ticinum he boarded a fast boat (cursoria) and sailed down to the Po; he jokes that among the poplars of the bank he thought of Phaethon’s sisters weeping amber (3).

s.h: The tributaries of the Po and Cremona
s.t: He sailed past the mouths of the Lambrus, the Addua, the Athesis and the Mincius, which rise in the Ligurian and Euganean mountains; he also rowed a little way up them and saw the groves of oak and maple along their banks and the birds nesting in the reeds (4). He reached Cremona, whose nearness the ‘Mantuan Tityrus’, that is Virgil, had once lamented (5).
At Brixellum he stopped only briefly while the boatmen changed crews – a glimpse of how the river service of the imperial post worked (5).

Turning right he reached Ravenna. He wonders whether ‘Caesar’s road’ between the old city and the new port (Classis) joins or separates them; a branch of the Po had been led round to guard the walls, but was also used for trade (5). Ravenna had plenty of goods and food, but the water was bad: the sea pressed in on one side, and on the other the barges stirred up the mud of the canals. Though almost standing in water, they were thirsty, for there was no clean aqueduct, cistern, spring or well (6). Ravenna was then the seat of the western imperial court.

s.n: The river Rubicon (near Savignano sul Rubicone; identification disputed)
s.t: He crossed the Rubicon, which according to Sidonius takes its name from the reddish colour of its gravel, and which was once the boundary between the Gauls and the Italians (7). Here in 49 BC Caesar crossed the frontier of Italy with his army. Which modern river is the ancient Rubicon was long disputed; since 1932 the Fiumicino has borne the name.
Sidonius mentions Ariminum for Caesar’s ‘rebellion’ (7): it was the first city Caesar took after crossing the Rubicon. Here begins the Via Flaminia, the main road to Rome.

Fanum was ‘stained’ by the death of Hasdrubal (7): at the nearby river Metaurus in 207 BC the Romans destroyed the army of Hannibal’s brother. The town took its name from a temple of Fortune built in memory of the victory.

Travelling along the Via Flaminia he had Picenum on his left and Umbria on his right. Heat, cold and the Tuscan air made him ill: fever and thirst tormented him. He longingly lists the rivers and springs he would have liked to drink from: the Velinus, the Clitumnus, the Anio, the Nar, the Farfarus and the Tiber (8). The springs of the Clitumnus are near Spoletium; the point is only symbolic, as Sidonius names no stop.

When Rome came into view he recovered. He went first to pray at the tombs of the Apostles, then rested in rented lodgings, where he wrote the letter (9). He had not yet been to the imperial court: he arrived just before the wedding of the patrician Ricimer to the emperor Anthemius’ daughter, and because of the celebrations filling the whole city he kept out of the way for the time being (10–11).

Ricimer, a general of Germanic descent, was then the real master of the western empire; the marriage was meant to seal the alliance of emperor and general. Five years later (472) Ricimer besieged Rome, and Anthemius was killed. Sidonius became prefect of the city in 468, then on returning home bishop of Clermont; in 475 he was held captive by the Visigoths.

t: St Severinus in Danubian Noricum (c. 454–482) and the Roman withdrawal (488)
intro:
The monk Severinus came from the East to Danubian Noricum (Noricum Ripense, today’s Upper and Lower Austria) and the neighbouring border of Pannonia after the death of Attila (453). He never revealed his origin; according to Eugippius his mother tongue was Latin. He lived here for almost thirty years, during the break-up of Roman rule, when frontier defence had ceased and the Danube towns were plundered by Rugii, Alamanni, Heruli and Thuringians. Severinus held no office, yet he became the leader of the Roman population: he organised food, ransomed captives, negotiated with barbarian kings and saved the people of the towns with his advice.

His life was written by his disciple Eugippius in 511 at the monastery of Lucullanum in southern Italy (Commemoratorium). The work is arranged by places and events rather than in chronological order; the walk therefore shows the places, not a single journey. It is one of the most important sources for the last decades of the Roman Danube frontier, next door to Pannonia. The numbers in brackets are chapters.

s.t: After Attila’s death Severinus arrived on the Pannonian border and stayed in the small town of Asturis. In the church he urged the people to repentance and fasting and foretold that otherwise the town would be destroyed. They did not listen, and the town soon fell to the enemy (1). The site of Asturis is uncertain; it is usually identified with Zwentendorf, sometimes with Klosterneuburg.

Severinus went on to nearby Comagenis, which was held under strict occupation by barbarians allied to the Romans. At his word the people fasted and prayed; terrified by an earthquake at night, the barbarian garrison panicked, cut one another down and fled (1–2). Later he healed the son of a Rugian noble here (33).

There was famine at Favianis; Severinus shamed the widow Procula, who had hoarded grain, and at his prayer the cargo boats from Raetia, frozen in the ice, were freed and arrived (3). He sent the tribune Mamertinus to recover captives from the raiders (4). Beside the town he built a monastery, which became the centre of his work; here he went barefoot even in winter and fasted strictly (4, 39).

Across the Danube lay the kingdom of the Rugii; their kings, Flaccitheus, then Feletheus (Feva) and his wife Giso, sought his advice (5, 8). To the young Odoacer, poorly dressed and on his way to Italy, he foretold that he would become king (7). Severinus died here on 8 January 482 (43).

Lauriacum, the former legionary fortress, was one of the last strong towns of Noricum Ripense. Here Severinus averted, with fasting and prayer, a blight threatening the harvest (18), and according to the Vita the oil for the poor multiplied (28). He foretold a night attack; the people kept watch, and the enemy withdrew (30).

The refugees of the towns further west all gathered here. Feva, king of the Rugii, came with an army to carry the Romans off; Severinus persuaded him to settle them peacefully in the Danube towns near his own country, where they lived in friendly alliance with the Rugii (31).

At the foot of the Alps, on the edge of inner Noricum, at Cucullis (Kuchl) Severinus exposed those secretly offering pagan sacrifice with a miracle of tapers, and drove off a plague of locusts with fasting (11–12). In a church near Iuvao, when no one could strike a fire for the evening service, the taper in his hand lit by itself; at Iuvao he healed a dying woman, who on the third day was already working in the fields (13–14).

s.h: Batavis: king Gibuldus and the last garrison
s.t:
Severinus often went to Batavis to help the inhabitants against Gibuldus, king of the Alamanni; the king received him trembling and released the captives (19). Here Eugippius tells the famous scene of the end of Roman frontier defence: while Roman rule lasted, soldiers paid from public funds were stationed in many towns, but this ceased, and only the garrison of Batavis remained. Some soldiers set out for Italy to fetch the last pay, but on the way they were killed by barbarians; the river carried their bodies back (20).

The people of nearby Quintanis (Künzing) fled from the Alamanni to Batavis; the Romans won, but in the end Severinus sent the population to Lauriacum (27).

s.h: His death and the Roman withdrawal
s.t: Severinus foretold that the Romans would leave the province and ordered that his body be taken with them (40). He died on 8 January 482 (43). After his death Ferderuchus, Feva’s brother, plundered the monastery, but within a month he was killed by his nephew. Odoacer, king of Italy, defeated the Rugii; his brother Onoulfus ordered the Romans to move to Italy, and count Pierius carried out the evacuation (44). By the usual dating this happened in 488. Before leaving they took up Severinus’ body, found intact after six years, and carried it with them on a wagon.

The refugees carried the coffin over the Alps into Italy and placed it in a fortress called Mons Feletrus (Mount Feleter); in the oratory, according to the Vita, a mute man regained his speech (44–45). The place is identified with today’s San Leo.

s.h: Lucullanum: the tomb and Eugippius’ monastery
s.t: A noblewoman named Barbaria, with Pope Gelasius’ approval, had the body brought near Naples; bishop Victor laid it in the mausoleum she had built in the fortress called Lucullanum, and the people of Naples received it solemnly (46). Here the monastery of Severinus’ monks was founded, where Eugippius wrote the Vita in 511. The Castellum Lucullanum stood on the Naples waterfront, around today’s Castel dell’Ovo and Pizzofalcone; here too the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, deposed in 476, lived out his last years.
